scope: Python-first foundations, automation, backend basics, and entry-level engineering practice

goals: Explain a variable, a value, and a type.
Call a function and distinguish return from print.
Write and trace arithmetic and boundary conditions.

sections.title: What a program actually does
sections.text: A program is a sequence of instructions applied to data. Python executes a file from top to bottom. A function definition stores a reusable set of instructions; its body runs when the function is called. The browser checks call your function with different inputs. They do not read your intentions, so the function name, arguments, and returned value must match the task.

sections.title: Values, names, and expressions
sections.text: An integer such as 8 is a whole-number value; a float such as 8.5 represents a fractional number; a string such as "8" is text. True and False are booleans. None represents an explicitly absent result. An expression produces a value: 8 + 2 produces 10. Assignment such as coins = 8 binds a name to a value. Later coins = coins + 2 reads the old value, computes the sum, and updates the binding. Assignment uses =; equality comparison uses ==.

sections.title: Syntax you need before the first challenge
sections.text: def starts a function definition. Parameters in parentheses name the inputs. A colon starts the indented body, conventionally four spaces. return gives a result back to the caller and exits the function. print displays text for a person; a function that only prints returns None. A # starts a comment and pass is a placeholder that does nothing. Python is case-sensitive, so Total and total are different names.

sections.title: Arithmetic and decisions
sections.text: Use +, -, *, and / for arithmetic; / produces a float. // is floor division and % is the remainder. Parentheses control grouping. Compare with <, <=, >, >=, ==, and !=. and requires both conditions, or requires at least one, and not reverses a boolean. An if/elif/else chain chooses a branch. Test exactly at each cutoff as well as on either side. Strings and numeric values do not combine automatically; convert deliberately with int(), float(), or str().

worked.code:
def remaining(coins, price):
    if coins < price:
        return None
    return coins - price

print(remaining(12, 5))
print(remaining(5, 5))
print(remaining(4, 5))
trace: The first call binds coins to 12 and price to 5. The comparison is False, so the final return gives 7.
At equal amounts the purchase is allowed, returning 0. An insufficient amount takes the early return.
print displays each returned value. Removing print would still compute values but a script would not display them.

mistakes: Using = instead of == in a condition.
Printing the answer instead of returning it.
Indenting return under the wrong branch or misspelling a parameter.
questions: Why is "12" + "5" different from 12 + 5?
What does a function return when it reaches its end with no return?
Which three inputs test the cutoff at price 5?

units.title: Start small
units.prerequisites: Start Here and basic computer file operations

plain.title: Read a Python instruction before writing one
plain.text:
A program is a sequence of instructions. Python normally runs the instructions in a file from top to bottom. A value is one piece of data: 6 is a whole number, and "tea" is text. Text values are called strings and need matching quotes. The quotes mark the text; they are not part of the text itself.

print(...) is a function call: ask an existing named operation to run. Parentheses enclose its inputs, called arguments. print displays its arguments for a person. A comma separates several arguments; print normally places a space between them. A # begins a comment that Python ignores. A blank line separates ideas for readers.
plain.code:
print("Hello")
print("Cups:", 6)
# This line is a comment, not an instruction.
plain.check: Which characters identify a string, a function call, and a comment?

plain.title: Assignment: a name refers to a value
plain.text:
A variable is a name referring to a value. In cups = 6, the single equals sign means assignment: calculate the right side, then bind the left-hand name to that result. An expression is code that produces a value, such as cups + 2.

An update reads the old value before assigning the new one. cups += 2 is shorthand for cups = cups + 2. Python names are case-sensitive: cups and Cups are different. Use descriptive names; names like cups_ready use underscores to separate words. You must assign a name before reading it.
plain.code:
cups = 6
cups = cups + 2
print(cups)
cups += 1
print(cups)
walk: Start with cups referring to 6.
Read the old 6, add 2, and make cups refer to 8.
The shorthand update adds 1 to the current 8.
plain.check: If you change the initial value, can you predict both printed values without running the code?

plain.title: Types and arithmetic have specific rules
plain.text:
A type describes the kind of value and the operations it supports. int is a whole number, float represents a fractional number, str is text, and bool has the values True and False. None means no value or no result; it is different from zero and from False. These spellings and capital letters matter.

Use + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. Division with / produces a float. // is floor division, rounding the quotient down; % gives the remainder. Parentheses group calculations. Multiplication and division happen before addition unless parentheses say otherwise.

The text "6" and the number 6 are different values. int("6") converts suitable text to an integer; float("6.5") converts it to a float; str(6) produces text. Python will not guess how to add a string to an integer. type(value) lets you inspect a value's type. Conversion can fail when the text is unsuitable; chapter 5 teaches how to handle that failure.
plain.code:
print(9 / 2, 9 // 2, 9 % 2)
print(2 + 3 * 4, (2 + 3) * 4)
print(int("6") + 1)
print("6" + str(1))
print(type(True))
walk: 9 divided by 2 is 4.5; the whole quotient is 4 and the remainder is 1.
With strings, + joins text instead of adding numbers.
type(True) reports bool, displayed by Python as <class 'bool'>. You do not need to write that display notation yourself.
plain.check: What is the difference between 6 + 1 and "6" + "1"?

plain.title: Define a function, then call it
plain.text:
A function packages instructions under a name. def introduces its definition. Names inside the parentheses are parameters: input names that receive values when the function is called. The colon starts its body, and four leading spaces show which lines belong to it. Defining a function stores the instructions; it does not run the body yet.

A call such as ribbon_length(3, 4) supplies two argument values in parameter order. Inside that call, count is 3 and length is 4. return sends a result back to the caller and ends that call. The caller can save that result in a variable. A function's local variables belong to that call; do not expect them to exist outside it.

The starter's pass is a placeholder meaning do nothing. Replace it with your own instructions when solving a challenge. Keep the required function name and parameters: the browser checks call exactly that interface.
plain.code:
def ribbon_length(count, length):
    total = count * length
    return total

needed = ribbon_length(3, 4)
print(needed)
walk: Python records the function when it reaches def.
The later call binds count to 3 and length to 4.
The multiplication produces 12. return gives 12 to the caller, which stores it as needed.
plain.check: Which names are parameters, which values are arguments, and where is the returned result stored?

plain.title: Returning a value is different from printing it
plain.text:
print displays information; return lets other code use information. A function that finishes without returning a value gives back None. Printing inside it does not change that. Forge's function checks compare returned values, so displaying the right text alone cannot satisfy a return-value contract.

A returned result can be used in another calculation or passed to another function. Keep calculation functions focused on returning results. Let main.py decide what to print. return also stops the function immediately: instructions after that return in the same execution path do not run.
plain.code:
def show_length():
    print(12)

def give_length():
    return 12

shown = show_length()
given = give_length()
print(shown)
print(given + 1)
plain.check: Why does shown contain None even though show_length displayed 12?

plain.title: Comparisons produce booleans
plain.text:
Use == to compare equality, != for inequality, < and > for strict comparisons, and <= and >= to include equality. Every comparison here produces True or False. The single = assigns a value; it does not ask a question.

and requires both conditions to be true. or needs at least one true condition. not reverses a boolean. Parentheses make combined rules easier to read. Test the exact boundary, one value below it, and one above it: an incorrect < in place of <= often hides there.
plain.code:
age = 12
print(age >= 12)
print(age > 12)
print((age >= 10) and (age <= 15))
print(not (age == 12))
plain.check: Which comparison would include both endpoints of a permitted range?

plain.title: Branches and indentation decide what runs
plain.text:
if condition: runs an indented block when the condition is true. elif means otherwise, if this next condition is true. else handles what remains. An if/elif/else chain chooses at most one branch. Indentation is part of Python syntax, not decoration. A line aligned with if runs after the branch instead of inside it.

A boolean parameter can be used directly as a condition: if enabled means run when enabled is True. You need not compare it with True. Check every path through a function: can each path produce the result its contract promises? A variable assigned only inside one branch will not exist on paths that skip that branch.
walk: At 8, 8 < 8 is false, so Python checks 8 < 18 and returns jacket.
At 18, both comparisons are false, so the else branch returns light clothes.
Only the chosen branch runs; return ends that function call.
plain.check: Trace values just below and exactly on each cutoff. Does every call return something?

plain.title: Build readable text with f-strings
plain.text:
An f-string begins with f immediately before its opening quote. Inside it, braces { } contain an expression whose value is inserted into the text. The braces are not printed. Python converts the inserted value to text for you. Ordinary strings without f keep their braces literally.

You can format an already-computed result, or call a function inside the braces. Saving an intermediate result often makes beginner code easier to inspect. The escape sequence \n represents a newline inside a string; it is not two printed characters.
plain.code:
visitor = "Mina"
length = 12
message = f"{visitor} needs {length} metres."
print(message)
print("First line\nSecond line")
plain.output:
Mina needs 12 metres.
First line
Second line
plain.check: What changes if you remove the f before the first message string?

plain.title: Connect files using imports
plain.text:
A module is a Python file. import math loads the standard-library math module; math.floor names its floor operation. A dot selects a named part of an object or module. The standard library comes with Python. floor(value) returns the greatest integer less than or equal to the value; ceil(value) returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to it. These move toward negative or positive infinity, not simply toward zero: floor(-3.2) is -4, and ceil(-3.2) is -3.

from math import floor loads the same operation under its short name. These are two spelling choices; you normally use one style consistently. For local labs, core.py contains your calculation functions and main.py imports and calls them. from core import some_name means load the function named some_name from core.py in the same project folder. Replace some_name with an actual function you wrote; it is not a special Python keyword. Saving a file matters: Python runs what is saved on disk. Keep files together, and run commands from that folder.

Python executes a module's top-level instructions when first importing it. Function definitions alone are safe to import; top-level input or printing will run too. Chapter 4 explains the __main__ guard for separating reusable definitions from executable programs.
plain.code:
import math
print(math.floor(3.8))

from math import ceil
print(ceil(3.2))
plain.check: In your lab, which file should calculate a result, and which file should display it?

plain.title: Write one small test without learning classes first
plain.text:
A test compares what your function actually returns with an expected answer worked out independently. Start with ordinary values, zero, and exact cutoffs. Do not compute the expected answer by calling the same function: that would only compare a result with itself. assert condition is a simple executable expectation. If its condition is false, Python raises AssertionError; when true, it moves on.

The lab's supplied test file uses unittest, Python's built-in testing library. You can use its existing scaffold before learning to design classes. class CoreTests(unittest.TestCase) groups tests; leave that structure in place. A method is a function inside a class. Each test method begins with def test_ and takes self, the name for the current test object. self.assertEqual(actual, expected) checks equality. Add your method inside the class at the same indentation as the existing test method, then indent its assertions another level.

Import the function you intend to test from core. The supplied test reads cases.json using library code; you need not rewrite that loader. The full roles of classes, files, and JSON are taught later. 'Ran 2 tests' counts test methods, not assertions: one method may contain several checks. OK means all checks that actually ran passed, not that every possible case is covered.
plain.code:
def ribbon_length(count, length):
    return count * length

assert ribbon_length(2, 3) == 6
assert ribbon_length(0, 3) == 0
print("Both expectations passed")
plain.check: Choose an independent expected result before adding a test. What mistake would that test detect?

plain.title: Find the part of the test scaffold you should edit
plain.text:
Here is a tiny standalone unittest scaffold for an unrelated multiplication function. A class groups the test methods, and unittest.TestCase supplies assertEqual. You are not expected to invent the class machinery yet; keep the supplied structure and add test_ methods following its pattern. The first indentation level places a method inside the class. The second places its assertions inside that method. self identifies the current test object, whose assertEqual method checks the two arguments.

In your lab, import your own function from core instead of copying its implementation into the test file. Then choose your inputs and an independently calculated expected answer. Run the test command from the setup guide in the chapter folder. Python's test discovery calls methods whose names begin with test_. The snippet below defines one such method; by itself it defines a test but prints nothing.

The supplied loader is infrastructure you can leave intact: json.loads parses the cases file, Path(__file__) locates the current test file, with_name chooses cases.json beside it, and read_text reads its contents. Chapters 6 and 10 teach file and class machinery more fully. for case in cases visits supplied cases; *case["args"] unpacks the stored list into separate positional arguments. with self.subTest labels a case so a failed assertion can identify its inputs. You do not need to duplicate that loader to write a direct assertion of your own. Add your assertions in a separate test method and keep the supplied cases unchanged.
walk: unittest is Python's built-in testing module; no extra installation is needed.
RibbonTests groups the tests. The existing lab uses CoreTests; keep that name in your file.
test_two_lengths contains two assertions, but test discovery counts it as one test method.
The expected numbers 6 and 0 are worked out independently of the function call.
plain.check: Which line imports the testing tool, which groups tests, and where would you add a new assertion?

plain.title: Use the lab as independent practice
plain.text:
A specification is the agreement about inputs and outputs. A streak is a supplied count of consecutive events; the first lab does not ask you to implement a history tracker. 'At least' includes the cutoff. 'Nonnegative' means zero or greater. A boundary case sits where a rule changes.

Before coding, record inputs and exact expected results. Afterward run both tests and main.py: passing calculation tests does not demonstrate that the program prints the requested reports. In README.md record the commands, actual output, one bug or difficulty, and help used. Explain how each function receives inputs and returns a result. You do not have to finish the first lab in the same session as setup.

The required GitHub workspace and Python setup guides tell you exactly which buttons to select and commands to run. Follow them when the chapter reaches its local lab. Keep the learner repository separate from Forge's app source. Browser progress backups and your local project files protect different things.

goals: Trace each iteration of a loop.
Build a new list without mutating the input.
Normalize strings and explain indexing and slicing.

sections.title: Lists and positions
sections.text: A list is an ordered collection: [3, 7, 2]. Its first index is 0, so values[0] is 3. A negative index counts from the end; values[-1] is 2. values[1:3] slices from index 1 up to, but excluding, index 3. len(values) gives its length. Indexing an empty list raises IndexError. Lists can change: append adds an element and pop removes one. Strings support indexing and slicing too, but cannot be changed in place.

sections.title: Loops and accumulators
sections.text: for item in values binds item to each value in sequence. range(3) produces 0, 1, 2; range(1, 4) produces 1, 2, 3. Use enumerate(values) when you need both index and item. An accumulator starts before the loop, updates inside it, and is returned after it. A misplaced return inside the loop stops after the first item. A while loop repeats while a condition holds; update the state so it can eventually stop.

sections.title: Filter and transform
sections.text: Filtering keeps selected items; mapping changes each item. Start with explicit loops so you can trace their behavior. Later, [x * 2 for x in values if x > 0] combines filtering and mapping in a comprehension. It builds a new list. A generator expression uses parentheses instead: (x * 2 for x in values) produces results one at a time when consumed. sum totals numbers, any returns whether at least one value is truthy, and all returns whether every value is truthy. For empty input, sum returns 0 by default, any returns False, and all returns True. Trace the equivalent loop before using the compact form. Do not remove items from the collection you are iterating unless you fully understand the consequences. A fresh result list makes the contract easier to reason about.

sections.title: Strings and boundaries
sections.text: strip removes whitespace from both ends, lower changes case, replace substitutes occurrences, split divides text, and join combines strings using a separator. These methods return new values. An f-string such as f"Score: {score}" formats a value into text. Decide whether repeated internal spaces should remain or collapse. A normalization function must reflect the spec, not your guess about what a clean name should look like.

trace: Start total at 0. Read 4 and add it, so total becomes 4.
Read -2; the condition fails and the accumulator stays 4. Read 3 and add it to get 7.
The return happens after the loop. An empty list never enters the loop, so its result is the initial 0.

mistakes: Resetting the accumulator inside the loop.
Returning after the first iteration.
Using a list index before checking that the list contains an item.
questions: What does range(2, 5) produce?
Where must return go to process every element?
Which version changes its input: values.append(3) or values + [3]?

units.title: Make it repeatable

plain.title: Lists, indexes, and empty input
plain.text:
A list stores items in order and allows duplicates. Square brackets create one; commas separate its items. [] is an empty list. len(items) returns its item count. An index selects one position, starting at zero: items[0] is the first. A negative index counts back from the end, so items[-1] selects the last.

Reading an index that does not exist raises IndexError. An empty list has no first or last item, even though its length is valid. Decide how empty input should behave before indexing. A slice such as items[1:3] creates a new list from index 1 up to, but excluding, 3. Unlike a direct index, a slice can safely select an empty range.
plain.code:
colours = ["blue", "gold", "blue", "green"]
print(len(colours))
print(colours[0], colours[-1])
print(colours[1:3])
print(colours[9:12])
plain.check: What is the difference between an item's value and its position?

plain.title: A method belongs to a particular value
plain.text:
A method is an operation reached through a value using a dot. items.append(value) means call the list's append method to add one item at its end. The parentheses supply the item to add. append changes the list in place and returns None, so do not replace your list with append's return value.

items.pop() removes and returns the last item. pop on an empty list raises IndexError. A list can change, which is called mutation. By contrast, first_list + second_list joins their items into a new list without changing either input. Some operations create new values instead; learn which behavior each method promises rather than assuming every dot call behaves the same way.
plain.code:
colours = ["blue"]
returned = colours.append("gold")
print(colours)
print(returned)
last = colours.pop()
print(last, colours)
plain.check: Why would colours = colours.append("gold") lose the list reference?

plain.title: A for loop visits one item at a time
plain.text:
for colour in colours: repeats its indented body for each item. colour is an ordinary variable name that receives the next value each iteration. 'Iteration' means one pass through the loop body. The collection is read in order. When no items remain, Python continues with the first line aligned outside the loop.

The loop variable contains an item, not automatically its index. An empty list runs the body zero times. Avoid adding or removing items from the same list you are visiting: it can change which items the loop reaches. Read the original and build a separate result when filtering.
plain.code:
colours = ["blue", "gold"]
for colour in colours:
    print("Visiting", colour)
print("Finished")
plain.check: Which line runs once for every item, and which line runs only after the loop finishes?

plain.title: Accumulators start before the loop
plain.text:
An accumulator remembers a growing result. Start it before the loop, update it in the body, and use it after the loop. A running sum adds values; a running count adds one per qualifying item. total += amount is the update shorthand introduced in chapter 1.

The example below totals word lengths, a different calculation from your challenge. return is aligned with for so every word is processed before returning. Putting return inside the loop exits on the first item. Initializing total inside the loop would reset earlier work. For empty input the initial zero is the result.
plain.code:
def character_total(words):
    total = 0
    for word in words:
        total += len(word)
    return total

print(character_total(["sun", "rain"]))
print(character_total([]))
walk: Before the loop total is 0.
For sun, len(word) is 3, so total becomes 3.
For rain, len(word) is 4, so total becomes 7.
The loop ends; return sends 7 back to the caller.
plain.check: Why must the initialization and return sit outside the repeated block?

plain.title: Filter into a separate list
plain.text:
Filtering selects items; transforming changes the selected values. Start a new result list, inspect each input, and append only the desired result. This keeps the original collection intact and preserves encounter order. Repeated input items stay repeated unless the specification explicitly requests deduplication.

Below, the selection rule is a word-length rule and the stored result is a length. Track what gets appended: it need not be the original item itself. For no qualifying items, the new list stays empty. len(result) gives its item count, and sum(result) totals numeric items. sum([]) is zero. min and max select the smallest and largest item but need a value or an explicit default for empty input.
plain.code:
words = ["owl", "sunshine", "rain"]
lengths = []
for word in words:
    if len(word) > 4:
        lengths.append(len(word))
print(lengths)
print(words)
print(len(lengths), sum(lengths))
plain.check: Would a word exactly four characters long be kept? Which operator decides?

plain.title: Trace the loop instead of guessing
plain.text:
A trace records the state after each iteration. It is a paper explanation, not another Python function. Write the input, the fixed condition, and the starting accumulator. Then make columns for current item, condition result, and accumulator afterward. A False condition leaves the accumulator unchanged if the only update is inside that condition.

For the example below the starting total is 0. The rows are: 3, True, 3; -2, False, 3; 4, True, 7. Notice that the condition is always number > 0; the cutoff does not change as the loop visits new numbers. Include both selected and skipped items so your trace demonstrates the branch. For an empty input there are no rows and the starting accumulator is the result.
plain.check: Create your lab trace by hand. Can you explain why each accumulator changed or stayed unchanged?

plain.title: Two names are not two copies
plain.text:
first = original gives the same list another name. Mutating that list through either name is visible through both. original.copy() creates a separate top-level list containing the same items. For a list of integers, this is enough to preserve a before-call snapshot. Chapter 3 explains why nested lists need more care.

To test input preservation, make the snapshot before calling the function and compare afterward. Comparing original with itself cannot detect mutation. Neither can comparing it with another name for that same object. A literal expected list is another valid independent reference.
plain.code:
original = [6, 2]
alias = original
snapshot = original.copy()
alias.append(9)
print(original)
print(snapshot)
print(original == snapshot)
plain.check: Which variable here records what the list contained before the append?

plain.title: String methods return new text
plain.text:
Strings are sequences too: you can use len, indexing, slicing, and a for loop on their characters. Unlike lists, strings cannot be changed in place. A string method returns a new value. Save that return value if you need it later.

strip() removes whitespace from the ends, not from the middle. lower() returns lowercase text. replace(old, new) replaces each occurrence of old with new. split(separator) returns a list of pieces; split() without an argument splits runs of whitespace. separator.join(pieces) joins strings with that separator between them. These are methods with different return types: split returns a list; join returns a string.

Do one operation per line while learning. Chaining methods means the next method receives the previous method's returned value, not the original string. Follow the exact normalization contract; replacing each space is different from collapsing all whitespace.
plain.code:
label = "  Red  Bird  "
clean = label.strip()
small = clean.lower()
changed = small.replace(" ", "-")
print(label)
print(changed)
parts = clean.split()
print(parts)
print("/".join(parts))
plain.check: Why are there two hyphens in the transformed text?

plain.title: range and nested loops
plain.text:
range(stop) supplies integers from zero up to, but excluding, stop. range(start, stop) begins at start. range(start, stop, step) also controls the increment. The excluded stop is a frequent source of off-by-one errors. range is useful when the numbers themselves matter, not merely because something needs repeating.

A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For each outer item, the entire inner loop runs again from its beginning. Read the indentation before predicting the output. The two-by-two grid below produces four pairs, not two. More nested-loop work can grow quickly; chapter 8 teaches how to describe that growth.
walk: list(range(1, 4)) constructs a list from the supplied integers so we can display them.
At row 0 the inner loop visits columns 0 and 1.
Then row becomes 1 and the inner loop starts again at column 0.
plain.check: How many body executions would three rows and four columns produce?

plain.title: Unpack pairs before using enumerate or zip
plain.text:
Assignment can unpack a fixed sequence into separate names. left, right = [2, 5] assigns 2 to left and 5 to right. The number of names must match the number of values. A tuple, written (2, 5), also holds a sequence; unlike a list its items cannot be replaced.

enumerate(items) supplies pairs containing an index and an item; unpacking names them in the loop header. start=1 is a keyword argument: it explicitly names the parameter being set, so the numbering begins at 1 rather than 0. zip(first, second) supplies one pair of items at a time from two collections. It stops at the shorter collection, so check lengths if silently losing unmatched items would violate your contract.
plain.output:
2 5
1 sun
2 rain
sun gold
rain grey
plain.check: What do the two names in each loop receive? What would happen if the second list passed to zip were shorter?

plain.title: Read compact collection syntax after understanding loops
plain.text:
A list comprehension is a shorter way to build a new list. In [len(word) for word in words if len(word) > 3], read it as: for each word, keep it if the condition is true, and store len(word). The expression at the left says what is stored. The for clause says where inputs come from; the optional if clause selects them.

A generator expression uses parentheses instead of list brackets and supplies results as another operation requests them. sum can consume a generator without first building the whole list. any returns True if at least one supplied value is truthy; all returns True if every supplied value is truthy. Truthy means treated as true by a condition; zero, False, None, and empty strings or collections are falsy, while nonempty collections and nonzero numbers are truthy. For empty input any is False and all is True. For now prefer explicit loops in exercises that require them. Shorter syntax is optional, not a sign that your loop is inferior.
plain.code:
words = ["sun", "cloud", "rain"]
lengths = [len(word) for word in words if len(word) > 3]
print(lengths)
print(sum(len(word) for word in words))
print(any([False, True]), all([True, True]))
print(any([]), all([]))

sections.title: Choose by operation
sections.text: A list preserves order and duplicates. A tuple is an immutable sequence, useful for a fixed pair such as (x, y). A dictionary maps unique keys to values and preserves insertion order. A set stores unique hashable values for membership tests; do not depend on its iteration order for a report. Strings, numbers, and tuples of hashable values can be keys; mutable lists cannot. Choose based on what you need to do, not which syntax looks shortest. For sets, a | b is union, a & b is intersection, and a - b is difference. These operations also work with dictionary key views. A membership test uses in; use not in for its opposite.

sections.title: Count and look up
sections.text: counts[item] raises KeyError if the key is missing. counts.get(item, 0) supplies a starting value without inserting it. Updating counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1 accumulates a frequency. Use key in mapping to distinguish a missing key from a stored value of None or 0. mapping.items() yields key/value pairs that can be unpacked in a loop.

sections.title: Objects and copies
sections.text: Assignment does not copy a collection: b = a makes both names refer to the same list. Modifying b can therefore change what a sees. a.copy() makes a shallow top-level copy; nested collections are still shared. A pure transformation returns a new result and leaves the caller’s input alone. You will need this distinction whenever a task says do not mutate.

sections.title: Sorting is a policy
sections.text: sorted(values) returns a new ordered list; list.sort() changes the list and returns None. key chooses a comparison value. lambda record: record["score"] is a tiny function returning a score. A tuple key such as (-score, name) means score descending, then name ascending. Stable sorting retains original order when keys compare equally. Define ties explicitly rather than relying on accidental order.

units.title: Think in collections

plain.title: A dictionary maps a key to a value
plain.text:
A dictionary stores key/value associations. In {"red": 4}, "red" is a key and 4 is its value. A colon separates a key from its value; commas separate entries. {} creates an empty dictionary. Unlike a list's numeric positions, dictionary brackets look up a key: stock["red"] means find the value associated with red.

Dictionary keys are unique. Assigning to a key replaces its previous value; assigning to an absent key adds an entry. Reading an absent key with brackets raises KeyError. Dictionaries preserve insertion order, but that does not automatically give the alphabetical or numeric display order a report might require.
plain.code:
stock = {"red": 4, "blue": 2}
print(stock["red"])
stock["red"] = 6
stock["green"] = 1
print(stock)
plain.check: Which assignment updates an existing entry, and which creates a new entry?

plain.title: Membership, missing keys, and get
plain.text:
key in mapping asks whether a dictionary contains that key, not whether it contains that value. not in asks the opposite. mapping.get(key, default) returns the stored value when present and the default when absent. It does not insert that default into the dictionary. If you omit the second argument, mapping.get(key) returns None for an absent key.

A missing key is not the same as a present key storing zero or None. Use membership to distinguish those situations when the contract cares. For a running count, read the previous value with a default of zero, compute the update, then assign it to that key. Separate those actions while learning instead of hiding the whole update in one line.
plain.code:
visits = {"garden": 0}
print("garden" in visits, "harbour" in visits)
previous = visits.get("harbour", 0)
print(previous, visits)
visits["harbour"] = previous + 1
print(visits)
plain.check: Does get change the dictionary? Which later line actually changes it?

plain.title: Loop over keys or key/value pairs deliberately
plain.text:
for key in mapping visits dictionary keys. mapping.values() supplies values. mapping.items() supplies pairs of key and value; the two-name loop header unpacks each pair, using chapter 2's unpacking rule. These are dictionary views: they reflect the current dictionary, not independent copies. Avoid adding or deleting entries while iterating over a view.

del mapping[key] removes an entry but raises KeyError if the key is absent. mapping.pop(key, default) removes a present entry and returns its value, or returns the default for an absent key. Before removing inventory entries in your lab, decide and document what missing or zero-count removal should mean. Python does not choose that policy for you.
plain.code:
stock = {"red": 4, "blue": 2}
for colour, amount in stock.items():
    print(colour, amount)
removed = stock.pop("blue", 0)
print(removed)
print(stock.pop("green", 0))
print(stock)
plain.check: Which operation merely reads entries, and which removes one?

plain.title: Choose list, tuple, dictionary, or set by the job
plain.text:
A list keeps order and duplicates. A tuple also holds an ordered sequence but its own items cannot be reassigned; (3, 4) is a two-item tuple and (3,) is a one-item tuple. A dictionary associates unique keys with values. A set stores unique elements for membership questions without promising a useful iteration order.

Dictionary keys and set members must be hashable: Python must be able to compute a stable lookup value for them. Strings and integers work. A tuple works only if all its members are hashable. Mutable lists and dictionaries cannot be keys or set members. Use a list for a history, a dictionary for per-item quantities, and a set for whether something has appeared. One project can need all three; they answer different questions.
plain.code:
position = (3, 4)
x, y = position
print(x, y)
print(["red", "red", "blue"])
print({"red": 2, "blue": 1})
plain.check: Why would a set lose information if you needed to remember how many times each event occurred?

plain.title: Create a set, then add or check one value
plain.text:
set() calls Python's set constructor with no arguments and creates an empty set. Do not use {}: that creates a dictionary. set(["red", "red", "blue"]) constructs a set from list items and removes duplicates. A nonempty set literal uses braces without colons, such as {"red", "blue"}.

seen.add(value) calls the set's add method. It inserts one element, doing nothing extra if that element is already present. add changes the set and returns None. value in seen checks membership without inserting it. The example below prints booleans and lengths instead of raw set contents because set display order is not a contract. If first-seen output order matters, keep a separate result list; a set alone cannot remember it.
plain.code:
seen = set()
print("red" in seen)
seen.add("red")
print("red" in seen)
seen.add("red")
print(len(seen))
seen.add("blue")
print(len(seen))
walk: set() creates a collection with no members.
The first add makes red a member; the second add of red leaves the size at 1.
Adding a different value increases the size to 2.
plain.check: What does add return, and why should you not write seen = seen.add(value)?

plain.title: Set operations combine membership rules
plain.text:
With sets, left | right is union: members from either side. left & right is intersection: members present on both sides. left - right is difference: left-side members absent from the right. These expressions produce new sets. The original sets stay unchanged.

Dictionary key views support these set-style operations too, but be explicit about whether you want keys, values, or full entries. sorted(collection) makes a new sorted list, which is useful for a deterministic display of set members. Do not confuse alphabetical display order with original encounter order; sorting cannot recover an order that the set never stored.
plain.check: Which operation answers 'present in both', and which answers 'only in the first'?

plain.title: Copy a dictionary without confusing names and objects
plain.text:
alias = original makes another name for the same dictionary. Mutating it through alias changes what original sees. original.copy() creates a new top-level dictionary. dict(original) is another spelling for a shallow dictionary copy: dict is a constructor, like list and set, and the argument supplies existing associations. dict() with no arguments creates an empty dictionary.

A shallow copy copies the outer container, not every object inside it. If a value is itself a list, both outer dictionaries still refer to that nested list. Replacing a top-level number in the copy is independent; appending to a shared nested list is not. For this chapter's item-to-integer counts a shallow copy is sufficient. A promise not to mutate input concerns the caller's data, not merely the variable name.
plain.code:
original = {"red": 4}
alias = original
alias["red"] = 5
print(original)
independent = dict(original)
independent["red"] = 9
print(original, independent)

nested = {"colours": ["red"]}
outer_copy = nested.copy()
outer_copy["colours"].append("blue")
print(nested)
plain.check: Which change in the example reaches the original through a shared nested value?

plain.title: Read nested data one level at a time
plain.text:
A list can contain dictionaries; a dictionary can contain lists. Each pair of brackets selects one level and gives a value that can be used by the next operation. In rows[0]["name"], first read index 0 from rows, then read the name key from that dictionary.

Break a long expression into temporary variables when the shape is unfamiliar. Distinguish a missing key from a missing list position. The data contract should say which fields are guaranteed and what empty input means. max and min on an empty list need an explicit policy; an example with one nonempty nested list does not establish that all real records have one.
plain.code:
rows = [{"name": "Mina", "sizes": [2, 5]}]
first_row = rows[0]
sizes = first_row["sizes"]
print(first_row["name"])
print(sizes[1])
print(rows[0]["sizes"][0])
plain.check: Describe the type of the value after each bracket operation.

plain.title: Sort basic values before introducing sort keys
plain.text:
sorted(values) returns a new list in ascending order, leaving the input container unchanged. For numbers ascending means smaller first; for strings it follows Python's character ordering, so do not assume a language-aware human collation rule. reverse=True is a keyword argument that requests descending order. In a call, values is supplied by position, while reverse=True names the parameter being set. That equals sign is part of an argument, not a new variable assignment or an equality comparison. key=some_function works the same way: explicitly supply the key parameter.

items.sort() is different: it rearranges that list in place and returns None. Use sorted when the contract says preserve input. Python's sort is stable: items with equal comparison keys retain their original relative order, even when reverse=True. Stability is a tie policy, and it differs from explicitly breaking ties alphabetically. Read the exercise's requested policy rather than copying a more complicated example.
plain.code:
sizes = [4, 1, 3]
ordered = sorted(sizes)
print(ordered)
print(sizes)
print(sorted(sizes, reverse=True))
returned = sizes.sort()
print(sizes, returned)
plain.check: Which operation would be unsafe if the caller requires their list to remain unchanged?

plain.title: A sort key is a function, not a field name
plain.text:
To sort records, Python needs a comparable value for each record. Define a normal function that receives one record and returns that value. Pass the function itself with key=function_name, without calling it. sorted calls that function for each record. Writing key=function_name() would call it immediately without the required record.

This is a new idea: a function can be passed as a value, just as a number or string can. The name without parentheses refers to the function; parentheses request a call. Below, the key function extracts a length field. Because the first two records have equal length, their input order remains intact. That behavior is stability, not an alphabetical tie break.
walk: sorted calls parcel_length on each parcel dictionary.
The resulting comparison values are 4, 4, and 2, so C comes first.
B and A remain in that order because their keys tie.
plain.check: Why is the key argument parcel_length rather than parcel_length()?

plain.title: A lambda is a small alternative to def
plain.text:
lambda parameter: expression creates a function without a def statement. It takes the parameter and returns the expression's value automatically; do not write return inside a lambda. It is useful for a short key function, but it is optional. A named def is equally valid and often easier to explain or debug.

In lambda parcel: parcel["length"], parcel is an ordinary parameter name, the colon separates parameter from expression, and the bracket lookup produces the comparison value. lambda does not itself sort anything; sorted performs the sorting and calls the function. Start with the named function from the previous section before choosing shorthand.
plain.code:
parcels = [{"tag": "B", "length": 4}, {"tag": "C", "length": 2}]
ordered = sorted(parcels, key=lambda parcel: parcel["length"])
for parcel in ordered:
    print(parcel["tag"])
plain.check: Rewrite the lambda as a named function in your notes. What input does it receive and what value does it return?

plain.title: Tuple keys express a deliberate tie policy
plain.text:
Python compares tuples from left to right. It compares the first elements; only if they tie does it compare the second elements. A key such as (length, tag) means ascending length, then ascending tag. A negative numeric first element changes that part's direction: (-length, tag) gives longer first, but still alphabetical tags for equal lengths.

This is an explicit secondary tie rule. It would be wrong for a contract requiring original input order on ties. reverse=True reverses the whole ordering policy, whereas negating one numeric component reverses only that component. Do not add a tie breaker merely because the syntax is available.

The final comprehension below extracts names after sorting. Chapter 2 taught that its left expression selects the stored value and its for clause supplies each input; it builds a new list. An ordinary for loop with append is equivalent and remains a good choice.
walk: Keys are (-4, B), (-4, A), and (-7, C). Smaller -7 comes first.
The two -4 keys tie on their first part; A sorts before B on the second.
The comprehension reads ordered and stores only each tag.
plain.check: Which tie rule does your browser exercise require? Which rule will you explicitly choose and document for your independent lab?

plain.title: A set comprehension is optional shorthand
plain.text:
After an ordinary loop is clear, a comprehension can build a set directly. {expression for item in collection} uses braces to collect unique results. It has no key:value colon, so it is a set comprehension rather than a dictionary comprehension. Like a list comprehension it may include an if condition after the for clause.

Uniqueness applies to the computed result: two different inputs can transform into the same member. This also discards first-seen order, so only use this form when the specification permits it. sorted can then produce deterministic ascending output, but that is a separate ordering policy. Your first implementation can stay an explicit loop with add; shorthand is not required to demonstrate understanding.
plain.code:
lengths = {len(word) for word in ["sun", "owl", "rain"]}
print(sorted(lengths))
plain.check: Why are there two results even though there are three input words?

plain.title: Build a collection policy before building the lab
plain.text:
For your inventory lab, decide what happens when an item is missing, a removal reaches zero, or a removal asks for more than available. The brief leaves these design choices to you; record them and test them. Use a list for event history and a dictionary for quantities. If you return a new inventory, test that the caller's original is unchanged.

For display, distinguish insertion order, first-seen order, alphabetical order, and a score-based order. They are different promises. Test repeated items, empty data, missing items, equal scores, and unsorted inputs. The supplied checkpoint tests cover only their required function, so your own new functions need their own tests. Write a short explanation of why each collection fits the operation rather than choosing a collection just because it appeared in the lesson.
plain.check: Can you explain the difference between deduplicating, counting frequencies, and sorting?

units.title: Build a game engine

plain.title: State is the information that changes over time
plain.text:
State is the current information needed to describe a system. A lift has a floor; a game may have position, health, and an inventory. A transition is one update: current state plus a command produces next state. A sequence of transitions feeds each result into the following step.

Begin with a tiny model that you can trace, not graphics. Below a heater's state is a temperature. Each command chooses an update. A command not covered by either branch leaves the state unchanged. That is a deliberate policy; another application could instead reject an unknown command.
plain.check: What is the state before the third command? Which line changes it?

plain.title: min and max enforce a chosen bound
plain.text:
An invariant is a rule that must stay true after each update. If a dial must stay between 0 and 5, enforce both limits whenever changing it. max(lower, candidate) chooses the larger value and prevents going below the lower bound. min(upper, candidate) chooses the smaller and prevents exceeding the upper bound.

Clamping means replacing an out-of-range candidate with the nearest permitted boundary. It is one possible rule, not a universal fix. Sometimes an invalid move must be ignored instead. Read the contract first. Separating candidate calculation from boundary handling makes both parts easier to inspect.
plain.code:
dial = 2
candidate = dial - 7
dial = max(0, candidate)
print(dial)
candidate = dial + 9
dial = min(5, candidate)
print(dial)
plain.check: How would rejecting an out-of-range change differ from clamping it?

plain.title: Coordinates and unpacking describe position
plain.text:
A two-dimensional coordinate uses two numbers. Decide and document the axes: in a conventional mathematical grid, x increases rightward and y increases upward. A list [x, y] can store the pair. Assignment such as x, y = position unpacks exactly two items, as in chapter 2.

A change can also be a pair, often called a vector: dx and dy mean change in x and change in y. A dictionary can map command names to vectors. Lookup with get supplies a deliberate default. The example uses a canvas-style row/column position with named commands, not your exercise's N/S/E/W contract. Keep the chosen coordinate convention consistent throughout your own program.
plain.code:
position = [2, 3]
column, row = position
changes = {"right": (1, 0), "down": (0, 1)}
dc, dr = changes.get("down", (0, 0))
print(column + dc, row + dr)
print(position)
plain.check: What does the default (0, 0) mean, and does this calculation mutate the original list?

plain.title: A while loop checks a condition repeatedly
plain.text:
A for loop obtains each next item from a collection. A while loop instead asks whether a condition is true before each pass. If true it runs the body, then asks again. If false on the first check, the body never runs. Something in the body must eventually make the condition false, or another explicit exit must occur.

Before writing a while loop, name its progress measure: what gets closer to stopping? In this countdown it is remaining. If the decrement were zero, the loop would never finish. An input that prevents progress requires a contract rule before entering the loop, not a hope that the time limit will stop it.
plain.code:
remaining = 3
while remaining > 0:
    print(remaining)
    remaining -= 1
print("Ready")
walk: Check 3 > 0, print 3, and reduce remaining to 2.
Repeat at 2 and 1.
At 0 the condition is false, so continue after the loop.
plain.check: What happens with an initial remaining of 0? What change would accidentally make the loop infinite?

plain.title: break, continue, and return have different scope
plain.text:
break leaves the nearest enclosing loop and continues after it. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and begins the next one. return exits the entire function, including any loops inside it. These are different actions, even when small examples happen to end at the same place.

Use them when they make the rule clearer. A sentinel is a special value meaning stop; choose one that is distinguishable from ordinary data. In a local command loop, a quit command can be a sentinel. Validate zero or negative progress values before a repetitive simulation so impossible inputs do not trap the program.
plain.check: Why is the final show command never visited?

plain.title: Terminal input returns text
plain.text:
input(prompt) prints a prompt, waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, and returns that line as a string. Even entering 4 gives the text "4". int(text) converts suitable integer text when you need a number; chapter 5 handles conversion failures. print displays information and does not ask for input.

Run this greeting in a local .py file using the lab's run command. With Mina entered, it displays Hello, Mina!. This is an interactive illustration, so Forge does not run it as an unattended example. Browser function quests already receive arguments from the test harness; do not add input() to those functions. Keep interactive input and display in main.py and testable calculations in core.py.

Decide a quit command before building a game loop. Explain what changes on every turn and what event ends the session. A program that cannot stop cleanly is not complete even if its individual calculations are right.
plain.code:
name = input("Name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}!")
plain.check: Which part of your local program interacts with the user, and which part can be tested without typing?

plain.title: Functions can hand results to other functions
plain.text:
Split a larger program into pieces with explicit inputs and returned results. One function might process a single update; another could call it for each command. To call a helper, use its name and supply the arguments it requires. A returned value does not update your state automatically: save it or pass it onward deliberately.

Do not make every function read global variables. Passing the needed state makes dependencies visible and lets tests supply tiny examples. The example's two helpers format a travel duration; they do not implement your game. Trace where the returned number becomes the next function's argument.
plain.code:
def minutes_from_hours(hours):
    return hours * 60

def describe_minutes(minutes):
    return f"Duration: {minutes} minutes"

minutes = minutes_from_hours(2)
message = describe_minutes(minutes)
print(message)
plain.check: Where is the first function's return value saved, and which function receives it next?

plain.title: Protect executable code with the main guard
plain.text:
Every Python module has a special __name__ variable. When you run a file directly, Python sets it to "__main__". When another file imports it, Python uses the module's name instead. if __name__ == "__main__": therefore means run this block only when this file is the entry point. The double underscores and spelling are part of Python's convention, not names you invent.

Defining a main function and calling it inside this guard keeps imports from starting an interactive program. Tests can then import calculation functions without a game immediately requesting keyboard input. The guard does not make a program correct; it separates reusable definitions from execution.
plain.check: Why would top-level input() inside an imported module interfere with automated tests?

Trace at least one multi-command sequence by writing before and after state. A boundary policy must be consistent with the specification.

For the local game, build the smallest usable path: initial state, one valid command, a displayed result, and a quit path. Add other rules one at a time. Document coordinate direction, boundaries, unknown commands, and when the session ends. Use fixed commands in tests; keep typing and display outside the pure transition functions. No graphics or third-party library is required for this chapter's terminal game.

sections.text: A syntax error prevents Python from parsing the program. A runtime exception happens during execution, such as accessing a missing key. A logic bug runs but produces the wrong answer. Use different evidence for each: a parser location, a traceback, or an expected/actual comparison. A red test is a starting point for investigation.

sections.title: Tracebacks and debugging
sections.text: Read the exception type and message at the end, then find the last relevant line in your own code. Reproduce the smallest failing input. Check variable values with a temporary print or a debugger breakpoint. Form one hypothesis and test it. When you fix the bug, preserve the input as a regression test so it does not quietly return.

sections.title: Exceptions and validation
sections.text: try protects code that might raise an expected exception; except ValueError handles that type. Do not put your entire program in except Exception and report success. int("4") succeeds, int("four") fails, and int("4.5") also fails. None can represent an invalid parsed result, but callers must handle it before arithmetic. Check types before calling methods or comparing missing values.

sections.title: Truth is not presence
sections.text: An empty list, empty string, zero, False, and None are falsy in conditions. They do not mean the same thing. if not scores is useful for rejecting an empty list, but if value may be 0, use an explicit check such as value is None. Short-circuit conditions help validate safely: check isinstance(name, str) before name.strip(). Avoid dividing by len(values) until you know the list is nonempty.

trace: The first conversion succeeds and zero passes the nonnegative rule.
The second conversion raises ValueError, handled by the specific except.
A caller must distinguish a legitimate count 0 from the invalid marker None.

mistakes: Catching every exception and hiding unrelated bugs.
Treating zero as missing.
Changing several things at once without a reproducible example.
questions: Is the failure syntax, runtime, or logic?
Why is if value is None different from if not value?

units.title: Handle messy inputs
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–4, especially build a game engine

plain.title: Separate syntax errors, exceptions, and wrong answers
plain.text:
A syntax error means Python cannot read the program: a missing colon or unmatched quote prevents execution. A runtime exception interrupts code that has started running, such as dividing by zero or requesting an absent dictionary key. A logic bug runs without an exception but computes the wrong answer.

Each needs different evidence. For syntax, inspect the indicated location and preceding line. For an exception, read its traceback. For a wrong answer, record the input, expected value, and actual value, then trace the first place the calculation diverges. Do not change several things at once: a testable hypothesis is more useful than random editing.
plain.check: If a function returns 4 instead of 5 without crashing, which kind of problem is that?

plain.title: Read a traceback from the error back to your code
plain.text:
A traceback lists the calls active when an exception escaped. The final line names the exception and its message. Above it are file names, line numbers, and relevant instructions. Start at the bottom, then find the nearest relevant line in your own code; library frames can provide context but are not usually where you should edit.

For ZeroDivisionError at return total / count, inspect count before division. For KeyError, inspect the key and actual dictionary contents. For TypeError, inspect the types being combined. Preserve the exact failing input before fixing anything so the failure can become a regression test. A regression test ensures an already-fixed mistake does not silently return.
plain.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "example.py", line 8, in <module>
    print(share(10, 0))
  File "example.py", line 2, in share
    return amount / people
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
plain.check: Which value would you inspect first, and what smallest input reproduces this problem?

plain.title: Convert text deliberately and catch expected failures
plain.text:
int(text) accepts integer text such as "8" or "-2". It rejects "eight" and "8.5" with ValueError. A try block encloses an operation that may raise an expected exception. except ValueError: handles that exception and lets you define the response. If the conversion succeeds, its except block is skipped.

Keep the try block small. Catching every Exception around your entire program can hide spelling mistakes and broken assumptions. An invalid input is not the same as an unexpected implementation bug. When a contract specifies None for invalid data, return None only for those declared failures and ensure callers check it before arithmetic.
walk: For -2, conversion succeeds and execution continues to the final return.
For warm, conversion raises ValueError and execution jumps to the matching handler.
The handler returns None immediately; the final return is not reached on that path.
plain.check: Why is int("8.5") not the same as float("8.5")?

plain.title: Validate a value after converting its representation
plain.text:
Parsing turns a representation into a value. Validation asks whether that value is acceptable for this application. A successful integer conversion does not prove the number lies in the allowed range. Keep these stages distinct when explaining your program.

A guard clause checks a rejected condition and exits early. Later lines can then assume that condition was passed. Test a lower bound, an upper bound, the values immediately outside, and malformed text. A default is a deliberate fallback policy; do not silently substitute it unless your contract allows that behavior.
plain.check: Which part parses, and which part applies a domain rule?

plain.title: False is not the same as missing
plain.text:
Conditions treat 0, False, None, empty text, and empty collections as falsy. That shorthand is useful for if not items when you mean an empty collection. It is dangerous when zero or False is a valid result. if not value would reject all of those different cases. bool(value) converts a value's truthiness into the actual boolean True or False; it does not tell you whether the value is present or valid for your application.

Use value is None when checking the missing-value marker specifically. is tests identity; None is a special singleton value, so this is its usual check. Use == for ordinary value equality. Do not replace all equality comparisons with is: two equal strings or numbers are not guaranteed to be the same object.
plain.code:
for value in [0, False, None, ""]:
    print(value, bool(value), value is None)
plain.output:
0 False False
False False False
None False True
 False False
plain.check: If your parser legitimately returns False, what check preserves it while rejecting None?

plain.title: Short-circuit validation protects later operations
plain.text:
Python evaluates and from left to right and stops when a condition is false; it evaluates or until one is true. This is short-circuiting. Put the prerequisite first: check that text has the needed type before calling a string method, or that a list is nonempty before indexing it.

isinstance(value, str) asks whether value is a string. Similar checks can name list, dict, int, or float. bool is a subclass of int in Python, so isinstance(True, int) is true; a strict integer-only contract may need a more precise rule. Validate the inputs your contract actually allows; extra rejection rules can break otherwise valid cases.
plain.code:
def has_visible_text(value):
    return isinstance(value, str) and value.strip() != ""

print(has_visible_text(None))
print(has_visible_text("   "))
print(has_visible_text(" note "))
walk: For None the type check is false, so .strip() is never attempted.
Whitespace text has the right type but becomes empty after stripping.
The final string leaves visible content after stripping.
plain.check: Why would reversing the two conditions make the None input unsafe?

plain.title: raise communicates a failure to the caller
plain.text:
Some APIs return a missing marker; others raise an exception. raise ValueError("message") creates an error with a meaningful explanation, stops the current function, and passes control outward until a matching handler is found. The caller must follow that API's chosen policy. Do not raise where an exercise explicitly requires None.

except ValueError as error names the caught exception so its message can be displayed or logged. The as name is available inside that handler. Keep unexpected failures visible instead of claiming every failure is ordinary bad input.
plain.output: Rejected: text must not be empty
plain.check: How is returning None different from raising ValueError for the caller?

plain.title: Use a debugger to inspect a hypothesis
plain.text:
A breakpoint pauses execution at a selected source line. In VS Code, open the local .py file, select the gutter beside a line before the suspected bug, and start the Python debugger for that file. A red dot marks the breakpoint. When paused, inspect the Variables panel or hover over names. Step Over runs the next line without entering every helper; Step Into enters a called function; Continue resumes to the next breakpoint or program end.

If execution never pauses, confirm that you saved the file, are running that same file with the selected environment, and are using a failing input that reaches the breakpoint. Do not place the breakpoint after an early return you never reach. Stop the debugger when finished. Record observed values and the hypothesis they support; a screenshot of a paused program alone does not explain the bug.
plain.check: Which line would let you inspect a converted number before the range checks run?

plain.title: Build a regression test and an honest bug note
plain.text:
Before correcting a bug, record expected and actual behavior for its smallest input. Add that input to your tests with an independently computed expectation. Run it to confirm it exposes the bug; after fixing the code, run it again and then run the existing suite. This red-to-green sequence shows the test would catch the original failure.

The settings lab needs separate policies for a numeric setting, a yes/no setting, and a name. Document accepted spellings, whitespace treatment, valid zero/False behavior, invalid markers or exceptions, and any defaults you choose. For a bug note, write expected, actual, cause, change, verification, and help used. It is fine to write that no failure was observed in a particular case; do not invent a bug to fill a heading.
plain.check: Which exact test would stop your original bug from returning next month?

goals: Read and write text using a context manager.

sections.title: Files and resources
sections.text: A file handle is a resource. with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle closes it when the block exits, including on an exception. Read mode does not create a missing file; write mode can overwrite existing content. Use a dedicated practice folder. The browser’s Python filesystem is temporary and separate from your computer, so real persistent file labs run locally.

sections.title: JSON is a format, not a Python expression
sections.text: json.loads reads JSON text into Python objects; json.dumps produces text. File-based json.load and json.dump use handles. JSON null maps to None and true/false map to Python booleans. Parsing successfully does not prove the result has the shape your application needs. Check that expected lists, keys, and value types are present before processing.

sections.title: CSV and text streams
sections.text: csv.DictReader reads headers into dictionary keys. Most CSV field values arrive as strings, so convert numeric fields deliberately. A quoted title may contain a comma; split(",") cannot reliably parse it. io.StringIO lets the same parser read an in-memory string for tests. Use newline="" when opening real CSV files and let csv handle delimiters and quoting.

sections.title: Paths and pure processing
sections.text: pathlib represents paths and their components. PurePosixPath computes components without touching a disk; Path can access the local filesystem. A suffix is not proof of valid file contents. Design a core that transforms records, then write a thin wrapper to read and write files. This prevents tests from needing a real filesystem for every calculation. A generator expression such as (row["minutes"] for row in records) produces those values as they are requested; sum(...) consumes them. It resembles a list comprehension but uses parentheses and need not first construct a list. An ordinary loop is an equally valid way to express the calculation.

worked.code:
import json
text = '[{"game": "Halo", "minutes": 12}]'
records = json.loads(text)
print(sum(row["minutes"] for row in records))
trace: Parse text into a list of dictionaries.
Each record has a minutes value; the generator provides it to sum.
The calculation knows nothing about the source filename, so it is easy to test with a tiny fixture.

mistakes: Splitting CSV by commas.
Assuming parsed JSON always has the expected schema.
Accidentally overwriting the input file during an experiment.
questions: How do loads and load differ?
Why can a quoted comma break manual CSV parsing?
What part of your program should own file I/O?
