units.title: Work with real data

plain.title: A format is not the same thing as a Python value
plain.text:
A Python list or dictionary exists as objects while the program runs. A data format describes text or bytes that can be stored or transferred. JSON and CSV are formats. Parsing converts their representation into usable values; serializing converts values back into a representation.

Keep your calculation functions independent of file locations. A pure processing function receives records and returns results; a thin outer layer reads text, parses it, calls the processing function, and writes output. This lets tests use a tiny in-memory fixture, meaning deliberately chosen sample data, rather than needing a real file for every calculation.
plain.check: Which part of a report program should know its input filename? Which part should only know records?

plain.title: JSON text becomes lists and dictionaries
plain.text:
import json loads Python's standard JSON library. json.loads(text) means load from a string; the final s stands for string. json.dumps(value) produces JSON text. json.load(handle) and json.dump(value, handle) are the file-handle variants, introduced after opening files below.

JSON uses double-quoted strings, true, false, and null. Python uses True, False, and None. JSON objects become dictionaries and arrays become lists. A successfully parsed document can still have the wrong shape for your application. The parser checks JSON syntax; your validation checks expected keys and types. Keep JSON text inside a Python string with matching outer quotes so Python can read the example itself.
plain.code:
import json
text = '{"open": true, "note": null, "colours": ["red", "blue"]}'
record = json.loads(text)
print(record["open"], record["note"])
print(record["colours"][1])
print(json.dumps({"ready": False}))
plain.check: Which value here is text, and which is a dictionary? What does the trailing s in loads indicate?

plain.title: Escape sequences and multiline data
plain.text:
Inside a Python string, \n represents a newline and \t a tab. A backslash before a quote puts a quote inside a double-quoted string without ending it. You can often avoid quote escaping by using single quotes around a string containing double quotes. Triple quotes can hold multiline text.

CSV data contains row boundaries; JSON data often contains quoted names. Distinguish the outer Python string syntax from the inner file-format syntax. Printing shows the interpreted text. repr(value) shows a developer-oriented representation with escape sequences, useful when invisible whitespace causes confusion. print normally adds a newline after its arguments; end="" names the end parameter and replaces that extra newline with empty text. This avoids adding an extra blank line when text already ends in a newline.
plain.code:
text = "colour,count\nred,2\n"
print(text, end="")
print(repr(text))
walk: Each \n in the source becomes a line break in the string.
end="" tells print not to add its usual extra newline.
repr exposes the newline characters using backslash notation.
plain.check: How would you tell an actual two-row CSV string from a string containing literal backslash and n characters?

plain.title: A text stream lets a parser read a string like a file
plain.text:
A stream is an object that supplies text as it is read. io.StringIO(text) wraps an existing string in an in-memory text stream. It does not open a file on your disk. import io makes the constructor available as io.StringIO.

CSV readers accept streams rather than raw text strings. If you pass the raw string directly, iteration would produce characters instead of rows. Keeping the stream in a named variable makes that boundary explicit. The stream's readline() method reads one line, keeping its final newline if present. Its read() method returns all remaining unread text. Reading advances the stream's position; reading again after reaching the end returns empty text. A fresh StringIO is often simplest for a separate test.
plain.code:
import io
stream = io.StringIO("red\nblue\n")
print(stream.readline(), end="")
print(stream.read(), end="")
print(stream.read() == "")
plain.check: Does StringIO require a file to exist on your computer?

plain.title: Read CSV fields with DictReader
plain.text:
CSV separates fields with delimiters, commonly commas, and uses quoting to allow delimiters inside fields. Splitting each line on a comma cannot handle a field such as "Harbour, evening" correctly. csv.DictReader reads the header row and gives one dictionary per data row, with header names as keys.

CSV fields generally arrive as strings. Convert a numeric field with int or float according to its contract before calculating. float accepts fractional numbers such as "2.5". The example displays a label and converted amount; it does not implement the chapter's total calculation. Blank and malformed rows need an explicit policy in your local project.
plain.code:
import csv
import io
text = 'label,hours\n"Harbour, evening",2.5\nGarden,1\n'
stream = io.StringIO(text)
reader = csv.DictReader(stream)
for row in reader:
    hours = float(row["hours"])
    print(row["label"], hours)
walk: DictReader consumes label,hours as the header, not as a data row.
The quoted comma belongs inside one label.
row["hours"] is text; float converts it before arithmetic could use it.
plain.check: Which dictionary keys does the header create? Why would split(",") break the first data row?

plain.title: Write CSV using a writer, not manual commas
plain.text:
csv.writer(stream) writes sequences of fields. writer.writerow(fields) writes one row and applies CSV quoting rules. csv.DictWriter(stream, fieldnames=[...]) instead writes dictionaries using the named column order; writeheader() writes the header once, and writerow(mapping) writes a record.

Use io.StringIO() with no initial text to collect output in memory. getvalue() returns everything written there as a string. Writers use their own line endings; lineterminator="\n" chooses one newline for this deterministic illustration. For real files, open with newline="" so the CSV library handles line boundaries. Then read the written text back with DictReader as a round-trip test: a comma-containing label must remain a single field.
plain.code:
import csv
import io
output = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.DictWriter(output, fieldnames=["label", "hours"], lineterminator="\n")
writer.writeheader()
writer.writerow({"label": "Harbour, evening", "hours": 2.5})
print(output.getvalue(), end="")
plain.check: Which method writes the header, and what determines the column order?

plain.title: Paths describe names separately from file contents
plain.text:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath imports a path class that interprets POSIX-style names without touching the disk. Construct it from a string. .name is its final filename, .suffix is its last extension including the dot, and .stem is the name without that last extension. These are attributes, so they are read without parentheses. Methods such as .lower() are called with parentheses.

Path is a related class for the current operating system and can perform real file operations. PurePosixPath is useful when an exercise explicitly supplies POSIX-style paths even on Windows. A suffix identifies a name convention, not proof that a file contains valid JSON or CSV. A filename without an extension has an empty suffix.
plain.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
path = PurePosixPath("records/June.CSV")
print(path.name)
print(path.stem)
print(path.suffix.lower())
print(PurePosixPath("records/README").suffix == "")
plain.check: Why use a path parser instead of assuming every name contains exactly one dot?

plain.title: Open a local file with an explicit mode
plain.text:
open(path, mode, encoding="utf-8") creates a file handle: an object for reading or writing. Mode "r" reads an existing file and fails if it is absent. Mode "w" creates a file or replaces existing content, so use a disposable practice folder. Mode "a" appends. encoding chooses how stored bytes represent text; use UTF-8 consistently.

with open(...) as handle: starts a context manager. The indented block uses handle, and Python closes it automatically when leaving the block, even on an exception. handle.read() returns all remaining text. handle.write(text) writes text. For CSV use newline="" on open and let csv handle quoting and row endings. Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory, not automatically from the source file's directory. Check the terminal folder when a file cannot be found.

The following is a local file recipe; create a disposable practice folder first and run it there. It writes note.txt and replaces that file if it already exists. The expected displayed line is Practice file. Browser worker files are temporary and separate from your local disk, so keep persistent lab files local.
plain.code:
with open("note.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    handle.write("Practice file\n")

with open("note.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    text = handle.read()
print(text, end="")
plain.check: Which mode can overwrite a file, and where does the relative filename point?

plain.title: Read JSON files and validate their shape
plain.text:
After opening a text file, json.load(handle) parses it directly. json.dump(value, handle) serializes into a writable handle. The string variants loads and dumps remain useful for browser practice and unit tests. Catch json.JSONDecodeError for invalid JSON syntax only when your application promises to handle it; a missing key later is a different problem.

Use isinstance(records, list) to verify a list shape and isinstance(row, dict) to verify each record. Check required keys with in and verify numeric fields before processing. A syntactically valid JSON string could represent a single number, null, or an unrelated object. Keep the project's documented invalid-data policy consistent: reject clearly, do not silently report misleading totals.

A test fixture should be small enough to total manually. Include repeated grouping keys, empty data, and punctuation in labels. Snapshot the records before calling a supposedly pure processor. Writing a report should not rewrite the input records.
plain.check: If json.loads returns a dictionary when your project expects a list, has JSON parsing failed or has application validation failed?

plain.title: Understand the generator in the worked example
plain.text:
A generator expression supplies one value at a time. In (row["hours"] for row in records), the for clause selects each row, and the expression at the left extracts its hours. sum(...) consumes those numbers. It is an alternative to initializing a total and adding each extracted value inside a loop.

The parentheses belong to the generator expression; they do not create a tuple of all results. When a generator is the only function argument, Python lets its parentheses share the call's parentheses. This saves an intermediate list but is not a requirement. The explicit loop is easier to trace while learning. Both require correctly shaped records and numeric values; syntax cannot replace validation.
plain.code:
records = [{"hours": 2}, {"hours": 3}]
total = 0
for row in records:
    total += row["hours"]
print(total)
print(sum(row["hours"] for row in records))
plain.check: Write the equivalent loop before using a generator in your own project.

plain.title: Connect the report pipeline without coupling its pieces
plain.text:
The lab combines input, calculation, and output, but those jobs need not live in one function. Read the fixture in main.py, pass ordinary records to your core, choose a deterministic display order, and write CSV with the library writer. Use the test suite to check calculations without files, plus a small integration check that reads your written CSV back.

Document how to choose a different input fixture without editing source code: for example a command-line filename, a prompt, or a clearly documented configuration file. Chapter 13 teaches a full argument parser; you do not need that machinery yet. Record input shape, invalid-data policy, output columns, manually computed totals, exact run commands, and an example output file. Do not confuse an in-memory return value with a file that actually exists.
plain.check: Can someone run your project on another fixture by following the README alone?

sections.title: Separate plan from action
sections.text: A file automation tool should first calculate a list of proposed operations. A preview shows source and destination so the user can inspect the plan. The execution layer receives an approved plan; it should not invent additional changes. In this course, start with a folder of disposable sample files and preserve the originals.

sections.title: Collisions are more than duplicate input
sections.text: Two differently spelled files can normalize to the same target. A target might also already exist without appearing in the plan. Case sensitivity differs between filesystems, so a rename that looks safe on one machine may collide on another. Your lab should state its target-platform assumptions and reject a conflicting plan before applying any part of it.

sections.title: Idempotence and reruns
sections.text: An idempotent transformation has the same result after applying it twice. Stripping and lowercasing a tag is often idempotent. A tool that appends a timestamp every run is not. Test reruns explicitly: a second normalization pass should produce no extra changes. Idempotence is a useful property, not a substitute for testing all side effects.

sections.title: A helpful audit
sections.text: An audit counts intended changes and conflict groups, not just raw rows. Keep counts and reasons so someone can understand why execution is blocked. A command-line dry run should make the planned actions clear without writing. When you later add writes, log the operation outcome and make failure behavior explicit rather than assuming every rename succeeds.

What happens if the third operation fails after two succeed?

units.title: Automate with care
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–6, especially work with real data

plain.title: A preview is data, not an action
plain.text:
Automation changes many things quickly, so calculate a plan before performing any change. A plan is ordinary data describing proposed actions. A read-only preview prints those actions for review. It should not call rename, unlink, write_text, or open files in write mode. A string describing a filename is not itself a filesystem operation.

The example creates a list of proposed label changes, not a file-renaming implementation. Each [old, new] pair records both identities for a reviewer. A good pure planner can be called repeatedly in tests without side effects. The independent lab explicitly stops at a preview; executing the plan is outside its scope.
plain.code:
before = ["draft", "approved"]
after = ["review", "approved"]
plan = []
for old_label, new_label in zip(before, after):
    if old_label != new_label:
        plan.append([old_label, new_label])
print(plan)
plain.check: Which lines construct data, and which line displays it? Does any line access a file?

plain.title: Normalize according to a written rule
plain.text:
Normalization chooses one representation for equivalent inputs. Lowercasing, trimming outer whitespace, and replacing a particular character are separate policies. Do not silently add or collapse characters unless the specification requests it. Store the original and proposed value so a user can understand what would change.

A normalized value is not automatically a safe filename. Filesystems have platform-specific restrictions and case rules. This chapter's exercises use explicit string contracts; your lab must document its assumptions rather than claiming to support every operating system. A name that needs no change need not appear as an action in the plan, but it still matters when checking occupied destinations.
plain.code:
source = "  Review Note  "
trimmed = source.strip()
normalized = trimmed.lower()
print(repr(source))
print(repr(normalized))
print(source == normalized)
plain.check: What would change if repeated internal spaces were preserved rather than collapsed?

plain.title: A collision means different sources want one destination
plain.text:
A collision occurs when two proposed operations require the same target identity. It is not the same as repeated source data. Decide whether identities are case-sensitive for the target filesystem. On a case-insensitive system, NOTE.txt and note.txt may refer to the same destination.

Before designing code, write a tiny example with two distinct sources and one shared destination. A count of conflicting destination groups differs from a count of participating rows. If three sources want one target, that is one conflict group involving three rows. A report must say which quantity it means. Dictionaries can count requests and sets can record membership; choose the structure for the information the audit needs.
plain.output:
first -> shared
second -> shared
third -> other
plain.check: How many operations and how many distinct conflicting destination groups does this proposal contain?

plain.title: Unchanged names can still occupy a target
plain.text:
A plan that lists only changes is incomplete evidence about what destinations are available. A file that stays unchanged may already own a name another file wants. Keep the original directory listing as well as the proposed changes when checking the whole batch.

For example, if report.txt stays unchanged and a different source proposes report.txt, duplicate-target counting inside the change list alone will not reveal the occupied file. Also consider whether a chain or swap of names is permitted; this read-only lab can reject cases it does not support rather than pretending they are safe. Document the policy. Detect problems before any execution, not after changing half the folder.
plain.check: What information would be lost if the collision checker received only changed pairs and never saw unchanged names?

plain.title: Idempotence means the second application makes no new change
plain.text:
An operation is idempotent when applying it again has the same result as applying it once. Removing surrounding whitespace is idempotent: once trimmed, trimming again changes nothing. Appending another exclamation mark on every call is not.

Test the property explicitly with once = operation(input), twice = operation(once), and an equality comparison. This proves it for that test input, not for all possible inputs. A string transformation can be idempotent while a file-changing program still has unsafe side effects; test both calculation and action boundaries. For your read-only planner, a plan generated from already-normalized names should contain no changes.
plain.code:
text = "  Review  "
once = text.strip()
twice = once.strip()
print(repr(once))
print(once == twice)

first = "Review" + "!"
second = first + "!"
print(first == second)
plain.check: Why does adding a timestamp on every run usually violate idempotence?

plain.title: Read a directory without changing it
plain.text:
Path.iterdir() visits direct children of a directory; it does not recurse into subfolders. child.name reads a child's final name. child.is_file() asks whether it is a regular file. These operations inspect; they do not rename or write. Directory iteration order is not a sorting promise, so sort names explicitly when a preview requires deterministic order.

Create a disposable sample folder manually before trying this local recipe. Run it from that folder to print its direct child filenames. Path(".") means the current working directory. If the output shows the wrong folder, inspect the terminal's location before doing anything else. Keep this lab read-only even though pathlib also offers mutation methods.
plain.check: Does this recipe visit grandchildren inside subfolders? Where does the dot path point?

plain.title: Dry-run output should explain why a batch is blocked
plain.text:
A dry run calculates and displays intended work without applying it. A --dry-run flag is a command-line option by convention; it has no effect unless a program implements it. This chapter's entire local tool is a read-only preview, so it does not need an execution mode at all. A later chapter builds a command-line parser.

A useful audit reports what would change, which destinations conflict, how many conflict groups exist, and whether the batch is acceptable under its policy. Keep conflicts visible and return structured information from the core; printing belongs in main.py. Do not print success just because planning completed when the plan itself contains blocking conflicts.
plain.check: Could someone tell from your preview why a batch was rejected without reading your source code?

plain.title: Test the preview's promises
plain.text:
Test a clean case, a repeated target, an occupied unchanged target, empty input, and an already-normalized input. Include case-only differences under your documented platform assumptions. Use a snapshot to check that the planner does not mutate supplied names or pairs. Use a second normalization pass to test the rerun property.

For the local integration check, create disposable sample names, record the directory listing before the preview, run the tool, and compare the listing afterward. No file should be created, removed, or renamed by the preview. Keep real documents out of the sample folder. Record your plan output and audit meaning in the README, including unsupported chains, swaps, or platform behavior.

plain.title: Restate the contract before searching for a technique
plain.text:
In an interview-style task, first say what inputs exist, what output is required, and which edge cases matter. Ask about duplicates, empty input, absent results, and tie rules. A returned index is a position, not an item value. A first-match rule is different from any-match or last-match.

Work one small example by hand. Describe a straightforward correct approach before optimizing. If you cannot explain why it works, a short clever expression is not an improvement. This chapter asks you to choose remembered information and justify it; the examples teach the tools without giving the practice functions' implementations.
plain.check: For each exercise, can you write one sentence describing the returned value and the absent-result rule?

plain.title: Indexes, sentinels, and ordered scans
plain.text:
enumerate(values) supplies (index, value) pairs beginning at index zero by default. This distinguishes where something appears from what it contains. When an ordered scan may stop at a match, return or break can avoid examining later items, but they have different scope: return ends the function and break only ends the nearest loop.

A sentinel is a special value representing an outcome such as not found. -1, None, and [] are different conventions, and you must follow the current contract. Be careful with -1: indexing a list at -1 selects its last element, so a missing index must be checked before indexing. Empty data runs no loop body and still needs the specified absent result.
plain.code:
letters = ["c", "a", "c"]
for index, letter in enumerate(letters):
    print(index, letter)
missing = -1
print(missing == -1)
plain.check: Why could using a not-found index directly in values[index] silently return a real item?

plain.title: Define input size before stating Big-O
plain.text:
Complexity describes how work or extra storage grows as input grows. First define n, often the number of input items. O(1) means the amount does not grow with n; it does not mean exactly one instruction or zero time. O(n) means proportional growth: twice as many items roughly doubles the counted work. O(n²) describes growth proportional to the square: doubling n roughly quadruples it.

Big-O is a growth description, not a stopwatch prediction. Constants, hardware, and actual data still affect runtime. Distinguish best-case and worst-case work: an early match may stop a scan immediately, while an absent match requires inspecting every item. State which case you are discussing.
plain.code:
for n in [3, 6, 12]:
    single_scan = n
    all_pairs = n * n
    print(n, single_scan, all_pairs)
plain.check: When n doubles here, what happens to the single-scan count and the pair count?

plain.title: Count loop work and extra storage separately
plain.text:
A loop that visits n items once is O(n) if each body operation is O(1). Two full nested loops over those items perform n times n body executions, giving O(n²). Not every nested loop is quadratic: a fixed four-step inner loop still gives 4n, which is O(n). Always inspect the ranges, not just indentation.

Extra space counts storage your algorithm adds beyond the input. A few counters use O(1) extra space; a set holding up to n distinct values uses O(n). Depending on the discussion, output storage may be counted separately; say which convention you use. Sorting is generally O(n log n) work; it is not free merely because the call is one line.
plain.check: How many checks would the same loops make with six values? Which extra variables grow with input size?

plain.title: Membership cost depends on the collection
plain.text:
Testing value in a list may scan up to all n positions. Dictionary and set lookup are average O(1) under ordinary hash-table assumptions, though worst-case behavior can differ. Therefore a loop containing repeated list membership can do quadratic work, while a loop using a set for the same membership question is often average linear work.

The faster lookup usually costs extra storage. A set also discards order and duplicates, so it cannot replace a list when those details are required in the output. Keep ordered results in a list and auxiliary membership information elsewhere if the design needs both. Explain what each structure remembers rather than calling a set universally faster.
plain.output:
read True
delete False
write True
plain.check: Which information would you lose if you converted an event history to a set?

plain.title: A dictionary can remember where something first appeared
plain.text:
Choose keys to represent the question you need to ask quickly, and values to represent the answer you need to retain. A dictionary can remember a resource's first location, not just whether it has appeared. When first occurrence matters, do not overwrite an existing entry on every visit.

Below the key is a desk name and the value is its first row number. The repeated desk keeps its earlier row. This is a general state-design example, not the pair-finding exercise. In your own contract, ask whether you need first, latest, count, or all positions before choosing the update policy.
walk: east is absent at row 0, so store its row.
west is absent at row 1, so store its row.
east is present at row 2, so do not overwrite its first location.
plain.check: How would unconditional assignment change the meaning of the stored values?

plain.title: Distinct elements and distinct positions are different rules
plain.text:
A task involving two items may require two different input positions even when the two values are equal. Decide whether you are allowed to reuse an item. If a left-to-right scan asks about earlier data, the remembered collection should contain only information from before the current position at the moment you query it.

An invariant describes what that remembered state means before each iteration. For example, a registry may contain first locations from previously visited rows. Changing whether you query before or after updating can change the invariant. Trace at least two elements and a repeated-value case by hand; do not rely on a single successful example. Preserve the specified first-occurrence and first-found rules rather than returning any mathematically valid result.
plain.check: In your exercise's tie rule, does 'first' describe a value, a position, or a pair discovered by a particular scan order?

plain.title: Frequency, membership, and text normalization answer different questions
plain.text:
Membership says whether an item appears at least once; a frequency records how many times it appears. A set cannot distinguish two occurrences from three. A dictionary of counts can. Comparing collections therefore requires choosing the right representation for the contract.

Text normalization is also part of the contract. Ignoring literal spaces and letter case does not automatically mean removing punctuation, tabs, or every kind of whitespace. .replace(" ", "") removes literal spaces; .split() without arguments treats many whitespace characters specially and would encode a different rule. Dictionaries compare equal when they have the same key/value associations regardless of insertion order; lists compare both values and order.

Use tiny test pairs that differ only in multiplicity, punctuation, or whitespace to check that you have implemented the intended comparison policy. Do not change the input contract merely because a broader cleanup rule sounds helpful.
plain.check: Could a set-based comparison notice that one string contains a letter twice and the other contains it once?

plain.title: Explain, test, then optimize
plain.text:
For each independent problem, record a simple approach and what repeated work it does. Then describe one possible improvement and its trade-off before implementing it yourself. Define n, state time and additional space, and explain the remembered-state invariant. If the improvement depends on average hash lookup, say so.

Test normal, empty, absent, repeated, and boundary cases. State any first-match or tie rule with an example that distinguishes it from alternatives. Explain the solution aloud without reading code, then change one requirement and see whether your reasoning adapts. Rebuilding later from a blank file measures retention better than recognizing yesterday's answer. Add a timer only after the reasoning is reliable; speed is not the first goal.
plain.check: Can you explain why your data structure helps, rather than only naming its Big-O?

sections.title: Two pointers
sections.text: Two indices can inspect a sequence from opposite ends or maintain a window. For a palindrome, outer pairs already checked must match, and each step moves inward. The loop ends when pointers meet or cross. A simple drawing of left and right often reveals an off-by-one bug more quickly than repeated code edits.

sections.title: Stacks and nesting
sections.text: A stack removes the most recently added item first. A list with append and pop implements this behavior. Parenthesis validation pushes an opener and pops on a matching closer. A closer with an empty stack fails immediately; unmatched openers fail at the end. Extending to several bracket types requires checking the opener type, not just the count.

sections.title: Sliding windows
sections.text: A fixed-size window sum can move by subtracting the outgoing value and adding the incoming one. Initialize the best result from a real window, not 0, or all-negative data may be wrong. If the window size is invalid, return the contract’s chosen result before taking a slice. Later you will extend this to a variable-size window.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.text: Binary search requires an ordered domain. For an inclusive interval [left, right], search while left <= right. After inspecting mid, discard it and the impossible side using mid + 1 or mid - 1. Every unsuccessful step must shrink the interval. Returning an index after sorting an originally unsorted list would refer to a different order; do not quietly change the meaning of an index.

For ab, the first comparison fails immediately.
The already-checked outer region remains valid throughout the scan.

units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–8, especially your first interview toolkit

plain.title: Before choosing a pattern: describe the remaining work
plain.text:
An algorithm is a sequence of steps for solving a problem. A pattern is a useful shape of algorithm, not a function to memorize. This chapter introduces positions moving through data, a stack of unfinished work, a moving range, and a shrinking search interval. Learn them separately before choosing one.

An invariant is a statement that remains true as a loop runs. Write one sentence describing what your variables mean before the loop, after one iteration, and at the end. This gives you a reason for each update and a way to find a bug. You already know lists, indexes, while, and comparisons; those are enough to build these patterns.
plain.check: For a list of four items, name its first and last valid indexes. What index represents the last item of an empty list? Why must you avoid reading it?

plain.title: Two positions and a simultaneous swap
plain.text:
A pointer here is just an integer index; it is not a special Python type. One index can start at the left edge and another at the right. left < right means there is still a distinct pair to inspect. After handling that pair, left += 1 and right -= 1 move inward.

In a multiple assignment, Python evaluates the right-hand values before assigning either left-hand destination. That lets a, b = b, a swap values safely. list(text) creates a list of characters because strings themselves cannot be changed. The string method separator.join(parts) joins strings using that separator; an empty separator joins without spaces.
plain.code:
letters = list("lamp")
left = 0
right = len(letters) - 1
letters[left], letters[right] = letters[right], letters[left]
print(letters)
left += 1
right -= 1
print(left, right)
print("".join(letters))
walk: The right-hand side first reads the old last and first characters: p and l.
The assignments change only those two positions. The middle pair has not been handled yet.
This is one step of a reversal, not a completed algorithm. Draw the next pair yourself.
plain.check: What statement describes the positions outside left and right after a completed step?

plain.title: A stack: append puts on, pop takes off
plain.text:
A stack removes the most recently added item first: last in, first out. Python lists already provide the operations. stack.append(value) adds one value at the end; stack.pop() removes the last value AND returns it. Unlike append, pop has a useful returned value.

Calling pop on an empty list raises IndexError. Check whether a list is nonempty before popping. In a condition, [] is false and a nonempty list is true. The last item can also be inspected with stack[-1] without removing it, but that too needs a nonempty stack. An undo history is a natural stack: the newest unfinished action is the first one undone.
plain.code:
history = []
history.append("draw circle")
history.append("draw square")
print(history[-1])
if history:
    undone = history.pop()
    print("undo:", undone)
print(history)
plain.output:
draw square
undo: draw square
['draw circle']
plain.check: After two pushes and one pop, how many unfinished actions remain? What should code do before attempting another pop?

plain.title: Nesting requires order, not just equal counts
plain.text:
Nested structures must close in reverse opening order. A cupboard inside a room must be left before the room is left. A stack remembers this unfinished work. Merely counting openings and closings misses a closing symbol that appears before its opening.

Separate three situations when designing a nested checker: a new opening, a closing when something is waiting, and a closing when nothing is waiting. At the end, decide what leftover openings mean. If the task supports several symbol types, remember which opening type is waiting, not only how many. If the contract says to ignore other text, ordinary letters should leave the state unchanged. This explains the model; write your exercise's own decisions and tests yourself.
plain.check: Without coding, compare () and )( . They have equal counts. Why do they need different results?

plain.title: A window is a consecutive slice
plain.text:
A window is a consecutive part of a sequence. A fixed-size window keeps exactly k items. In values[start:stop], start is included and stop is excluded, so the length is stop - start when those indexes are valid. sum(values[0:3]) adds the first three values.

As a window moves one position right, exactly one item leaves and one arrives. You can update the previous total instead of summing the whole slice again. Keep the meaning of the endpoints explicit. First validate the requested size: zero, negative, or too large cannot describe a real window under this chapter's contract.
plain.code:
readings = [4, -2, 7, 1]
first = readings[0:2]
window_total = sum(first)
print(first, window_total)
outgoing = readings[0]
incoming = readings[2]
window_total = window_total - outgoing + incoming
print(readings[1:3], window_total)
walk: The first window contains indexes 0 and 1, totaling 2.
Moving right removes 4 and adds 7; -2 remains inside.
The new total is 2 - 4 + 7 = 5. The slice confirms which values it describes.
plain.check: If all window totals are negative, why is zero a misleading starting value for a best-so-far total?

plain.title: Best-so-far values need a real starting candidate
plain.text:
A running maximum remembers the greatest candidate seen so far. Starting at zero silently assumes that zero is a valid candidate or that some candidate cannot be smaller. That assumption fails for all-negative data. Once you have confirmed a nonempty set of candidates, initialize from its first actual candidate.

An empty result needs its own policy before this initialization. In the window exercise, None means the requested size is invalid; it is not the same as a total of zero. Keep 'no result exists' separate from 'the result exists and equals zero'.
plain.check: Trace best after every candidate. Which wrong result would initializing best = 0 produce?

plain.title: Binary search: ordered data lets you discard a half
plain.text:
Binary search needs data already sorted according to the comparison you use. In an inclusive interval, low and high are both candidate indexes. The middle index is (low + high) // 2; // keeps a whole-number index. Compare the middle value with the target, not the middle index with the target.

If the middle value is too small, sorted order proves everything at or left of it is too small. The next low is mid + 1. If it is too large, the next high is mid - 1. Excluding the already-checked middle guarantees progress. When low > high, no candidate remains. Do not sort the input silently: the task's indexes refer to its original supplied order.
plain.code:
shelf = [3, 6, 10, 14, 19, 25, 31]
wanted = 25
low = 0
high = len(shelf) - 1
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(mid, shelf[mid])
low = mid + 1  # 14 was too small
mid = (low + high) // 2
print(mid, shelf[mid])
walk: Initially candidate indexes are 0 through 6, inclusive.
Index 3 holds 14, so the second probe uses only indexes 4 through 6.
Index 5 holds 25. These are two probes, not a completed search function.
plain.check: Draw the intervals for a missing target. How does low > high represent an empty range?

plain.title: Practice and lab: test the invariant, not a memorized example
plain.text:
Use separate trace tables for each pattern. A two-pointer table needs left, right, compared items, and the next indexes. A stack table needs the current item and the unfinished stack. A window table needs its range and total. A binary-search table needs low, high, mid, and the discarded region.

Try empty and size-one inputs where allowed, missing targets, reversed nesting, and all-negative windows. The browser exercises have precise contracts; for example, text comparisons may deliberately be case-sensitive. Do not add cleaning rules that were never requested. For the independent lab, write each function's invariant in your README and change one requirement only after the original tests pass.
plain.check: Before coding, identify which practice tasks require sorted data and which must preserve the supplied order.

sections.title: Objects and methods
sections.text: A class defines a type; an instance is a particular object of that type. __init__ initializes each instance. self refers to the instance whose method is being called. Put per-player values on self so two players do not accidentally share state. A class-level mutable collection is shared and can create subtle bugs if you intended separate inventories.

sections.title: Functions or classes?
sections.text: Use a function for a straightforward transformation. A class helps when data and operations belong together over time, such as a wallet or game state. Do not create a class merely to hold unrelated utility functions. Composition lets one object use another for storage or formatting while keeping responsibilities distinct.

sections.title: Interfaces and invariants
sections.text: An interface is the behavior callers can rely on: arguments, results, errors, and side effects. A wallet may promise balance never becomes negative. Test that invariant after every transaction, especially rejected ones. Return values and exceptions should follow documented policies so callers do not have to inspect implementation details.

sections.title: Readable pipelines
sections.text: A small pipeline might normalize input, filter records, rank candidates, then format output. Give each step a name that describes its result. A list comprehension is appropriate when it remains readable; a short loop is often clearer when there are several conditions or validation steps. Prioritize code a teammate can inspect and change safely.

An unaffordable spend returns False without changing state.

units.title: Make code maintainable

plain.title: An object is state plus operations
plain.text:
A function is often enough for a calculation. A class is useful when individual things keep state across several operations. A class defines a type; calling the class creates an instance of that type. An attribute is a named value belonging to an object. A method is a function accessed through an object. The dot in lamp.brightness reads the brightness attribute of lamp, just as a dictionary lookup reads a value by a key.

Start with one object and one attribute. You do not need inheritance or a large architecture to use a class. The goal is to make ownership of changing values clear.
walk: class Lamp: introduces a new type; its indented block defines that type's behavior.
Lamp(4) creates an instance and runs __init__ with the new instance and brightness 4.
self.brightness stores 4 on that instance. desk is the caller's name for the instance.
plain.check: Which is the class, which is the instance, and which is the attribute?

plain.title: self means the particular object receiving the call
plain.text:
self is a conventional parameter name, not a separate global object. Python supplies it when a method is called through an instance. desk.adjust(2) passes desk as self and 2 as amount. That is why method definitions include self even though callers do not type it.

A parameter like amount is temporary input for one call. An attribute like self.brightness stays on the instance after that call returns. Two instances share method code but normally keep their own instance attributes. Put mutable collections inside __init__ when each instance needs its own collection; a list created directly in the class body is shared.
plain.check: In desk.adjust(2), what does self refer to? Why does hall remain at 9?

plain.title: Initialization and methods have different jobs
plain.text:
__init__ has two underscores on each side; it is a special name Python recognizes. It establishes starting state. Ordinary methods perform later operations. A method can return a result just like any function; changing an attribute and returning a value are separate decisions. A method with no return gives back None even if it changed state.

Classes can be defined at module level. They can also be defined inside a function: the indented class definition creates the local type when that function runs. One exercise asks for that local arrangement. Follow its requested wrapper and return value so the browser can call it; do not replace the required function with only a top-level class.
plain.check: Explain the difference between constructing Lamp(4), reading desk.brightness, and calling desk.adjust(2).

plain.title: Guard an invariant before changing state
plain.text:
An invariant is a promise that stays true after every accepted operation. If a container cannot hold more than its capacity, calculate the proposed state first, reject invalid changes, then store an accepted result. Rejection should leave the previous state intact.

State the input assumptions too. A check against going above capacity says nothing about negative additions unless the contract handles them. Tests must include rejected operations and confirm the state afterward. A successful return alone cannot prove a rejection left the object unchanged.
walk: The first proposal fits and becomes the new state.
The second proposal would be 7, beyond capacity 6.
The early return happens before assignment, so level remains 4.
plain.check: What assertion would detect a rejected operation that accidentally changed the level?

plain.title: Separate normalization, selection, and ordering
plain.text:
A pipeline is a sequence of small steps where each output becomes the next input. In a text search, decide which values should be normalized for comparison and which original values should be returned. For example, stripping whitespace and lowercasing a search term does not require replacing every original display string.

Substring membership uses small_text in larger_text. It is different from item membership in a list. sorted(strings) returns a new alphabetically ordered list and leaves the source list alone. An empty substring is contained in every string, so the specification must decide whether an empty query is allowed. Functions with one clear responsibility are easier to combine and test than one long function doing all stages.
plain.code:
labels = ["Studio", "Kitchen", "study"]
needle = "  STU ".strip().lower()
selected = []
for label in labels:
    if needle in label.lower():
        selected.append(label)
print(sorted(selected))
print(labels)
plain.check: Why do the results retain their original capitalization even though the comparison ignores case?

plain.title: Best-per-key data: missing is not always zero
plain.text:
A dictionary can store one best-so-far value for each distinct key. Before updating, distinguish 'this key has never appeared' from 'its current best is zero'. A default of zero would incorrectly beat legitimate negative measurements. Membership with key in mapping answers existence; lookup answers the stored value.

Decide whether you want a total, latest value, or maximum. Those are different update policies. In your lab, document the policy and test an inferior update after a superior one, a new key, and tied values. Keep storage separate from ranking so a change in presentation does not alter the recorded state.
plain.code:
coldest = {"north": -4}
print("south" in coldest)
print("north" in coldest, coldest["north"])
print(coldest.get("south", 0))
# The returned 0 is a fallback, not an actual south measurement.
plain.check: Why would treating a missing key as a real measurement of zero give a wrong best-so-far result?

plain.title: A ranking key is a tuple of priorities
plain.text:
Review the chapter-3 sorting rule: sorted receives a key function, and calls it for each item. A tuple compares its first field, then its second only when the first ties. Negating a numeric field changes its direction within an otherwise ascending key. A name used as a second field makes ties deterministic.

Define a named key function first so each operation is visible. The equivalent lambda is a short anonymous function: lambda item: expression. It has a parameter, a colon, and one returned expression. It is optional shorthand, not a different sorting algorithm. Do not negate text. Decide tie policies from the task rather than copying a key from another example.
plain.check: Write the three key tuples by hand. Why does A appear before B?

plain.title: Inheritance is a later option, not a requirement
plain.text:
The compact material mentions inheritance. class Child(Parent): defines a specialized type that can reuse the parent's methods. Overriding means defining a method with the same name in the child. super() gives access to the parent's implementation for the current instance.

Understand the call sequence before using it. This example changes the volume step of a speaker; it does not require reimplementing initialization. Inheritance is useful for a genuine 'is a kind of' relationship. An ordinary helper function or an object stored in an attribute is often simpler. You do not need inheritance for the main chapter exercises.
walk: QuietSpeaker inherits Speaker.__init__, so construction sets volume to zero.
The child method calls the parent method first: volume becomes 2.
Its own adjustment then makes volume 1.
plain.check: Which method runs when radio.turn_up() is called, and why?

plain.title: Special methods connect objects to Python syntax
plain.text:
Names such as __str__, __len__, and __eq__ are special methods. Python calls __str__ to obtain a readable string, __len__ for len(object), and __eq__ for equality. Return the kind of value the operation requires: text for __str__, a nonnegative integer for __len__, and an equality result for __eq__.

Without a custom equality policy, ordinary user-created objects usually compare by identity. If you implement equality, check the other object's type before reading its attributes. isinstance(value, Type) asks whether value is an instance of that type or a subtype. NotImplemented is a special response meaning this comparison method does not support the other type. These extension hooks are optional here; first make your state and method calls clear.

plain.title: Lab readiness: choose responsibilities before code
plain.text:
For your independent score service, write down who owns stored state, which operation updates it, which operation ranks it, and which layer prints or saves it. A class is optional unless the exercise explicitly requires one. A plain data transformation can remain a function.

If you use classes, create two instances in a test and change only one to prove their state is separate. Test ties, negative values where allowed, and rejected updates. When refactoring a long function, first capture its behavior in tests; change the structure while preserving its inputs, outputs, and documented side effects. A neat class diagram cannot replace those observable promises.
plain.check: Can a caller know whether an operation mutates state from your function name and documentation? If not, state that policy explicitly.

plain.title: A tool starts with an input/output promise
plain.text:
A complete tool connects several smaller operations. Before implementation, choose one ordinary input and its exact expected output. Name the accepted types, missing-value policy, duplicate policy, ordering, and failure behavior. 'Supports import' is a feature name; 'reads these records and produces this table' is a testable promise.

Work in stages: read external input, validate and normalize it, combine values, order results, format output. Keep the middle stages as ordinary functions returning ordinary Python values. File access and terminal printing belong at the outer boundary. You can then test decisions without having to create files or launch an interactive program for every case.
plain.check: Write a tiny example involving two records that refer to the same thing with different capitalization. What duplicate policy will your tool promise?

plain.title: Normalize once, without losing the display value
plain.text:
Normalization chooses a consistent representation for comparisons: stripping outer whitespace, making text lowercase, and converting numeric text deliberately. It should follow the specification, not silently invent a new identity rule. Two labels can normalize to the same key, so preserve a separate display label if the user needs original capitalization.

A chain such as text.strip().lower() first calls strip, then calls lower on the returned string. Both return new strings. int(text) converts numeric text and raises ValueError for invalid numeric text; only skip error handling when the contract guarantees conversion. Missing keys, None, and empty strings are different inputs and may need different policies.
plain.code:
raw = {"label": "  Morning Walk ", "steps": "120"}
display = raw["label"].strip()
key = display.lower()
steps = int(raw["steps"])
print(display)
print(key, steps)
print(raw["label"] == "  Morning Walk ")
plain.check: Which values are useful for display, and which for identity matching? Did the original record change?

plain.title: Unique cleaned values: loop first, comprehension second
plain.text:
To normalize a collection, first write the explicit loop: clean one item, reject an empty result, and add acceptable results to a set. set.add(value) keeps one instance of each unique value. Sets do not promise presentation order, so sort them when returning a list.

A set comprehension uses {expression for item in collection if condition}. Read it as: visit each item, keep those passing the condition, compute the expression, and collect unique results. It is a compact form of a loop, not required syntax for the task. A dictionary comprehension instead has a colon between a key and a value. Use the loop if repeating normalization in a short expression makes it less clear.
walk: The first blue is inserted; the second blue is already present and creates no duplicate.
The empty string is false, so it is not added.
Both implementations return the same sorted presentation; the loop makes each stage explicit.
plain.check: What distinguishes {} from set()? Why would returning a set directly make output order unreliable?

plain.title: Grouping combines records according to a policy
plain.text:
A group key says which records belong together. A dictionary can hold one accumulated value per key. The update policy might sum quantities, preserve the latest value, or keep the maximum; these policies are not interchangeable. Decide it before writing the update.

mapping.get(key, default) returns a value without inserting the default. An assignment is still needed to store an updated value. Trace the first occurrence separately from later occurrences: the first starts from the documented default, while later ones use the previous accumulated value. Do not mutate the original records unless the contract explicitly permits it.
plain.check: If this policy were 'largest delivery' rather than 'all boxes delivered', which conceptual step would change?

plain.title: CSV writing: let the library handle commas and quotes
plain.text:
CSV is text containing rows and fields. A field can itself contain a comma, quotation mark, or newline. Joining values with commas cannot represent all those cases correctly. csv.writer(file_like_object) creates a writer that quotes fields when necessary. writer.writerow(sequence) writes one row.

io.StringIO() is an in-memory text stream: it behaves like a small text file without touching disk. It starts empty. The writer adds text to it, and getvalue() retrieves the complete string. repr(text) displays escape sequences such as \r\n so you can inspect exact line endings. The output below shows the representation of the string; the returned CSV itself contains real line breaks.
plain.code:
import csv
import io
output = io.StringIO()
writer = csv.writer(output)
writer.writerow(["place", "visits"])
writer.writerow(["Park, east", 2])
text = output.getvalue()
print(repr(text))
walk: The first row supplies two headers.
The comma inside Park, east belongs to one field, so the writer surrounds that field with quotes.
The default writer line terminator is carriage return plus newline; tests may deliberately check those exact characters.
plain.check: Why would ','.join(...) misrepresent the place in this example?

plain.title: Dictionary comprehensions and stable exports
plain.text:
A dictionary comprehension produces key/value entries: {key_expression: value_expression for item in collection}. The colon separates each key from its value. Dictionary keys must be unique; if two generated entries have the same key, the later value replaces the earlier one. That makes a comprehension unsuitable for aggregation unless you have already resolved duplicates.

Iteration over a dictionary yields its keys. sorted(mapping) therefore gives sorted keys, not values or key/value pairs. To export a deterministic report, choose an ordering explicitly and look up each key's value. This preserves the mapping and separates aggregation from presentation.
plain.check: Why would a dictionary comprehension alone lose information if repeated records must have their quantities summed?

plain.title: A safe entry point: import without starting the program
plain.text:
Python executes a module's top-level statements when it is first imported. A test importing your functions should not immediately ask for input or overwrite an export. Put the run sequence in main(), then use a main guard.

__name__ is a module variable set by Python. It equals the string '__main__' when that file is launched directly; it is the module's import name when imported. The comparison if __name__ == '__main__': therefore runs main only in the direct-launch case. Defining functions and classes at import time is normal; performing unrelated external actions at import time makes reuse and testing difficult.
plain.check: Which lines define reusable behavior and which line starts the run? What should happen when a test imports headline?

plain.title: Tests describe behavior, not the current implementation
plain.text:
A useful assertion compares the observed result with an answer independently chosen from the specification. unittest discovers methods whose names start with test_ inside unittest.TestCase subclasses. self.assertEqual(actual, expected) reports a failure when the values differ. The self here is the test instance; it is unrelated to the object your program may be testing.

Use one small input that exposes a specific bug. A duplicate test should actually contain duplicates after normalization. A quoted-field test needs text requiring quoting. An empty test should check the chosen output shape, not just that nothing crashes. The example runs a self-contained test case directly; in your lab keep tests in test_core.py and run unittest discovery from that folder.
plain.check: What wrong implementation would this specific test catch? What empty-input test would you add?

plain.title: From functions to a local CLI, one command at a time
plain.text:
A CLI is a command-line interface: the terminal supplies arguments, the program performs a task, and output goes back to the terminal. A minimal first version can choose an action from a small list of argument strings before you study argparse in chapter 13. Keep the command choice outside your normalization and export functions.

sys.argv contains strings: index 0 is the launched script name, and sys.argv[1:] is the remaining argument list. 'list' and 'export' are strings your program chooses to interpret. Use small synthetic files in a separate lab folder. For CSV files opened locally, pass newline='' and encoding='utf-8'; the CSV module should control line endings. For JSON, use the parse/write techniques from chapter 6. Start with one working command, then add the others rather than writing every branch at once.
plain.code:
import sys
# A real CLI reads sys.argv[1:]. This fixed list demonstrates its shape.
arguments = ["list", "sample.json"]
command = arguments[0]
path_text = arguments[1]
print(command, path_text)
plain.check: What should happen if no command was supplied? Write that policy before indexing an argument list.

plain.title: Lab handoff: another person should reproduce your result
plain.text:
The independent lab asks you to build import, list, search, and CSV export using your own design. Before writing it, choose exact input formats, normalization and duplicate rules, and ordering. Reuse your tested functions rather than putting every calculation in the CLI. Include a tiny synthetic dataset with ordinary, duplicate, empty, and quoted-text examples.

Your README should contain setup commands, actual run commands, representative output, test commands, limitations, and help used. Test instructions from a clean folder or environment, since hidden dependencies on your current directory can make a correct function unusable as a tool. The supplied checkpoint tests cover one slice of the project; passing them does not prove the full import/export workflow.

plain.title: Independence means choosing steps, not guessing syntax
plain.text:
This chapter combines earlier ideas into new contracts. Reduced guidance should mean you decide the plan yourself; it should not mean a new language feature is hidden in an example. Review the needed building blocks here, then close the examples before solving the tasks. Looking up syntax is normal.

Start with one input and exact output, then write the steps in ordinary words. Separate validation, grouping, filtering, ranking, and presentation. For each step, name the data shape it receives and produces. A dictionary of totals is a different shape from a list of [name, total] pairs. Many bugs happen when one stage returns the wrong shape for the next.
plain.check: For your chosen project, write down the input shape and output shape without writing Python.

plain.title: Unpack pairs and include categories with zero activity
plain.text:
A record such as ['east', 'west'] is a two-item list. Writing first, second = record assigns its two items to separate names; it requires exactly two items. A loop can unpack each record in its header.

When several roles appear in a record, think about which roles must exist in your result. Some entities may need a zero entry even when they never receive an increment. 'Not in the mapping' and 'present with zero' convey different facts. Establish the population separately from deciding which values change. Then the accumulation policy can remain simple.
plain.code:
routes = [["pier", "park"], ["park", "hill"]]
places = set()
for origin, destination in routes:
    places.add(origin)
    places.add(destination)
print(sorted(places))
plain.check: Which place would be lost if you recorded only destinations? Which if you recorded only origins?

plain.title: Split once when the remainder may contain separators
plain.text:
str.split(separator, maxsplit) limits how many cuts are made. split('|', 1) cuts only at the first vertical bar, preserving any later bars inside the message. Without the limit, you may get more fields than expected. Before unpacking into two names, decide what to do when no separator exists.

.strip() removes outer whitespace, while .upper() returns uppercase text. Applying them to a category label does not imply you should change the message too. An allow-list is a collection of permitted values checked with membership. It is useful when unknown labels must be ignored or reported rather than silently accepted.
plain.code:
line = "  notice | open gate | slowly"
parts = line.split("|", 1)
label = parts[0].strip().upper()
message = parts[1].strip()
print(label)
print(message)
print(label in {"NOTICE", "ALERT"})
plain.check: What is returned by 'no separator'.split('|', 1)? Why would blindly reading parts[1] fail?

plain.title: Counting first, then scanning in original order
plain.text:
Some tasks need a global fact before deciding which original item qualifies. A counting pass can build how often each value occurs. A later scan can then inspect that count while preserving original input order. These are two passes, not a nested scan of the entire input for every item.

Two O(n) passes still take O(n) time: doubling the input roughly doubles the total work. The count mapping needs storage for distinct values. Do not confuse dictionary iteration order with an arbitrary ranking policy; when the answer is defined by original order, scan the original sequence explicitly. Decide how to represent 'nothing qualifies' before writing a return.
plain.check: How many dictionary lookups happen in the second pass? How would that compare with recounting the whole string for every character?

plain.title: Rank by several fields, then apply the limit
plain.text:
A multi-field tuple key expresses priority: compare the first component, use the second to break ties, then the third if needed. A negative numeric component sorts larger numeric values first while leaving later text components ascending. Use a named function when that makes the rule easier to explain.

Filtering, ranking, and limiting are separate operations and usually need that order. Taking the first few inputs before sorting can discard a better candidate. A slice [:limit] selects up to that many items from the sorted result. If negative limits are not meaningful, validate or clamp according to your contract rather than accidentally using Python's negative-slice meaning.
plain.check: Write the key tuples by hand. Which comparison is decided by space, and which by walking distance?

plain.title: Read compact syntax only after the steps are clear
plain.text:
A lambda is a one-expression function: lambda item: expression means receive item and return expression. Passing it with key= supplies a sorting rule. A list comprehension [expression for item in items] builds a new list from each result. These are abbreviations for a function and a loop you can already write explicitly.

If a compact line combines filtering, lookup, sorting, and formatting, expand it before debugging. Put intermediate results in well-named variables and print their values or inspect them in a debugger. Shorter source code does not imply a simpler explanation or faster algorithm.
plain.code:
weights = {"small": 2, "large": 7}
ordered = sorted(weights, key=lambda name: (-weights[name], name))
pairs = [[name, weights[name]] for name in ordered]
print(pairs)
walk: Iterating weights yields the names small and large.
The key function looks up each weight and reverses only that numeric priority.
The comprehension builds a new two-item list for each already-ordered name.
plain.check: Can you replace the lambda with a named function and the comprehension with a loop without changing the result?

plain.title: Test transfer with a changed requirement
plain.text:
A remembered answer is useful recall, but transfer means adapting the reasoning when a rule changes. After completing a task, choose one small variation: a different tie-break rule, a different permitted category, a different limit, or a different duplicate policy. Write a new expected result before changing code.

Include empty inputs, exact boundaries, duplicates, and ties where relevant. Preserve input when the contract says so: make a separate snapshot before calling your function, then compare afterward. Test assumptions too. For example, an input contract allowing negative values needs tests that would expose a default of zero. Record any help honestly and revisit the work later from a blank file.
plain.check: Name one test that distinguishes your intended ranking rule from a plausible but wrong rule.

plain.title: Independent lab: a small specification and evidence
plain.text:
Choose one of the chapter's project directions, then define a narrow useful version. Your written specification should state valid input, expected output, duplicate and tie behavior, invalid-input policy, and what is deliberately outside scope. A useful limitation is specific, such as supporting one documented file format rather than all spreadsheets.

Keep the implementation, tests, examples, loop trace or algorithm explanation, and run instructions together. State one tradeoff: for example, a clearer two-pass implementation may use more memory than a streaming approach. Do not label yourself ready or unready based on one exercise. Evidence that you can explain, debug, test, and modify the result is the point of this chapter.

sections.text: A terminal runs commands in a current directory. The Python executable launches your script; the interpreter selected in VS Code should be the same environment your terminal commands use. Create .venv with python -m venv .venv. On Windows you can invoke .venv\Scripts\python directly without activating; on macOS/Linux use .venv/bin/python. Install project dependencies through that interpreter using -m pip. Record dependencies for a clean setup rather than relying on packages installed elsewhere.

sections.title: Git’s three locations
sections.text: Your working tree contains editable files. git add places a snapshot into the staging area. git commit records the staged snapshot, not every subsequent edit. Use git status, git diff, and git diff --staged to inspect each location. Start a branch for a focused change, commit useful checkpoints, and review the diff before sharing. A remote is another repository; pushing a commit is distinct from creating it locally.

sections.title: Entry points and arguments
sections.text: Write main() to parse arguments, call a core function, present results, and return an exit code. if __name__ == "__main__": raises SystemExit(main()) only when launched as a script. argparse can provide --help, value conversion, defaults, and flags. Parse values once at the boundary and pass them as ordinary arguments. Environment variables also arrive as strings and need explicit validation.

Exclude .venv, generated outputs, and secrets in .gitignore. If you encounter a conflict, inspect both intended changes rather than deleting markers blindly.
