plain.title: The command boundary: terminal, interpreter, script, arguments
plain.text:
A terminal accepts commands. Its current directory decides how relative paths are resolved. cd changes that directory; dir on Windows or ls on macOS/Linux lists its contents. The interpreter is the Python executable that reads and runs your script. Everything after the script name is an argument supplied to that script.

In python report.py --copies 3, python is the interpreter, report.py is the file, and --copies plus 3 are argument strings. Do not type these commands into a .py file or at Python's >>> prompt. Save code in the editor, then run the command from the terminal in the folder containing the file. Paths containing spaces need quotes when supplied as a single command argument.
plain.check: In your terminal, identify the current directory and the Python executable you intend to use before running anything.

plain.title: An environment selects the interpreter and installed packages
plain.text:
A virtual environment is a project-specific Python installation area. It lets this project use its own packages rather than accidentally relying on packages installed for another project. Creating .venv does not move your code into it. Keep source files beside .venv, not inside it. The VS Code interpreter selection and your terminal command should use the same environment.

From the lab folder on Windows, create it with py -m venv .venv and run its interpreter as .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe. On macOS/Linux, create it with python3 -m venv .venv and use ./.venv/bin/python. You do not need to activate it when you use that explicit path. -m means run an installed Python module as a command. Use the environment's interpreter with -m pip when installing a dependency; the standard library needs no installation.
plain.check: What does the explicit interpreter path tell you that a bare pip command does not?

plain.title: argparse creates a parser object and declares options
plain.text:
argparse is Python's built-in command-line parsing module. ArgumentParser() creates a parser object. parser.add_argument(...) declares an accepted option; it does not yet read user input. A keyword such as default=2 names an argument to add_argument. type=int passes the int conversion function itself, so the parser can convert incoming text.

parse_args(list_of_strings) reads those strings and returns a Namespace object. Its attributes contain parsed values. In type(args.copies).__name__, type finds the value's type and __name__ reads that type's name as text, such as int. Passing a list makes examples and tests deterministic. In a real CLI, parse_args() with no explicit list reads the terminal arguments. The automatically provided --help explains declared options and exits. This chapter's browser task supplies valid arguments; a full CLI should also be tried with invalid input.
plain.code:
import argparse
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Choose print copies")
parser.add_argument("--copies", type=int, default=2)
args = parser.parse_args(["--copies", "3"])
print(args.copies, type(args.copies).__name__)
print(parser.parse_args([]).copies)
walk: The declaration says that --copies takes a value converted with int.
The text '3' becomes integer 3 on the returned Namespace.
An empty list supplies no override, so the default is used.
plain.check: Why is type=int written without parentheses? What would int('3') do immediately instead?

plain.title: Flags are present-or-absent choices
plain.text:
A flag such as --quiet does not need a following value. action='store_true' sets its result to True when present and leaves it False when absent. Hyphens in long option names become underscores in the Namespace attribute by default: --show-path is read as args.show_path.

Do not pass the text 'False' to a store_true flag: its presence already means true. A dry-run flag is a product promise, not magic provided by argparse. Your program must use its boolean value to print a proposed plan without applying changes. Keep plan calculation separate from the part that writes files so the flag can reliably suppress side effects.
plain.code:
import argparse
parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--show-path", action="store_true")
print(parser.parse_args([]).show_path)
print(parser.parse_args(["--show-path"]).show_path)
plain.check: Which part of your code must enforce 'preview only': argument parsing, planning, or applying changes?

plain.title: Git has a working tree, staging area, and history
plain.text:
Your working tree contains files you can edit. The staging area holds the exact snapshots selected for the next commit. A commit records those staged snapshots in local history. git add file.py updates the staged snapshot at that moment. If you edit the file afterward, the new edit is not automatically part of that snapshot.

Use git diff to compare working files with the staging area, and git diff --staged to compare the staging area with the previous commit. git status summarizes all three. A remote is another repository, often on GitHub. git push uploads commits; it does not create the local commit or include uncommitted edits. You already practiced the basic flow in earlier labs; this chapter explains why it works.
plain.check: If you stage a file and then edit it again, which version would git commit record? Which diff would show the later edit?

plain.title: Read the two status columns separately
plain.text:
git status --short represents each tracked file with two status columns. The first describes the staging area compared with the last commit; the second describes the working tree compared with staging. A space means no change in that column. MM can mean a staged modification plus a later unstaged modification in the same file. Count these independently.

The special prefix ?? means an untracked file; it is not two ordinary modification columns. A leading space matters, so do not strip the line before examining status positions. Your exercise receives simplified status strings with a fixed two-character prefix. It is a parser exercise, not an attempt to execute Git inside the browser.
plain.check: Which example represents both staged and unstaged work? Why would line.strip() destroy useful information?

plain.title: Branches, commits, and pull requests describe different steps
plain.text:
A branch is a named line of commits. Creating one lets you make a focused change without moving your main branch immediately. git switch -c name creates and switches to a branch; git switch name switches to an existing branch. A pull request is a review proposal on GitHub, comparing branch changes. Opening a pull request does not itself merge the changes.

For the local lab, make a small tested change in your own learning repository. Review the diff, commit only intended files, push the branch, and open a practice pull request in GitHub. Give it a description of the problem, resulting behavior, and checks. If a conflict appears, stop and inspect both intended changes rather than deleting unfamiliar markers or force-pushing. The first-time workspace guide remains the source for repository setup and sign-in.
plain.check: Explain which actions are local and which require communicating with GitHub.

plain.title: Configuration arrives as text, including booleans
plain.text:
An environment variable is a named setting provided to a process by its surroundings. os.environ is a mapping of those names to strings. .get(name, default) uses the default only when the key is missing; an invalid existing value should not silently become the default unless that is the documented policy.

The nonempty strings '0' and 'false' are both truthy, so bool(text) does not parse a boolean setting. Compare against allowed text values instead. Convert integer settings explicitly, catch the expected conversion error, then validate the allowed range. A test can pass an ordinary dictionary to your parsing function; this avoids changing the machine's real environment and makes tests reproducible.
plain.code:
settings = {"RETRIES": "0", "VERBOSE": "false"}
raw = settings.get("RETRIES", "2")
retries = int(raw)
verbose = settings.get("VERBOSE", "").lower() in ("1", "true")
print(retries, verbose)
print(bool(settings["VERBOSE"]))
plain.check: How should your function distinguish a missing setting, text that cannot convert, and a converted number outside the allowed range?

plain.title: Exit codes are a second output channel
plain.text:
A command prints messages for people and returns an exit code for other programs. Zero normally means success; nonzero means some failure category chosen by the tool. Your core function can return a result dictionary describing the code and message; a real command boundary translates that result into printing and process exit.

raise SystemExit(code) asks Python to end the process with that code. Put it under the main guard so importing the module does not exit the test process. In this example, main returns a code; merely calling main does not automatically exit. The browser exercises model exit decisions as data so they can be tested without closing the worker.
plain.code:
def main():
    print("preview complete")
    return 0

code = main()
print("returned code:", code)
# A local entry point can use raise SystemExit(main()).
plain.check: Why should a conflict take priority over a preview-success message when both conditions are present?

plain.title: Secrets and generated files belong outside version history
plain.text:
A .gitignore lists untracked paths Git should ignore, such as .venv/, __pycache__/, local output, and secret configuration files. It does not remove a file already tracked or erase a secret from earlier commits. If a real secret was committed, revoke or rotate it; deleting the current line is insufficient. Do not put real keys in a practice dataset or terminal transcript.

Before your lab commit, inspect git status, git diff, and git diff --staged. Test --help, defaults, explicit arguments, and the preview mode. Record the supported Python version and exact environment commands in the README so another person can reproduce your setup without packages installed elsewhere.
plain.check: Can your dry run be tested without changing real files? Can your configuration be tested without editing the actual environment?

plain.title: A test has arrange, act, and assert stages
plain.text:
Arrange creates a small controlled input. Act performs the operation. Assert compares what happened with the promised result. Keep the expected result independent of the implementation: copying its calculation into the test can reproduce the same bug. A useful test should distinguish correct behavior from at least one plausible wrong behavior.

Python's assert condition raises AssertionError when the condition is false. An optional message after a comma explains the failure. Assertions are useful in tests; they are not appropriate runtime validation for untrusted input because Python can disable them with optimization. Validation should use explicit conditions and documented returns or exceptions.
plain.code:
def twice_length(text):
    return len(text) * 2

# Arrange
text = "oak"
expected = 6
# Act
actual = twice_length(text)
# Assert
assert actual == expected, "wrong doubled length"
print("passed")
plain.check: What plausible bug does this test catch? Would it detect a problem that occurs only on an empty string?

plain.title: The test runner discovers methods, not individual assertions
plain.text:
unittest discovers TestCase methods whose names start with test_. One method may contain several assertions, so 'Ran 2 tests' means two methods ran, not necessarily two example inputs. Separate methods give clearer failure names. subTest labels individual cases inside a loop without treating each case as a discovered method.

assertEqual compares values, assertTrue checks a condition, and assertRaises checks an expected exception. Exception testing matters because a function can promise to reject bad input. Do not catch the exception inside the test unless you are checking it deliberately; otherwise an unintended exception can be hidden as a passing test.
plain.check: Why would a test that accepts any exception be weaker than one expecting TypeError?

plain.title: pytest uses ordinary test functions
plain.text:
pytest is a third-party test runner, not a built-in Python keyword or part of unittest. Files named test_*.py contain functions named test_*. Each function can use plain assert statements. Keep imports separate from running a program: the tested module's main guard should prevent input prompts or file writes during import.

In your local .venv on Windows, install it with .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install pytest, then run .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest -q. On macOS/Linux use ./.venv/bin/python in those commands. The existing lab's unittest tests continue to work; pytest can discover them too. Record the dependency for a clean environment. Browser teaching does not install pytest or contact a package server.
plain.check: What makes a function discoverable by pytest? Why should you invoke pip and pytest through the same environment's interpreter?

plain.title: pytest.raises and parametrize introduce a context and a decorator
plain.text:
pytest.raises(ExpectedError) is a context manager. Place the operation expected to fail inside its with block. The test fails if the operation does not raise the expected error. This is the same testing idea as unittest.assertRaises, expressed through pytest.

A decorator is an @ line immediately above a function that supplies information or changes how that function is used. @pytest.mark.parametrize lists example arguments so pytest runs the test once per supplied tuple. The first string names the test parameters; each tuple supplies their values in that order. These are local test-file illustrations, not commands to paste into the terminal.
plain.check: How many parameterized examples are supplied? Which operation is required to raise ValueError?

plain.title: An error object has a type and a message
plain.text:
raise stops normal execution and passes an exception to the caller. A caller can catch a specific exception with except ErrorType as error; the name error then refers to that exception object. str(error) obtains its message as text. Keep the type and text distinct: the type lets a caller choose which failure to handle, while the message explains the specific case.

A custom exception class can name a domain-specific problem. class MissingSeat(Exception): pass creates such a type by inheriting the standard Exception behavior. pass is an empty statement used where a block is required. Catch the narrowest expected error and let unrelated programming mistakes surface.
plain.check: Why could except Exception hide a misspelled variable or a different bug you did not intend to handle?

plain.title: A fake dependency is an ordinary callable you control
plain.text:
A dependency is something your function relies on: a clock, database, or network fetcher. Dependency injection means passing that dependency in rather than hiding it inside the function. Because functions are values, you can pass a function as an argument, then call the received parameter.

A fake is a simple substitute with predictable behavior. It should follow the same input/output interface as the real dependency. A list of calls can record interactions as well as returned values. This lets you prove that a cached value prevented a fetch, for example, rather than merely proving that the final answer happened to be right. Prefer this small explicit fake to complicated mocking of internal implementation details.
plain.code:
def show_time(clock):
    return f"time: {clock()}"

calls = []
def fake_clock():
    calls.append("clock")
    return "09:30"

print(show_time(fake_clock))
print(calls)
walk: fake_clock is passed without parentheses so show_time receives the function itself.
clock() inside show_time calls the supplied function.
The fake returns controlled text and records that it was called once.
plain.check: What would change if you passed fake_clock() instead of fake_clock?

plain.title: Existence, truthiness, and emptiness are different questions
plain.text:
A dictionary can contain a key whose value is 0, False, None, or an empty collection. key in mapping tests existence. mapping.get(key) retrieves a value, but testing that value's truthiness does not answer whether the key exists. Cache code often breaks when it confuses these questions.

Similarly, a task asking for a value other than None and the empty string is not asking for a truthy value. [] and 0 are false in conditions but may be allowed answers. is None checks the special absence object by identity; == '' checks an empty string. Use the exact exclusion policy in the contract rather than a broader if value shortcut.
plain.code:
stored = {"attempts": 0, "answer": None}
print("attempts" in stored, bool(stored["attempts"]))
print("answer" in stored, stored["answer"] is None)
print("missing" in stored, stored.get("missing") is None)
plain.output:
True False
True True
False True
plain.check: Why do the second and third lookups both produce None even though only one key exists?

plain.title: Type hints and docstrings document an interface
plain.text:
A type hint is a note to readers and analysis tools. In def label(text: str) -> str, : str documents the parameter and -> str documents the return. These annotations do not automatically reject incorrect runtime input. You still validate untrusted values when your contract requires it.

A docstring is the first string inside a function or class. Triple quotes let it span lines. Explain what the function accepts, returns, changes, and may raise. A useful docstring describes behavior rather than narrating every assignment. Type hints express shapes; the docstring explains policies such as whether empty input is allowed or the original collection is preserved. The function attribute __doc__ holds its docstring as text; printing frame.__doc__ shows the documentation, not the function's returned value.
plain.code:
def frame(text: str) -> str:
    """Return text inside brackets; do not change its content."""
    return f"[{text}]"

print(frame("note"))
print(frame.__doc__)
plain.output:
[note]
Return text inside brackets; do not change its content.
plain.check: Would annotating an argument as int automatically prevent a caller from passing a string?

plain.title: Debug by checking one hypothesis at a time
plain.text:
Start from a reproducible discrepancy: input, expected result, actual result. Reduce to the smallest case that still fails. State a hypothesis about the line responsible, then inspect values at that line. A temporary print is enough for a small loop. A debugger breakpoint pauses a local program so you can inspect variables before continuing.

In VS Code, set a breakpoint in the left margin and choose Run and Debug for the current Python file with the lab interpreter. 'Step over' runs a line, while 'step into' enters a called function. breakpoint() also opens Python's local debugger, but do not put it in browser exercises or unattended tests. After finding the issue, remove temporary debugging code and keep a regression test that failed before the correction.

plain.title: Lab: prove the failure and the correction separately
plain.text:
Your lab asks you to introduce or reproduce a small parser or cache bug, write a failing test, inspect the wrong decision, and make a focused correction. First watch the test fail for the intended reason. A syntax error or bad test import is not proof that it caught the logic bug. Then run the corrected test and the rest of the suite.

Use a fake dependency to check both the stored-value case and the absent-key case. Record call counts or arguments where relevant. Add public-function type hints and docstrings, then document the reproduction command, diagnosis, changed behavior, test results, and limitations. No test suite proves every possible behavior; explain which risk each example addresses.

sections.title: Patterns and parsing
sections.text: re.fullmatch checks an entire value against a pattern. Prefer ASCII ranges when your format requires ASCII digits or letters. A raw string such as r"[0-9]{4}" keeps backslashes for the regex engine. Regex is good for a defined text grammar; calendar validity and general HTML need appropriate parsers instead.

sections.title: Dates and money

A timestamp needs a timezone policy; use aware UTC values internally when measuring instants. Use integer cents or Decimal constructed from text for currency. Decide how to reject or round extra precision rather than inheriting binary-float artifacts.

units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–14, especially test and debug deliberately

plain.title: Parsed data is not necessarily valid data
plain.text:
JSON parsing proves that text follows JSON syntax. It does not prove that a record has the fields, types, or ranges your application needs. Validate in an order that makes each later operation safe: verify a required key or choose a missing policy, check its type, normalize text, then check the allowed value.

Calling .strip() on None raises an error before your intended validation can respond. Comparing an absent quantity with zero has the same problem. Use small independent validators so you can test each rejection rule. Keep the original source and a row position when reporting errors, so someone can repair the actual input rather than guessing which record failed.
plain.check: Why must the type check happen before normalization? What result does .get produce for a missing key?

plain.title: Python booleans are also a special kind of integer
plain.text:
isinstance(value, int) accepts ordinary integers and booleans because bool is a subclass of int. That relationship is useful in some Python arithmetic but can be surprising in record validation: a quantity of True often should not mean one item.

When the policy requires exactly an integer and excludes booleans, type(value) is int checks the exact type. is compares object identity; int here is Python's integer type object. Do not use exact-type checks everywhere automatically: choose them only when the input contract requires this distinction. A nonnegative range check must still happen after the type check.
plain.code:
print(isinstance(True, int))
print(type(True) is int)
print(type(3) is int)
print(True + 1)
plain.check: Which two checks would a policy need to accept zero but reject both negative integers and booleans?

plain.title: A regular expression describes a small text grammar
plain.text:
A regular expression, or regex, describes allowed patterns in text. Python's re module supplies the functions; the pattern itself is a string. Start with literal characters: BIN- in a pattern means those exact characters. [A-Z] means one ASCII uppercase letter, [0-9] one ASCII digit, and {2} means exactly two repetitions of the preceding part. The r before the quote creates a raw string: it keeps backslashes for the regex engine rather than having Python consume them first. This example has no backslash, but the convention prepares for patterns that do.

re.fullmatch(pattern, text) requires the entire input to match. It returns a match object on success and None on failure; bool(...) turns those into True and False. A prefix-only match could accept unwanted suffixes, so use fullmatch when validating a whole identifier. Do not strip or lowercase the input unless the format explicitly allows those changes.
plain.code:
import re
pattern = r"BIN-[0-9]{2}"
print(bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, "BIN-47")))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, "BIN-470")))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, "bin-47")))
walk: The literal prefix requires uppercase BIN followed by a hyphen.
[0-9]{2} requires two ASCII digits, not an arbitrary length.
fullmatch rejects the extra digit and the wrong-case prefix.
plain.check: Which input would distinguish fullmatch from checking only whether the start matches?

plain.title: Raw strings, captures, and replacement have separate meanings
plain.text:
A raw string has r before its opening quote. It keeps most backslashes as literal characters for the regex engine, instead of Python consuming them first. Regex \d matches Unicode decimal digits, which is broader than ASCII [0-9]. Regex \w includes Unicode word characters and underscore; it is not simply English letters. + means one or more repetitions.

Parentheses make a capture group. re.findall returns all matched strings, or captured pieces when the pattern has a capture. re.sub(pattern, replacement, text) returns a new string with matching regions replaced. Learn each operation separately; a pattern that validates one field need not parse a complete document, HTML, or a calendar date.
plain.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r"@([A-Za-z]+)", "ask @Mia or @Bo"))
print(re.sub(r"[0-9]+", "#", "batch 12, shelf 4"))
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+", "１２")))
plain.check: In the first pattern, why are the returned names missing the @ sign? What does + permit?

plain.title: Calendar dates need a calendar parser
plain.text:
A string cannot safely calculate month lengths or leap days. datetime.date represents a calendar date. date.fromisoformat(text) parses an ISO date; date(year, month, day) constructs one from integer components. Invalid calendar values raise ValueError. The chapter exercises guarantee their date inputs, but your local validator should document and handle rejected dates.

Subtracting two date objects returns a timedelta: a duration. Its .days attribute is a signed integer, so reversing the subtraction changes the sign. Adding timedelta(days=...) moves through the calendar correctly. Date objects do not include a time of day or timezone; they represent calendar dates rather than worldwide instants.
plain.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date.fromisoformat("2024-02-28")
finish = start + timedelta(days=2)
print(finish.isoformat())
print((finish - start).days)
print((start - finish).days)
plain.check: Why is subtracting parsed dates safer than subtracting their day-of-month text?

plain.title: Date presentation and timezone policies are explicit choices
plain.text:
isoformat() turns a date object back into stable year-month-day text. strftime(format) uses formatting directives: %Y is a four-digit year, %m a two-digit month, and %d a two-digit day. Month-name directives can depend on the machine's locale, so numeric ISO output is easier to reproduce.

A datetime includes a time of day. A timezone-aware datetime also identifies how that local time relates to UTC. A naive datetime lacks that timezone information. Do not compare or combine them without an explicit policy. The current date-only practice needs date, not a timestamp. If your project later records worldwide instants, use aware UTC values internally and convert for display rather than guessing a local timezone.
plain.code:
from datetime import date, datetime, timezone
day = date(2025, 1, 6)
print(day.strftime("%Y/%m/%d"))
instant = datetime(2025, 1, 6, 9, 30, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print(instant.isoformat())
plain.check: Does a birth date necessarily need a timezone? Does a timestamp for an online purchase need a timezone policy?

plain.title: Money needs a representation and a precision policy
plain.text:
Binary floating-point numbers cannot represent every decimal fraction exactly. The small difference in 0.1 + 0.2 matters when an application promises exact currency arithmetic. Store whole cents as integers, or use decimal.Decimal constructed directly from text. Constructing Decimal from an already-rounded float preserves that float's approximation instead of recovering the original decimal amount.

Decimal('1.20') represents a decimal quantity. Multiplying a validated amount by 100 converts currency units to cents. int(...) truncates rather than rounding, so that conversion is valid only after you have enforced a suitable precision policy. The browser task guarantees at most two fractional digits. For a local validator, decide whether extra digits are rejected or rounded, and document the chosen rounding rule.
plain.code:
from decimal import Decimal
print(0.1 + 0.2)
amount = Decimal("1.20") + Decimal("0.35")
print(amount)
print(int(amount * 100))
plain.check: Why is Decimal('1.20') safer than Decimal(1.20) when the user supplied decimal text?

plain.title: Sum Decimal values from a Decimal starting point
plain.text:
sum(collection, start) begins with start, then adds every item. The second argument is optional and defaults to integer zero. Passing Decimal('0') makes the intended numeric type explicit and gives an empty collection a Decimal result too. A generator expression can supply converted values one at a time: (conversion(item) for item in items). This is the same mapping idea as a list comprehension without constructing a list first.

You can also use a plain loop with a Decimal accumulator if that is clearer. Do not convert each decimal to float as an intermediate step. Validate each field first; malformed decimal text can raise decimal.InvalidOperation, a specific exception from the decimal module.
plain.code:
from decimal import Decimal
weights = ["0.75", "1.25"]
total = sum((Decimal(text) for text in weights), Decimal("0"))

sections.text: A relational table has named columns and rows. A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key relates it to another table. SELECT chooses columns and WHERE restricts input rows. units.title: Store and query data

plain.title: Tables, rows, columns, and a schema
plain.text:
A relational database stores structured tables. A row is one record; columns name its fields. A schema defines those tables and constraints. TEXT stores text, INTEGER stores whole numbers, and a primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key identifies a related row in another table; it is not a copy of that row's display name.

SQL is the language used to define, query, and change tables. A SQL statement is text interpreted by the database, not Python syntax. Python sends it through the sqlite3 library. Start by creating a tiny in-memory database: the special path ':memory:' means temporary data inside this connection, with nothing saved after it closes.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE shelves (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT)")
print("table ready")
connection.close()
plain.check: Which part of the example is Python and which part is SQL? Why does closing this database lose its data?

plain.title: A connection sends statements; a cursor holds results
plain.text:
sqlite3.connect(...) returns a connection object. connection.execute(statement, parameters) sends one statement and returns a cursor. For a SELECT query, the cursor lets you retrieve result rows. fetchall() returns a list of row tuples. fetchone() returns one row tuple, or None if no row remains. A query selecting one column still returns one-item tuples such as ('east',), not bare strings.

close() releases the connection. Use explicit cleanup after the example's operations. In a real program, a try/finally can close it even when an operation raises an error. A connection's with block controls transaction commit or rollback; it does not automatically close that connection. Those are separate responsibilities.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE shelves (label TEXT)")
connection.execute("INSERT INTO shelves VALUES (?)", ("east",))
cursor = connection.execute("SELECT label FROM shelves")
rows = cursor.fetchall()
print(rows)
print(rows[0][0])
connection.close()
plain.check: What are the types of rows, rows[0], and rows[0][0]?

plain.title: Bind values with placeholders, including the one-item tuple
plain.text:
The ? in SQL is a parameter placeholder. Pass values separately as a tuple or sequence: execute('... WHERE label = ?', (wanted,)). The comma in (wanted,) makes it a one-item tuple. (wanted) alone is only parentheses around a value, not a tuple.

Parameter binding keeps a quote inside a value from turning into SQL syntax. Never use an f-string or string concatenation to insert external values into SQL. Parameters stand for values, not table or column names; choose identifiers from trusted program code or an explicit allow-list. Binding is one key protection, alongside permissions, schema rules, and input policies; it is not a complete security system by itself.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE shelves (label TEXT)")
wanted = "O'Neil"
connection.execute("INSERT INTO shelves VALUES (?)", (wanted,))
row = connection.execute("SELECT label FROM shelves WHERE label = ?", (wanted,)).fetchone()
print(row)
connection.close()
plain.check: Why should a title containing SQL-looking text still be treated as one ordinary value?

plain.title: Insert several rows with executemany
plain.text:
executemany(statement, rows) repeats one parameterized statement for each supplied row. Each inner tuple or list supplies one set of parameter values in column order. The number of values must match the number of placeholders. This is more reliable than building a SQL string by joining external data.

Name columns in INSERT statements when clarity matters; column order then becomes explicit. A Python list of pairs is not already a database table: inserting transfers those values into the table's rows. Validate or choose a rejection policy before inserting real-world records, and use constraints for important database invariants too.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE parcels (label TEXT, mass INTEGER)")
rows = [("blue", 6), ("amber", 3), ("green", 8)]
connection.executemany("INSERT INTO parcels (label, mass) VALUES (?, ?)", rows)
print(connection.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM parcels").fetchone()[0])
connection.close()
plain.check: How many times is the INSERT statement applied, and which input shape supplies one execution?

plain.title: SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY answer different questions
plain.text:
SELECT chooses returned columns. FROM chooses the source table. WHERE filters rows according to a condition. ORDER BY requests an output order; without it, do not rely on the sequence rows happen to arrive in. ASC is ascending and is the default; DESC is descending. Multiple ORDER BY fields specify tie-break priorities.

Filtering in SQL does not change the table. The result is a new sequence of rows. If your Python contract requires a list of strings, explicitly extract each row's first item rather than returning the cursor or tuple rows unchanged. Keep the expected return shape visible at the boundary.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE parcels (label TEXT, mass INTEGER)")
connection.executemany("INSERT INTO parcels VALUES (?, ?)", [("blue", 6), ("amber", 3), ("green", 8)])
rows = connection.execute("SELECT label FROM parcels WHERE mass > ? ORDER BY label", (4,)).fetchall()
labels = []
for row in rows:
    labels.append(row[0])
print(labels)
connection.close()
plain.check: Which clause determines whether a row qualifies, and which determines its position in the result?

plain.title: GROUP BY produces one result per group
plain.text:
An aggregate combines several rows: SUM adds values, COUNT counts rows or non-NULL values, and MAX chooses a greatest value. GROUP BY separates input rows into groups before calculating an aggregate for each group. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after the aggregate has been calculated.

Every selected non-aggregate column should identify the group clearly. ORDER BY still matters after grouping. With no matching rows, COUNT returns zero, while SUM can return SQL NULL. NULL means missing or unknown; it is not zero. Decide whether a zero replacement is meaningful before using one.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE deliveries (district TEXT, boxes INTEGER)")
connection.executemany("INSERT INTO deliveries VALUES (?, ?)", [("east", 2), ("west", 1), ("east", 3)])
query = "SELECT district, SUM(boxes) FROM deliveries GROUP BY district HAVING SUM(boxes) >= ? ORDER BY district"
print(connection.execute(query, (2,)).fetchall())
connection.close()
plain.check: Why does east contribute one result row even though it has two input rows?

plain.title: JOIN connects records through keys
plain.text:
Suppose a table holds one row per location and another holds many visits. A JOIN combines matching rows using a relationship condition. SQL aliases are short temporary names: places AS p lets p.id mean the id column from places. ON describes which rows match, often a child foreign key equals a parent primary key.

An INNER JOIN includes only matching pairs. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, even when the right side has no match. The missing right-hand columns are NULL. One left row can appear several times if several child rows match. This multiplicity is expected; account for it before counting or summing.

The setup below uses executescript to run several fixed SQL statements separated by semicolons. Triple quotes let the Python string span lines. Keep this setup script trusted and fixed; bind external values with execute or executemany, not by adding them to the script text.
walk: Garden matches two visit rows, so it appears twice before aggregation.
Lake has no visit row; LEFT JOIN preserves it with a missing right-hand value.
sqlite3 translates SQL NULL to Python None.
plain.check: Which row would disappear under INNER JOIN? Why would COUNT(*) count the preserved lake row as one?

plain.title: COALESCE and COUNT handle missing children deliberately
plain.text:
COALESCE(expression, fallback) uses the first value that is not SQL NULL. It is not a general falsy-value check: a numeric zero remains zero. COUNT(child_id) ignores NULL values, whereas COUNT(*) counts every joined row. For a left-side row with no child, this distinction separates zero real children from one preserved placeholder row.

SQL uses IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test missingness. A comparison such as value = NULL does not act like a Python value is None check. WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true, so use the correct NULL test.

When a report promises to include entities with no activity, start from the full parent table and use a LEFT JOIN. Choose whether a missing aggregate should be zero or remain unknown. SQL NULL and Python None represent missingness at the boundary; the meaning must come from your application's policy.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
row = connection.execute("SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 0), COALESCE(0, 99), COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT 1)").fetchone()
print(row)
connection.close()
plain.check: Why would checking a value's truthiness in Python fail to model COALESCE accurately?

plain.title: Foreign-key constraints protect relationships
plain.text:
A foreign key says a child value must refer to an existing parent key. In the schema clause FOREIGN KEY(place_id) REFERENCES places(id), place_id is the child column and places.id is its allowed source. Both are SQL column names, not Python variables. Enabling enforcement matters: SQLite connections need PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON before related data is inserted.

An invalid relationship raises sqlite3.IntegrityError rather than quietly creating an orphan. This does not replace a useful validation message at the program boundary; it is a final consistency rule shared by every caller. The example demonstrates only the schema and one rejected relationship. Your lab must choose its own entities, fields, insertion functions, and error policy.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE places (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE visits (place_id INTEGER, FOREIGN KEY(place_id) REFERENCES places(id))")
try:
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO visits VALUES (?)", (9,))
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    print("missing parent")
    connection.rollback()
connection.close()
plain.check: Why is checking an existing parent's name in Python weaker than enforcing the relationship by its stable ID in the database?

plain.title: Transactions keep related changes together
plain.text:
A transaction is a group of database changes treated as one unit. commit() accepts the changes. rollback() undoes uncommitted changes. If two related inserts must succeed together, commit only after both succeed; on an expected database failure, roll back. A connection's with block can perform commit or rollback on exit, but the connection must still be closed separately.

Constraints such as UNIQUE and FOREIGN KEY protect data even when a caller makes a mistake. In SQLite, enable foreign-key enforcement on the connection with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON before starting related operations. A constraint failure raises a specific sqlite3 exception. Catch failures you have a plan to report rather than hiding every programming error.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE labels (name TEXT UNIQUE)")
connection.commit()
try:
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO labels VALUES (?)", ("blue",))
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO labels VALUES (?)", ("blue",))
    connection.commit()
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    connection.rollback()
    print("rolled back")
print(connection.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM labels").fetchone()[0])
connection.close()
walk: The schema exists before the demonstrated transaction begins.
The second insertion violates UNIQUE, so the first insertion must not remain half-applied.
rollback removes the first pending insertion; the final count proves neither remained.
plain.check: Why would committing immediately after the first insertion prevent the intended all-or-nothing result?

plain.title: File persistence, indexes, and migrations are separate concerns
plain.text:
A file path such as 'practice.sqlite3' creates or opens a persistent database rather than a ':memory:' database. It is relative to the process's current directory. Commit intended changes, close the connection, reopen the same path, and query again to prove persistence. Use only a disposable lab folder and synthetic data while learning.

An index is an additional lookup structure that can speed selected queries; it also consumes storage and costs work on writes. It does not replace correct WHERE or ORDER BY clauses. A migration changes an existing schema or stored representation and needs a plan for old data; recreating an empty table is not a migration. Your lab should test quoted input as data, zero-activity reports, transaction rollback, and close/reopen persistence. Keep schema, query, and return-shape decisions documented.

sections.title: The request/response boundary
sections.text: An HTTP request specifies a method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body. The response has a status, headers, and body. GET commonly retrieves a resource; POST commonly creates or processes one. A successful transport response does not prove the data has the schema you expect. Check the service’s contract before processing its JSON.

sections.title: A reliable local client
sections.text: Use a maintained client such as Requests locally. Set timeouts and handle connection and HTTP errors. Requests timeout behavior is not a whole-operation stopwatch; it bounds waiting for relevant network activity. Decode JSON only when appropriate and validate the result. Build query parameters through the library rather than concatenating a user string containing &, spaces, or ?.

sections.title: Pagination and retries
sections.text: An API may return a page and a next token. Bound the page count and detect a repeated token. Deduplicate through stable ids when the service can return overlaps. Retry only when the operation and error justify it, with a limit and backoff. A retryable read differs from a potentially duplicate write. Respect the service’s published rate-limit policy.

The browser challenges operate on such fixtures. The local lab adds the real HTTP adapter. This keeps correctness checks reproducible and avoids mistaking a service outage for your algorithm’s bug.

units.title: Talk to services
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–16, especially store and query data

plain.title: Start here: a client, a server, and a contract
plain.text:
An API is an interface through which one program asks another for data or an operation. A client sends the request; a server receives it and sends a response. HTTP is the message protocol used by many APIs. A request describes a method, address, headers, and sometimes a body. The method expresses the operation: GET usually reads, POST often creates or processes, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes.

A response contains an integer status code, headers, and a body. Headers are named metadata such as Content-Type; the body is the actual content. JSON is common, but an error page might be HTML or plain text. This chapter's browser exercises use supplied values instead of contacting the internet. That lets you test the rules without an account, outage, or changing service data.
plain.check: Which parts describe the operation, and which describe its result?

plain.title: Status codes: transport success is not valid application data
plain.text:
The status is a number with a documented meaning. 2xx means an HTTP success, 3xx a redirect or related redirection response, 4xx a client-side request or access issue, and 5xx a server-side failure. 404 means a resource was not found; 429 means requests are being limited. These categories describe the protocol result, not who deserves blame. A legitimate request can receive 404, and a 200 body can still have the wrong fields.

Python's chained comparison 200 <= status < 300 means both 200 <= status and status < 300. Follow the exercise contract exactly: a particular practice task may accept only 200 even though other 2xx statuses exist. Do not broaden the contract without deciding what every successful status's body means.
plain.check: Why might attempting to decode the body of a 204 response fail?

plain.title: Decode JSON only at the correct boundary
plain.text:
json.loads(text) decodes JSON text into a Python value. The plural-looking loads means load from a string; it does not perform a network request. Invalid JSON raises json.JSONDecodeError. Valid JSON can produce a dictionary, list, number, string, boolean, or None. Decoding alone does not establish that a title field exists.

Check the status before handling a success body. Then decode, check the outer type, and validate required fields before using them. Do not call .get on a list, or .strip on a number. The example separates decoding from checking the shape rather than hiding both steps inside one expression.
plain.code:
import json
text = '{"label": "Map room"}'
data = json.loads(text)
print(isinstance(data, dict))
label = data.get("label")
print(isinstance(label, str))
print(label.strip())
walk: loads creates a dictionary from the JSON string.
isinstance checks that dictionary methods are appropriate.
The label value is checked separately before string operations.
plain.check: Choose an invalid JSON string and a valid JSON list. How should their failures differ?

plain.title: Build query parameters with urlencode
plain.text:
A URL has a scheme such as https, a host such as example.com, a path such as /search, and optionally a query after ?. A query contains name/value pairs joined by &. A literal ampersand inside a search phrase must be encoded so it is not mistaken for a separator.

from urllib.parse import urlencode imports one standard-library helper. Give urlencode a dictionary and it returns the encoded query text. In that text, spaces commonly become + and a literal & becomes %26. Encoding preserves the structure; it does not make a URL trustworthy or provide authentication. The dictionary's insertion order determines the order of these parameters.
plain.code:
from urllib.parse import urlencode
parameters = {"author": "Lee & Kim", "edition": 2}
query = urlencode(parameters)
print(query)
print("https://example.com/books?" + query)
plain.check: Which ampersand separates parameters, and which represents part of an author's name?

plain.title: A fixture is controlled example data
plain.text:
A fixture is known data supplied to a test. It can represent a response without a real connection. A fake fetch function accepts the same kind of argument as the real fetch function but returns a fixture. Passing that function into other code is dependency injection: the caller chooses how the dependency works. No special framework is required.

Keep the transformation separate from the request library. You can then simulate a success, missing resource, invalid schema, or failure on the second request. A test should assert the visible result, not merely that the fake was called. Reset mutable fixtures between tests or copy records before changing them.
walk: fixture_lookup without parentheses passes the function itself.
fetcher(path) calls whichever fetch function was supplied.
The example performs no HTTP operation.
plain.check: How would you supply a 503 fixture without changing show_status?

plain.title: Pagination: continue only while progress is possible
plain.text:
Pagination divides a large result into pages. An API may return items plus a next token: an opaque value identifying the next page. Opaque means use the token as documented, rather than guessing its internal structure. None often means there is no next page, but check the service contract.

A client needs several independent stopping rules: no next token, a repeated token, a page limit, or a failed request. Track visited tokens outside the loop. A set's .add(token) remembers the token, and token in visited tests membership. Seeing the same token twice indicates lack of progress; blindly requesting it forever would be a bug. The exercise containing a list of pages focuses on processing supplied pages; the local client adds actual fetching.
plain.code:
tokens = ["page-a", "page-b", "page-b"]
visited = set()
for token in tokens:
    if token in visited:
        print("stopped: repeated token")
        break
    visited.add(token)
    print("visit", token)
plain.output:
visit page-a
visit page-b
stopped: repeated token
plain.check: What second limit would stop a server that generates endless different tokens?

plain.title: Nested loops and stable identifiers
plain.text:
Pages are often a list of lists. The outer loop selects one page; the inner loop selects a record from that page. An id is a stable identifier, not a list index: the record can move between pages while retaining its identity. Decide explicitly whether the first or last occurrence wins.

Remembering identifiers across the entire run prevents overlaps from appearing twice. A set created inside the outer loop forgets previous pages. Use a list for ordered output and a separate set for membership; a set alone cannot promise first-seen display order. This is a design pattern to apply independently to your practice contract.
walk: enumerate supplies a page number and one page list.
The inner loop finishes all titles on page 1 before page 2 begins.
plain.check: Where must a remembered-id collection live if duplicates can cross page boundaries?

plain.title: Retry budgets and exponential backoff
plain.text:
An attempt is one request. A retry is an additional attempt after a failure. A maximum of three attempts allows at most two waits before retries. Backoff means waiting before trying again; exponential backoff multiplies the wait each time. ** is Python's exponent operator, so 2 ** 0 is 1, 2 ** 1 is 2, and 2 ** 2 is 4.

An offline exercise calculates delays and does not actually sleep. Only record a delay when another attempt will occur. A retry policy should decide which failures are temporary and whether repeating the operation is safe. A GET read is different from creating a payment: a response can be lost after the server already completed the write. A fixed limit is necessary even for retryable failures.
plain.code:
waits = []
for retry_number in range(3):
    waits.append(2 ** retry_number)
print(waits)
print("three waits permit four total attempts")
plain.output:
[1, 2, 4]
three waits permit four total attempts
plain.check: If the very first request succeeds, how many delays should you record?

plain.title: Local Requests adapter: response methods and exceptions
plain.text:
Requests is a third-party HTTP library, so install it into this chapter's environment rather than Forge's browser runtime. In an activated environment run python -m pip install requests, then record the installed version in your project's dependency file. On Windows you can replace python with .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe if the environment is not active; on macOS/Linux use ./.venv/bin/python.

For a request you choose from a service's documentation, requests.get(url, params=..., timeout=(3, 10)) encodes query parameters and sets connect/read timeouts in seconds. A read timeout limits waiting for network activity; it is not a total-operation deadline. response.status_code is an attribute. response.raise_for_status() raises for HTTP error statuses; response.json() decodes the body and may fail separately. Catch requests.exceptions.Timeout and requests.exceptions.ConnectionError when handling those expected failures. Do not catch every exception and call the result success. No live request is needed to complete the browser practice.
plain.code:
python -m pip install requests
python -m pip show requests
plain.check: Before a live request, identify the documented URL, required parameters, rate limit, and timeout policy.

plain.title: Configuration, secrets, and an honest failure result
plain.text:
The base URL is the shared address prefix, while a token is a credential. Keep both configurable; keep credentials out of committed source, screenshots, and logs. os.environ.get('SERVICE_TOKEN') reads a process environment variable or returns None if absent. Reading an environment variable does not create it. Use a synthetic fixture with no credential for the default demo.

Decide what a failed middle page means. You might return an explicit partial result with errors, or fail the operation without claiming completeness. Document that choice and test it. Do not silently return the first page as if every page succeeded. For the lab, write tests covering repeated tokens, overlapping ids, invalid data, and a timeout through a fake fetcher before connecting Requests.
plain.output:
fixture
Use fixture data; no credential required.
plain.check: What visible evidence would distinguish a complete result from a partial one?

sections.title: Functions and scope
sections.text: Parameters and local names belong to a function call. Defaults are created when a function is defined, so a default list may persist across calls. Use a None sentinel and construct fresh mutable state when needed. Keyword arguments improve clarity at call sites, and a docstring should describe meaning, errors, and side effects rather than merely repeat the function name.

sections.title: Organize responsibilities
sections.text: Keep parsing, domain rules, storage, and presentation distinct. Small modules can expose a few documented functions or classes. Importing a module should not automatically run the application. Composition lets a service use a repository object; avoid deep inheritance trees when a small explicit dependency is enough. Streaming a file line by line can reduce memory while still requiring state for any aggregate you maintain.

units.title: Design maintainable Python

plain.title: Local scope and keyword arguments
plain.text:
A function call receives its own parameters and local variables. A local assignment does not overwrite a caller's variable just because the names match. Mutating a supplied list is different: both caller and function may refer to the same object. Recall this distinction when refactoring.

Positional arguments match parameters by position. Keyword arguments name them explicitly, as width=4. Defaults allow callers to omit an argument. After using a keyword argument, do not place an ordinary positional argument after it. Clear keyword names make multi-option calls easier to understand, but the names become part of your public interface.
plain.code:
def frame(width, border="*"):
    return border * width

width = 7
print(frame(width=4, border="-"))
print(width)
plain.check: Which width belongs to the function call, and which belongs to its caller?

plain.title: Safe defaults: omitted input is not shared state
plain.text:
Python evaluates a default expression when it executes def, not every time the function is called. A default list therefore stays attached to the function and can retain mutations between calls. Use None to mean 'not provided', then create the fresh list inside the call. is None tests that exact sentinel; if not items would also match a supplied empty list.

Decide whether your helper should mutate a supplied collection. Returning old_items + [item] constructs a new list; old_items.append(item) changes the existing one and returns None. Neither choice is automatically correct: document the intended contract and test two calls with no argument as well as a call supplying an existing list.
plain.check: Why does creating a list inside the function avoid a hidden connection between calls?

plain.title: Docstrings and type annotations are different tools
plain.text:
A docstring is the first string inside a function or class. Describe inputs, return meaning, possible errors, and mutation. Triple quotes allow a string to span lines. Type annotations such as text: str and -> int document expected types for readers and checking tools. Python does not automatically reject a wrong argument merely because a function has an annotation.

list[str] means a list whose elements are expected to be strings. int | None means an integer or None. A colon inside a parameter list introduces an annotation; a colon ending the def line starts its body. These uses have different roles. Run a type checker separately if your project chooses one, and still validate untrusted runtime input.
plain.output:
4
Return the character count without changing the input.
plain.check: Would annotations alone stop somebody passing an integer to this function?

plain.title: Fresh instances and composition
plain.text:
An instance is one object made from a class. Values assigned to self inside __init__ belong to that instance. A mutable class attribute would instead be shared through the class unless overridden; that can accidentally connect unrelated objects. Use independent instances for independent state.

Composition means an object uses another object to do a job. For example, a notifier can use a recorder supplied by its caller. The notifier need not inherit from the recorder or know whether it records in memory or a file. This makes it possible to test with an in-memory substitute. Agree on the small method interface first.
walk: MemoryRecorder creates its own messages list.
Notifier stores a reference to the supplied recorder.
announce calls that dependency's save method.
plain.check: What method would a file-backed recorder need to support for this notifier?

plain.title: Modules and the import guard
plain.text:
A module is a .py file. Importing it executes its top-level statements, then makes defined names available. Put reusable rules in a module that does not start a CLI or network request merely because a test imports it.

Python sets __name__ to '__main__' when a file is the entry point, and usually to its module name when imported. The familiar if __name__ == '__main__': guard calls main only for direct execution. Double underscores here are part of the special name. Split modules by responsibility—parsing, rules, storage, output—when that helps somebody find and test behavior, rather than making a file for every function.
plain.check: Which statements in an imported file still run even when its main call is guarded?

plain.title: An iterator gives you one value at a time
plain.text:
An iterable is something a for loop can read, such as a list or range. iter(iterable) obtains an iterator that remembers progress. next(iterator) asks for one value. After the final value, another next normally raises StopIteration; next(iterator, fallback) instead returns a chosen fallback.

A list can provide a new iterator every time, but a particular iterator does not automatically rewind. This distinction matters when tests read a stream twice. Materializing with list(iterator) consumes all remaining values into a list and uses memory for them.
plain.code:
letters = iter(["a", "b"])
print(next(letters))
print(next(letters))
print(next(letters, "finished"))
print(list(letters))
plain.check: Why does the final list contain no letters?

plain.title: yield creates a generator, not a returned list
plain.text:
A function containing yield is a generator function. Calling it creates a generator object; its body starts when somebody requests a value. yield hands out a value and pauses, retaining local state. The next request resumes after that yield. return ends the generator.

A generator can avoid an intermediate list, but its consumer may still keep every result. A loop uses it lazily; list(generator) requests all values. A file line iterator follows the same consume-as-needed idea. Start with a simple trace rather than assuming that shorter code is faster.
plain.code:
def positions():
    for value in range(2, 7, 2):
        yield value

stream = positions()
print(next(stream))
print(list(stream))
print(list(stream))
walk: range(start, stop, step) produces 2, 4, 6; stop 7 is excluded.
next consumes only 2.
The first list consumes what remains; the second sees an exhausted generator.
plain.check: How would you obtain a fresh generator after exhausting this one?

plain.title: Slices and generator expressions
plain.text:
values[start:stop] creates a list slice from start up to but excluding stop. A stop beyond the list's length is allowed. range(0, length, step) generates starting positions separated by step; step must not be zero. Decide what an invalid size means before using it in range.

A generator expression resembles a list comprehension but uses parentheses: (value * 3 for value in values). It yields results as requested rather than building a list immediately. sum(expression) can consume these numeric values directly. This syntax is an optional shorthand; you can write an explicit loop first.
plain.code:
values = ["p", "q", "r", "s", "t"]
print(values[3:9])
print(list(range(0, len(values), 2)))
print(sum(number * 3 for number in [1, 2, 3]))
plain.check: Which operation creates a new list, and which operation requests values one by one?

plain.title: Configuration: distinguish presence from truthiness
plain.text:
Configuration precedence says which source wins when two sources supply the same setting. A dictionary's .update(other) copies other's keys into that dictionary and replaces existing values; it mutates its receiver and returns None. Make a copy first when the original must stay unchanged.

Test key membership when an explicitly supplied False, 0, or None has meaning. value or default is a truthiness fallback; it cannot distinguish an omitted key from a supplied false value. Python's {**mapping} syntax unpacks dictionary entries into a new dictionary, and later entries with the same key win. Read and test the longer .copy/.update version before using multiple ** expressions.
plain.code:
options = {"sound": True, "volume": 8}
local = options.copy()
local.update({"sound": False, "volume": 0})
print(local)
print(options)
print({**{"theme": "light"}, **{"theme": "dark"}})
plain.check: Why would local.get('volume') or 8 lose a valid setting?

plain.title: Function arguments can be collected and unpacked
plain.text:
Before reading decorators, learn the star syntax they often use. In def collect(*args, **kwargs), *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects keyword arguments into a dictionary. The names args and kwargs are conventions; the stars determine the behavior.

At a call site, the direction is reversed: function(*values) passes collection elements as positional arguments, and function(**options) passes dictionary entries as keyword arguments. Do not use this flexibility when a fixed signature would be clearer. A wrapper uses it when it needs to forward a function's arguments without changing them.
plain.code:
def describe(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)
    print(kwargs)

describe("map", 2, color="blue")

def rectangle(width, height):
    return width * height

print(rectangle(*[3, 4]))
print(rectangle(**{"width": 2, "height": 5}))
plain.check: Which star usage collects values, and which unpacks them?

plain.title: Decorators: wrap a function in small steps
plain.text:
A function is a value you can assign, pass, and return. A decorator accepts a function and returns a replacement callable. The wrapper can call the original before or after adding behavior. A nested function can remember names from its enclosing function; that remembered environment is called a closure.

Writing @decorate above a def applies the decorator when the function is defined. It is equivalent to name = decorate(name). First understand that explicit assignment. functools.wraps(original), used above a production wrapper, copies useful function metadata such as its name and docstring; it is not needed to understand the behavior in this small example.
walk: with_brackets receives the welcome function without calling it.
It returns wrapped, a new function that remembers original.
The final call uses the wrapper, which calls the remembered original.
plain.check: Where does the original greeting run, and where are brackets added?

plain.title: Dataclasses, properties, and validation
plain.text:
A dataclass is a class for named fields. @dataclass asks Python to generate methods including initialization, a useful text representation, and field-based equality. Field annotations state intended types; ordinary dataclasses do not enforce them at runtime. A default after = is used when the field is omitted. For a mutable dataclass field, use dataclasses.field(default_factory=list) rather than a shared list.

@property makes a method readable like an attribute: parcel.total instead of parcel.total(). Its value is recalculated when read, so it can reflect current fields. It does not automatically validate those fields. Decide whether a simple class, dictionary, or dataclass best explains your record; this is a tool, not a requirement for every function.
plain.check: Which decorator creates record methods, and which changes how total is accessed?

plain.title: Context managers and cleanup
plain.text:
A with statement uses a context manager to perform setup and cleanup. It calls __enter__ before the block and __exit__ as the block ends, including when an exception leaves the block. In with manager as value, value receives the result of __enter__. __exit__ receives information about an exception; returning False lets it propagate rather than suppressing it.

Cleanup behavior depends on the manager. A file manager closes its file; a SQLite connection context commits or rolls back a transaction and does not itself close the connection. Do not generalize one manager's behavior to every with block. Abrupt process termination can prevent Python cleanup from completing. You rarely need to implement these methods yourself; use an existing manager when appropriate.
plain.check: What would label contain if __enter__ returned None?

plain.title: Apply the chapter without overengineering
plain.text:
Refactoring changes structure while preserving the promised behavior. Before moving code, record existing CLI outputs and run regression tests. Then separate only responsibilities that make a concrete difference: argument parsing, core calculations, storage, and presentation. An injected dependency or settings record can help tests, but adding every technique in this chapter would make a small script harder to follow.

For the lab, keep the public command and output stable. Move one responsibility at a time, rerun tests, and compare actual output. Document configuration precedence and input mutation. Demonstrate streaming only where consuming one record at a time helps; a generator that is immediately converted to a list still stores all of those results.

sections.title: Recursion and traversal
sections.text: A recursive solution has a base case and a smaller subproblem. Trace one call chain and its returns. Python has a finite recursion depth, so deep input may require a stack-based version. A linked-list traversal follows next until None; reversing a chain requires preserving the next reference before overwriting it.

sections.title: Queues and graph search
sections.text: BFS uses a first-in, first-out queue and visits an unweighted graph by increasing path length. collections.deque supports efficient popleft. Mark a node seen when enqueuing it so cycles do not cause repeated work. With adjacency lists the usual traversal work is O(V + E), where V is visited vertices and E is examined edges. Weighted shortest routes need a different algorithm.

sections.title: Priority and pattern selection
sections.text: A heap makes the smallest priority available without fully sorting on every insertion. Include a sequence number to preserve a tie order. Sorting once may be simpler for a static batch; a heap becomes useful when work arrives dynamically. For interviews, learn to explain why a stack, queue, map, or heap fits the behavior, and practice unfamiliar variations.
