units.title: Broaden your problem-solving toolkit

plain.title: Recursion: smaller calls and returning answers
plain.text:
Recursion means a function calls itself. A base case handles an input without making another call; a recursive case reduces the problem toward the base case. Each call gets its own local variables and waits for the smaller call's result. Trace both the downward calls and the upward returns.

The example counts characters recursively to make the control flow visible. text[1:] is a slice omitting the first character. The empty string ends the calls. This is a teaching example, not an improvement over len: repeated string slicing costs extra time and memory. Python limits nesting depth, so correct recursion can still fail for sufficiently deep input; RecursionError is not proof that the base case is wrong.
walk: 'sun' waits for 1 + letter_depth('un').
'un' waits for 1 + letter_depth('n').
'n' waits for 1 + letter_depth('').
The empty string returns 0; pending calls then return 1, 2, and 3.
plain.check: What progress measure decreases on every recursive call?

plain.title: Nested data and type-based decisions
plain.text:
Nested data contains collections inside collections. Before recursing, decide which values are leaves and which values contain children. isinstance(value, list) asks whether the value is a list. A list might be empty; its loop simply runs zero times. Make the allowed leaf types explicit rather than assuming every non-list value is a valid number.

A stack is an alternative way to remember pending work. A recursive call stack stores that work implicitly; an explicit list stack stores it visibly. list.pop() removes and returns the final item. Do not modify the collection you are currently iterating over unless the algorithm deliberately accounts for it.
walk: pop takes the nested list first because it is last on the stack.
reversed visits its children backward so subsequent pops restore their left-to-right order.
The original 'cover' item remains pending until both children are processed.
plain.check: How does a stack's last-in-first-out behavior affect output order?

plain.title: Trees, graphs, vertices, and directed edges
plain.text:
A vertex, or node, is an item in a graph; an edge is a connection. In a directed graph, a connection from A to B does not automatically imply a connection from B to A. A dictionary can map each node to a list of outgoing neighbors; this is an adjacency list. graph.get(node, []) treats a missing key as having no outgoing neighbors.

A tree is a connected graph without cycles, with additional direction or root conventions depending on representation. Graphs in general can revisit a node through cycles or multiple routes. A traversal must therefore remember visited nodes. The number of edges along a route is a distance only when every edge has equal cost.
plain.code:
routes = {"hall": ["desk", "stairs"], "desk": ["hall"]}
print(routes["hall"])
print(routes.get("stairs", []))
print("hall" in routes["desk"])
plain.check: Which two dictionary entries form a cycle?

plain.title: deque: a queue that removes from the front
plain.text:
A queue processes the oldest waiting item first: first in, first out. collections.deque is a double-ended queue. deque([...]) constructs one, .append(value) adds on the right, and .popleft() removes and returns the leftmost item. Removing from an empty deque raises IndexError, so a while queue loop checks that items remain.

A list's pop(0) also removes the front but shifts later elements. deque.popleft is designed for efficient front removal. A queue item can be a tuple containing a node and its distance. node, distance = item unpacks that two-part tuple into two names; it does not make two queue removals.
plain.code:
from collections import deque
waiting = deque([("door", 0)])
waiting.append(("desk", 1))
while waiting:
    node, distance = waiting.popleft()
    print(node, distance)
plain.check: Which item would a stack remove first from the same two entries?

plain.title: Breadth-first traversal: process one distance level first
plain.text:
Breadth-first search, or BFS, uses a queue to explore nodes in increasing number of edges from the start. A node's unvisited neighbors join the back with distance one greater. Mark a neighbor visited when you enqueue it, so two parents cannot both queue it before it is processed.

Keep the queue and seen collection outside the loop. If the queue becomes empty, all reachable nodes have been processed. A goal absent from that reachable set is unreachable. For adjacency lists, the usual traversal cost is O(V + E): each reachable vertex is queued once and each outgoing edge is examined once. BFS does not solve weighted shortest-route problems in general.
walk: entry is seen before processing begins.
Both neighbors join behind the current entry at depth 1.
left's edge back to entry is skipped because entry is already seen.
plain.check: Why would marking only on removal allow duplicate waiting items?

plain.title: Route reconstruction needs a predecessor map
plain.text:
Finding a distance is different from returning the actual route. To reconstruct a route later, remember the predecessor that first discovered each node. A predecessor map stores child -> parent, with a sentinel such as None for the start. Follow these links backward from a found goal until the sentinel, then reverse the collected sequence.

The snippet shows only the stored relationship. You still need to design how your own search records it, what to return for an unreachable goal, and how start equal to goal behaves. In a grid, decide which moves are legal before translating cells into graph connections. Coordinate tuples can be dictionary keys because tuples of integers are hashable.
plain.code:
predecessor = {"gate": None, "bridge": "gate", "tower": "bridge"}
print(predecessor["tower"])
print(predecessor["bridge"])
print(predecessor["gate"])
plain.check: Which order would you encounter these places while following links backward?

plain.title: Linked nodes are references, not neighboring list positions
plain.text:
A singly linked node holds a value and a reference to the next node. None marks the end. A Python dictionary or a small Node class can represent one. next is a descriptive field name here, not a command that automatically traverses the chain. A loop must repeatedly assign its cursor to that next reference.

Two nodes can live anywhere in memory; their relationship comes from the stored reference. Reaching the third node requires following earlier links rather than indexing directly. For reversal, draw the chain and preserve the next reference before overwriting a link, or you can lose access to the rest. A cycle would prevent an ordinary until-None traversal from ending.
plain.check: Does assigning another name to first copy the chain? Why not?

plain.title: A Node class and the reversal drawing
plain.text:
The class form gives the same two fields attribute syntax: node.value and node.next. Each constructor call creates a fresh object. Class and dictionary nodes teach the same reference model; the practice contract specifies which representation it expects.

Before reversing three links, draw previous, current, and following. First save following = current.next; only then redirect current.next toward previous. Move the names forward after preserving the remainder. Apply this reasoning yourself in the lab rather than copying a memorized loop. Test an empty chain and a one-node chain too.
plain.code:
class Link:
    def __init__(self, value, next_link=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next_link

last = Link("b")
head = Link("a", last)
print(head.value, head.next.value)
print(last.next is None)
plain.check: Which reference must you save before changing a node's next field?

plain.title: Heaps: the smallest item is ready, not the whole list sorted
plain.text:
heapq provides min-heap operations on a normal list. heappush(heap, item) inserts while maintaining heap rules. heappop(heap) removes and returns the smallest item. Both change the list. The internal list is not a fully sorted display; only the heap property is promised. heap[0] is the smallest while the heap is nonempty.

Use repeated pops to obtain priority order. Adding or removing costs O(log n); reading the smallest costs O(1). Sorting a fixed batch once can be simpler, while a heap helps when work arrives dynamically and you repeatedly need the next priority.
plain.code:
import heapq
waiting = []
heapq.heappush(waiting, 6)
heapq.heappush(waiting, 2)
heapq.heappush(waiting, 4)
print(waiting[0])
print(heapq.heappop(waiting))
print(heapq.heappop(waiting))
plain.check: Why should a report not print the raw heap and call it sorted?

plain.title: Heap tuple keys and stable ties
plain.text:
Tuple comparison examines components from left to right. A heap entry (priority, sequence, payload) compares priority first, sequence next, and payload only if both earlier values tie. Give every arrival a unique increasing sequence number when ties should keep arrival order. This also avoids asking Python to compare arbitrary payload objects.

A name in the second position would instead break ties alphabetically. That might be valid for another contract, but it does not preserve arrival order. Choose the tie rule explicitly before choosing the entry shape. enumerate supplies a convenient unique sequence for a fixed input batch.
plain.code:
import heapq
heap = []
heapq.heappush(heap, (1, 0, "zebra"))
heapq.heappush(heap, (1, 1, "apple"))
print(heapq.heappop(heap))
print(heapq.heappop(heap))
plain.check: Why does zebra come before apple even though a sorts before z?

plain.title: Memoization is an optional extension with a contract
plain.text:
Memoization stores answers for inputs already computed. functools.lru_cache is a decorator that can do this for functions with hashable arguments. maxsize=None permits an unbounded cache. The function should return the same meaningful result for the same arguments and should not depend on changing hidden state.

Caching trades memory for avoided repeated computation; it does not make all recursion linear. Keep this separate from first learning recursion or BFS. Inspect the cache statistics to see whether inputs actually repeat. Do not cache a function whose intended behavior is to produce a fresh timestamp, perform a write, or read changing data without an invalidation plan.
plain.code:
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def badge_width(text):
    return len(text) + 2

print(badge_width("north"))
print(badge_width("north"))
print(badge_width.cache_info().hits)
plain.check: Which resources grow if you cache millions of distinct inputs without a limit?

units.title: Build a small backend
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–19, especially broaden your problem-solving toolkit

plain.title: A route is an HTTP boundary around ordinary code
plain.text:
A backend is a program listening for requests. Routing chooses a handler based on the HTTP method and URL path. The handler translates request data into domain inputs, calls your tested rules, and translates the result into a status and public response. A repository is the component that reads or writes stored records.

Keep these responsibilities separate. A browser practice function returning a dictionary with a status field models a decision; it is not itself an HTTP server. The lab introduces a real local framework. Start with synthetic data and localhost, then connect your tested SQLite repository after you can verify one tiny route.
plain.check: Which part should still be testable when the web server is not running?

plain.title: Type checks before normalization
plain.text:
Untrusted JSON may contain missing fields, None, booleans, or the wrong type. Read a field, check its type, then normalize. .strip removes outer whitespace from a string; calling it on None fails. A nonempty stripped string is different from a merely nonempty original string containing spaces.

Python treats bool as a subclass of int: isinstance(True, int) is True. When the contract allows ordinary integers but excludes booleans, type(value) is int is an explicit exact-type check. Perform range checks only after the type is known. A validation model and a domain rule may use different conversion policies; document whether numeric strings are coerced or rejected.
plain.output:
True True False
0 True True
'4' False False
None False False
plain.check: Why could a truthiness check accidentally reject zero while accepting True?

plain.title: Public fields and consistent errors
plain.text:
An allowlist names exactly the fields a client may receive or edit. Construct a fresh public dictionary from those fields instead of serializing a storage row wholesale. Deleting one known secret field is fragile because a future internal field may then leak.

Use a documented error shape and suitable HTTP status. 200 means ordinary success, 201 creation, 204 success without a response body, 401 missing or invalid authentication, 403 denied permission, 404 not found, 409 a conflict, and 422 a validation failure in common FastAPI responses. Do not use 500 as an intentional ordinary validation result. A tutorial's particular status policy is a contract to follow, not a universal rule for all APIs.
plain.check: What would happen to a new internal field if you returned stored directly?

plain.title: Offset, limit, and nonmutating sorting
plain.text:
An offset counts items to skip; a limit caps items to return. These are counts, not page numbers. A slice values[start:stop] excludes stop, so offset plus limit gives an end position. Sort consistently before selecting the slice, or pages can vary even when the dataset is unchanged.

sorted(values) returns a new list; values.sort() changes the original and returns None. A negative offset in Python indexing normally counts from the end, so a contract that clamps offsets to zero requires an explicit decision before slicing. A limit of zero should follow the endpoint contract, rather than accidentally selecting the full list.
plain.code:
labels = ["west", "east", "north", "south"]
ordered = sorted(labels)
print(ordered)
print(ordered[1:3])
print(labels)
plain.check: Which two items does an offset of 1 and limit of 2 select here?

plain.title: Partial updates: absent is different from False or null
plain.text:
A PATCH-style partial update changes only supplied fields. If a key is missing, leave that value alone. An explicit False is still a supplied value. JSON null becomes Python None and may mean clear a field only if your contract allows it. Use key in changes to test presence; changes.get(key) by itself loses this distinction.

Start from a copy when the original must be preserved, apply only editable fields, then validate the complete candidate before saving it. A shallow copy duplicates the outer dictionary; nested mutable values are still shared. When nested updates exist, choose and test a suitable copying or reconstruction policy.
plain.code:
change = {"enabled": False, "description": None}
print("enabled" in change, change["enabled"])
print("description" in change, change["description"] is None)
print("name" in change)
plain.check: Why would if change.get('enabled') skip a requested change?

plain.title: Authentication and authorization are separate
plain.text:
Authentication establishes an identity using a trusted mechanism. Authorization checks whether that authenticated identity can perform this action on this resource. A caller-provided owner id is not proof of identity. A hidden button is not access control: a client can send a request without using your interface.

The browser exercises teach permission rules using trusted supplied inputs. For the lab, a fake identity boundary makes route tests reproducible. Label it as practice-only. Do not present a hard-coded user or a header anybody can choose as production authentication. A real deployment should use maintained identity tooling and enforce permissions server-side for every relevant operation.
plain.check: Which value in your service comes from a verified identity boundary, and which values come from the caller's payload?

plain.title: Install and start one local FastAPI example
plain.text:
Run these commands in your activated week environment, not in a Python source file. fastapi[standard] requests FastAPI plus its standard development tools; quotes keep the brackets together in shells. httpx supports the test client shown later. Record tested dependency versions in your project rather than depending forever on whatever happens to be newest.

Next create a separate local file named demo_api.py using the following section. The final command starts a local development server and keeps the terminal occupied. Open http://127.0.0.1:8001/notice in a browser; http://127.0.0.1:8001/docs opens interactive API documentation. The command deliberately uses port 8001 so it can run beside Forge on port 8000. Stop the server with Ctrl+C. This is a local teaching example, not your game-library lab solution.
plain.code:
python -m pip install "fastapi[standard]" httpx
python -m pip show fastapi httpx
python -m uvicorn demo_api:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001
plain.check: What file and object does demo_api:app tell the server to load?

plain.title: Read the route decorator before running the server
plain.text:
Save this illustration in demo_api.py. FastAPI() creates the application object. @app.get('/notice') registers the following function for GET requests at /notice; this uses the decorator idea from chapter 18. The decorator is configuration, not a call that runs the handler immediately. A regular def is enough for this example; async programming is not required here.

Returning a dictionary allows the framework to serialize JSON and produce a response. Here code is a path parameter from the URL, and its int annotation asks FastAPI to parse and validate it. /notice/7 succeeds; /notice/not-a-number produces a validation response. The separate /notice route has no parameter. Compare this with an ordinary Python function annotation, which by itself does not validate calls.
walk: The app object holds route registrations.
{code} in the path captures a URL component.
FastAPI uses the annotation at the request boundary; ordinary direct calls remain Python calls.
plain.check: Which requests exercise a normal result and a validation failure?

plain.title: Request models and validation policy
plain.text:
A request model describes named fields in a JSON body. Pydantic's BaseModel is the base class used by FastAPI for this purpose. Field annotations describe types; Field adds constraints such as a minimum length or a nonnegative value. StrictBool and StrictInt can reject coercions when your contract requires exact JSON types.

For example, class MessageBody(BaseModel): followed by text: str defines a required string field. A default makes a field optional to supply. body.model_dump() creates a dictionary from a model; model_dump(exclude_unset=True) keeps only explicitly supplied fields for a partial update. Do not confuse omitted fields with fields supplied as False or None. The local lab requires you to design its own request/response fields and reuse tested domain rules; a model does not replace every business check.
plain.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, StrictInt

class MessageBody(BaseModel):
    text: str = Field(min_length=1)
    priority: StrictInt = Field(ge=0)

body = MessageBody(text="Hello", priority=0)
print(body.model_dump())
plain.check: Does a minimum string length of one reject a string containing only spaces? What additional rule is needed?

plain.title: Test a route without launching a live server
plain.text:
FastAPI's TestClient sends requests to your application in the test process. It exercises routing and validation without opening a public listening port. Import TestClient, pass the app, then call client.get or client.post. The result exposes status_code and .json(), matching concepts from HTTP clients. assert checks a condition and fails the test if it is false.

For the separate demo_api.py file above, save these assertions as a local test or try them in a separate script. These tests do not need network access. For your lab, add fixtures and a fresh temporary repository for each test; exercise invalid bodies, missing ids, denied operations, and successful cases. A fake user must be supplied through a deliberate test boundary, not trusted from arbitrary request data.
plain.code:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from demo_api import app

client = TestClient(app)
response = client.get("/notice/7")
assert response.status_code == 200
assert response.json() == {"code": 7}
assert client.get("/notice/not-a-number").status_code == 422
plain.check: Which of these assertions would catch accidentally removing the int annotation?

plain.title: Connect storage only after the boundary is understood
plain.text:
A repository hides storage details behind a small interface such as find, list, or save. A route should not need to know SQL formatting. Use parameterized SQL from chapter 16 inside the repository, and commit related changes together. Public response models should allowlist fields instead of returning internal objects wholesale.

To finish the lab, document methods, routes, body examples, statuses, pagination limits, and authorization assumptions. Run both core and route tests. Try the API locally through /docs or a documented client request and record its actual response. Do not deploy this practice service as a secure multi-user application merely because its local tests pass.
plain.check: Can you replace the persistent repository with a fresh in-memory test repository without changing the domain rule?

sections.title: Observability with a purpose
sections.text: A useful log explains an event, relevant counters, and context such as a run id. Use severity to distinguish ordinary progress from partial rejection or failure. Avoid logging entire payloads or credentials. A structured event dictionary can be tested before deciding how to format or send logs.

sections.title: Idempotent imports
sections.text: Stable ids and a documented upsert policy prevent reruns from duplicating data. A unique database constraint reinforces the rule. Decide whether a repeated id replaces, merges, or rejects the record. Test both repeats within one batch and re-importing the entire file. A partial failure must not leave a misleading success summary.

sections.title: File and write boundaries
sections.text: Accept only the filename forms your tool needs. A lexical allowlist helps reject traversal components, but a real write must still stay in a controlled directory and consider resolved paths and symlinks. Use temporary test directories. For important output files, consider writing a temporary file and replacing the destination after the full result is ready.

sections.title: Reconciliation and recovery
sections.text: A batch report should account for every input record. Separate invalid rows from extra valid duplicate ids. Keep original input and a rejection report for repair. Transactions can ensure related database changes are coherent, while a retry policy must avoid duplicating already-applied work. Demonstrate reruns and a forced failure rather than assuming recovery works.

units.title: Make automation dependable
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–20, especially build a small backend

plain.title: Dependable means reruns and failures are understandable
plain.text:
An unattended batch job must report what it did, keep data consistent, and behave predictably when run again. Idempotent means applying the same operation twice has the same intended final effect as once. It does not mean the program never writes logs or that every counter must be identical. Decide which data state is promised.

Separate validation, planning, application, and reporting. A dry run executes the planning stage and describes proposed changes without writing them. A successful exit should mean the documented success condition was met, not just that an exception was swallowed. A partial failure needs a visible outcome and a recovery plan.
plain.check: For your importer, does a duplicate id replace, merge, skip, or reject? Write the policy before implementing it.

plain.title: Structured events before log formatting
plain.text:
A structured event is a dictionary with stable field names: an event name, relevant counts, and a severity. INFO describes ordinary progress, WARNING highlights an unexpected or partially rejected condition, and ERROR describes a failure. Choose severity according to a documented policy, rather than printing every event as an error.

Keep event construction testable without the logging system. An event should include enough context to investigate, such as a run identifier or row number, while excluding secrets and unnecessary personal data. A log message is evidence about an operation; it is not proof that every input was accounted for.
plain.check: Which fields would help compare two runs without logging their entire input payloads?

plain.title: logging methods and formatting placeholders
plain.text:
The standard logging module routes messages according to severity and configuration. logging.getLogger(name) obtains a named logger. .info, .warning, and .error emit at different levels. basicConfig commonly sets a minimum level and a display format at the application's entry point; libraries should generally leave overall configuration to their caller.

logger.warning('row %d: %r', index, value) supplies a format string and separate arguments. %d formats a number; %r uses repr, which shows quotes and escapes helpful for debugging. %(levelname)s and %(message)s in a logging configuration refer to event metadata. Do not confuse these placeholders with f-string braces. The snippet formats one record without changing the page's global logging configuration.
plain.code:
import logging
record = logging.LogRecord("demo", logging.WARNING, "sample.py", 1, "row %d rejected", (4,), None)
formatter = logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s %(message)s")
print(formatter.format(record))
plain.check: Why should an application avoid logging a secret token even when a request fails?

plain.title: Upsert policies and copies of records
plain.text:
Upsert combines update and insert. A stable id lets you find an existing record; if it is present, follow the update policy, otherwise insert a new one. A dictionary naturally associates one id with one value, but the code still needs an explicit first-wins or last-wins rule.

Copy a supplied record when your result must not share the same mutable outer dictionary. A list copy alone leaves its record dictionaries shared. A shallow record copy is sufficient only when nested mutation is not part of the operation. Sorting ids before building a report makes output deterministic; arrival order and id order are different policies.
plain.check: What would happen if registry stored source directly instead of source.copy()?

plain.title: Regular expressions start with a tiny alphabet
plain.text:
A regular expression is a pattern describing strings. re.fullmatch(pattern, text) succeeds only if the whole string matches; re.search can find a match inside a longer string. The return is a match object on success or None otherwise. bool(match) converts that result to True or False.

Square brackets describe one allowed character: [A-Z] means one uppercase ASCII letter. + repeats the preceding item one or more times; {2,4} means two through four repeats. A dot normally means any character, so \. means a literal dot. r'...' is a raw Python string that keeps backslashes convenient for the regex parser. Learn these pieces independently before assembling the lab's filename policy.
plain.code:
import re
pattern = r"[A-Z]{2,4}\.txt"
for name in ["AB.txt", "A.txt", "AB.txt.extra", "ab.txt"]:
    print(name, bool(re.fullmatch(pattern, name)))
plain.output:
AB.txt True
A.txt False
AB.txt.extra False
ab.txt False
walk: [A-Z]{2,4} allows a two-to-four-letter uppercase base.
\.txt requires the exact extension, including the dot.
fullmatch rejects trailing content that a substring search might accept.
plain.check: Which part of the pattern controls length, and which controls the permitted characters?

plain.title: Filename validation and actual filesystem boundaries
plain.text:
A lexical filename rule validates text before it becomes a path. A strict allowlist is easier to reason about than trying to remove every dangerous fragment. Path traversal such as ../private.txt attempts to leave the intended directory. Windows also recognizes backslashes, so a forward-slash-only test is not a complete cross-platform policy.

Even a well-formed base name does not establish where a write will occur. Join it to a controlled directory, consider resolved paths and symlinks, and test in temporary directories. pathlib.Path.resolve follows filesystem structure; PurePosixPath manipulates path syntax without proving a real location is safe. The browser regex exercise is deliberately a text-validation exercise, not a complete secure file writer.
plain.code:
from pathlib import PurePosixPath
path = PurePosixPath("reports/summary.txt")
print(path.name)
print(path.parts)
plain.check: Why does extracting .name from an untrusted path fail to prove the original input was acceptable?

plain.title: Account for every row exactly once
plain.text:
A reconciliation report explains where every input went. Invalid rows and duplicate valid rows are different categories. Validate before deciding a row is an acceptable duplicate; a repeated id does not excuse a malformed title. When categories are exclusive and exhaustive, their counts add up to the input length.

Normalize a string only after checking its type. Check exact integer type when booleans are excluded. Keep a rejection reason where useful, but avoid placing sensitive raw payloads in logs. A test should include invalid rows before and after a valid row with the same id, so the chosen policy is explicit.
plain.code:
counts = {"processed": 4, "rejected": 2, "skipped": 1}
accounted = counts["processed"] + counts["rejected"] + counts["skipped"]
print(accounted)
print(accounted == 7)
plain.check: Would adding one row to two categories make the reconciliation misleading?

plain.title: Transactions and atomic replacement solve different problems
plain.text:
A database transaction groups related database changes so they can commit together or roll back on failure. A uniqueness constraint can reinforce an id policy. Transactions do not automatically include unrelated filesystem writes or network calls. Record what is inside the transaction boundary and what is outside.

For a report file, write the complete result to a temporary sibling file, then replace the destination after the write succeeds. os.replace is designed to replace a destination atomically when the platform and filesystem support the operation; it does not by itself guarantee recovery from every power failure. Use a temp file on the same filesystem. Preserve original input so a rejected or failed batch can be investigated and rerun.
plain.check: If the database commits but writing the report fails, what will your tool tell its caller?

plain.title: Test recovery by making failure happen on purpose
plain.text:
A happy-path run cannot show that recovery works. Use a fake dependency that fails after a known number of operations, or an isolated temporary database, and inspect the resulting state. Do not test failure recovery against your only copy of valuable files.

For this lab, compare state after importing the same fixture twice, then force a failure partway through. Verify your documented all-or-nothing or partial-result policy. Test --dry-run by comparing state before and after; its output alone cannot prove that it avoided writes. Record actual counts and a recovery action in the README, rather than only 'it works'.
plain.check: Which assertion would demonstrate that a dry run changed no stored records?

units.title: Maintain and collaborate

plain.title: Map an unfamiliar project before editing
plain.text:
Start by running the documented command and tests. Record pre-existing failures rather than claiming a clean baseline you did not observe. Locate the entry point, the parser or HTTP boundary, one domain function, storage, and output. Search for a relevant function's name and its callers instead of reading every file in order.

A code map can be a short chain: command -> parser -> rule -> repository -> formatter. Follow one concrete input through it. Existing tests show expected behavior, but they may omit a boundary or encode an old requirement. Check the documented contract before calling surprising behavior a bug.
plain.check: For an earlier project, name the file that starts execution and the function that decides the result you want to change.

plain.title: Missing keys and explicit None are different states
plain.text:
dictionary.get(key) returns None for an absent key unless a different default is given. That can hide the difference between {} and {'note': None}. Test membership with key in mapping when absence itself matters. Comparing dictionaries' values is not enough when the requirement distinguishes missing from explicit null.

A schema is the agreed field names and types for a record. A migration translates old schema to new schema. Decide precedence by key presence, preserve valid False and 0, construct a fresh result when inputs must remain unchanged, and test both versions. Do not use a truthy fallback when an explicitly supplied zero should win.
plain.check: Which test distinguishes absence from an explicitly stored None?

plain.title: Type hints help readers; adapters preserve callers
plain.text:
A function annotation describes a contract to readers and optional type-checking tools. record: dict means a dictionary is expected; -> str means a string result is intended. Runtime validation remains your responsibility. More specific annotations such as dict[str, int] describe key and value types but do not guarantee that data loaded from JSON obeys them.

An adapter accepts one interface or data shape and produces another. During a transition, keep compatibility intentionally rather than renaming a field and hoping every caller updates at once. Test the old record, the new record, a record containing both, and a new field whose value is zero or False. Document when the old form can be retired.
plain.code:
def measurement_label(value: int) -> str:
    """Describe a measurement for presentation."""
    return f"{value} units"

print(measurement_label(0))
plain.check: If you change a public parameter name, which keyword-argument callers may break?

plain.title: Set union, intersection, and difference
plain.text:
A set stores unique values. set(list_of_names) removes duplicates without promising output order. The | operator is union: values in either set. & is intersection: values present in both. A - B is difference: values in A but not B. Reversing the subtraction usually changes the result. sorted(set_result) gives a predictable list for a report.

These are useful for coverage and change comparisons. A requirement set defines what matters; unrelated completed work should not automatically become an accepted requirement. First write each category in ordinary words, then choose its operation. These operators on sets differ from arithmetic subtraction or bit operations in other contexts.
plain.check: Which operation means 'in both', and why is difference directional?

plain.title: Regression tests establish the before-and-after behavior
plain.text:
A regression test preserves a bug's smallest reproducing example so it cannot quietly return. First verify that the new test fails for the relevant reason on the old implementation. A syntax error or missing import is not the same evidence as an assertion showing the wrong behavior. Then make a focused change and confirm the test passes.

Run related tests and the full relevant suite afterward. A refactor should preserve public behavior; a behavior change should state exactly what changes. Review the diff for unrelated edits and unexpected generated files. Keep your reproduction input and expected result with the change.
plain.check: Can you demonstrate that your new test detects the original bug instead of passing both before and after?

plain.title: Branches and pull requests: a reviewable proposal
plain.text:
A Git branch names a line of commits. git switch -c creates a branch and switches to it; it does not copy the working folder into a second directory. A pull request proposes merging that branch into a target branch and displays its diff. Creating or updating a PR can notify reviewers, so in practice use your own repository or an agreed collaboration workflow.

Run these commands only in the intended learning repository after reviewing git status. git diff shows unstaged changes; git diff --staged shows what the next commit will contain. The example branch and commit describe a hypothetical documentation change, not a solution to the lab. After pushing, use GitHub's Compare & pull request action to review the proposal.
plain.code:
git status
git switch -c clarify-run-instructions
git diff
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Clarify local run instructions"
git push -u origin clarify-run-instructions
plain.check: Which command shows the exact README content selected for the commit?

plain.title: A useful PR description and review comment
plain.text:
Describe the concrete problem, the resulting behavior, and the evidence. For example, explain which command previously failed, what it does now, and which test command passed. Record limitations such as a platform not tested. A screenshot alone rarely explains a reproducible bug.

A useful review comment points to a consequence: 'This fallback discards a configured zero, so the zero case should be tested.' A preference such as 'I dislike this name' needs a clarity reason to be actionable. When receiving review, check the behavior and update the code or explain the tradeoff with evidence. Keep factual findings separate from guesses.
plain.check: Write a three-sentence handoff: what was wrong, what changed, and how you checked it.

plain.title: Conflicts require understanding both changes
plain.text:
A merge conflict means Git could not combine overlapping edits automatically. The conflict markers show competing text, not instructions about which side is correct. Open both intended changes, decide the combined behavior, edit deliberately, and rerun tests. Removing markers without understanding the code can produce a syntactically valid but incorrect result.

Practice only in a disposable branch or your own small repository with committed work. git status tells you which files need resolution. After resolving, stage the reviewed files and follow Git's instructions for completing or aborting the merge. Do not use force-push or discard commands as a shortcut around an unfamiliar conflict.
plain.check: What two requirements must remain true after combining the competing changes?

plain.title: Failure triage is a comparison, not a diagnosis
plain.text:
Triage sorts evidence into categories so you know where to investigate. A newly failing test was absent from the earlier failure set; a resolved failure disappeared; an unchanged failure is present in both. Set comparison can identify these groups, but it cannot tell you the cause of a failure. A service outage, flaky timing, changed fixture, or regression can look similar at first.

For your maintenance lab, preserve a baseline, give reproduction steps, add a regression test, and make one focused change. Report the test command, actual outcome, affected scope, and any existing failures. Complete a practice PR and conflict resolution only after the local behavior is understood.
plain.check: How would you word a report that distinguishes an observed new failure from an unverified theory about its cause?

plain.title: A complete workflow has an explicit boundary
plain.text:
A portfolio project should solve a small real problem from input through output. Choose a coherent workflow, such as reading a synthetic collection, searching it, and writing a report. State the supported inputs and exact success criteria before adding more commands or an interface.

A dispatcher selects an operation from a command name. Keep dispatch separate from printing and storage so unknown commands can be tested. A public representation should select fields intentionally rather than exposing everything in a database row. This chapter assembles earlier skills; it does not require a new clever algorithm.
plain.check: What is the smallest end-to-end task another person can complete using your project?

plain.title: Make expected output and limitations reproducible
plain.text:
A demo should use committed synthetic sample input with a documented command and actual output. A screenshot may be useful, but text input/output lets another person repeat the result. Explain ordering, empty input, invalid rows, and known limits. Keep generated reports and private databases out of source unless they are intentional fixtures.

A README should state what the program does, the supported runtime, setup, dependencies, run commands, test commands, sample data, and limitations. Document the working directory for each command. Test your instructions literally rather than silently relying on an activated environment, a secret file, or a globally installed package.
plain.check: Which undeclared file or global package could make the project work only on your current machine?

plain.title: Clean installs use the chosen interpreter
plain.text:
A clean-install test starts from a separate clone or copy and a fresh virtual environment. Use the same interpreter for installation and execution: python -m pip calls pip associated with that python, unlike an ambiguous standalone pip command. The lab's explicit .venv interpreter paths work without activation.

Run the commands below from a fresh project copy after creating its environment and activating it, or replace python with the environment's interpreter path. requirements.txt lists third-party runtime dependencies; built-in modules such as json and unittest do not need pip packages. If your project has no third-party dependencies, document that instead of inventing a requirements file. Record versions you tested, and review changes when updating them.
plain.code:
python --version
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m unittest -v
python main.py
plain.check: Which commands should a reviewer run if your project uses only the standard library?

plain.title: Exit status is how automation detects failure
plain.text:
A terminal command returns an integer exit status. Conventionally zero means success and nonzero means failure. Test runners return a failing status when assertions fail, so an automation system can stop without reading human text. A script that prints 'error' but exits zero may be mistaken for a successful job.

In Python, raise SystemExit(1) or sys.exit(1) requests a failing process exit; do this in the CLI boundary, not in a reusable core function. In PowerShell, $LASTEXITCODE reports the most recent native program's exit code. A CI summary should derive success from actual exit codes, not just log messages.
plain.check: What exit status should your automated test command report after one failed assertion?

plain.title: all and generator expressions, read slowly
plain.text:
all(iterable) returns True when every item is truthy, and stops at the first false item. For an empty iterable it returns True: there is no counterexample. If a contract requires the actual boolean True, compare with is True instead of merely trusting a value's truthiness. A string such as 'yes' is truthy but is not True.

A generator expression can supply checks one by one. In all(flag is True for flag in flags), read the inner phrase as 'for each flag, produce whether it is exactly True'. Write a loop first if the one-line form is hard to trace. Do not assume all validates the meaning of an evidence note; it only combines the checks you supply.
plain.code:
print(all([True, True]))
print(all([]))
print(all(["yes", 1]))
flags = [True, "yes"]
print(all(flag is True for flag in flags))
plain.check: Why can a list of truthy strings pass all without proving a boolean-only contract?

plain.title: CI runs your known checks in a fresh environment
plain.text:
Continuous integration, or CI, automatically runs checks for changes. A job is a group of steps on a runner machine. Typical steps check out the source, select Python, install declared dependencies, and run the project's test command. The runner starts without your local .venv or uncommitted files, exposing hidden setup assumptions.

CI is useful only when its checks detect real problems. A green badge cannot establish correctness for behaviors never tested. First make the commands reliable locally, then automate those same commands. Workflow execution and any service usage limits depend on the hosting plan and repository settings; check GitHub's current Actions documentation instead of assuming unlimited usage.
plain.check: Which exact local test command should the runner execute, and what nonzero result should make the job fail?

plain.title: Read a GitHub Actions workflow before adapting it
plain.text:
A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file under .github/workflows/. YAML uses indentation to nest mappings and - to begin list items. name labels the workflow; on chooses triggers; jobs groups named jobs; runs-on selects the runner; steps is an ordered list. uses invokes a reusable action, while run executes a shell command.

Save the example as .github/workflows/python-checks.yml at the root of your Forge Work repository. It runs on pushes and pull requests. checkout downloads the committed files into the runner; setup-python selects Python 3.12. The @v6 and @v5 suffixes select action versions, not Python versions. These choices follow GitHub's documented Python examples; review maintained versions when updating your workflow. permissions: contents: read permits reading the repository.

The default working-directory is week-23 because this learning repository keeps code in chapter subfolders. Change that folder only if your project lives elsewhere. Every run step starts there, while uses steps operate on the repository. The example runs standard-library tests; if your project needs third-party packages, add a run step for python -m pip install -r requirements.txt before testing, with that dependency file in the same chapter folder. Check the Actions log reports the expected number of tests: a green run with zero tests is not evidence. Push a practice branch and inspect its Actions run before relying on the workflow.
plain.code:
name: Python checks
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: week-23
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m unittest discover -s . -v
plain.check: Why would this structural illustration need checkout before it could find your test files?

plain.title: Prove CI can fail, then restore the passing change
plain.text:
On an isolated practice branch in your own repository, introduce one deliberately failing assertion and observe the failing job. Then repair it and observe a passing run for the repair commit. This checks that the runner discovers the tests and respects their exit status. Do not merge the deliberate failure into your main branch.

Distinguish a test failure from infrastructure failure: a dependency download or missing interpreter can fail before any test executes. Read the job logs and verify how many tests ran. The lab evidence should name the branch or commit, command, and failing-then-passing outcome. Never put credentials in the workflow file or echo their values into a job log.
plain.check: What log evidence proves tests were discovered rather than the command succeeding with zero tests?

plain.title: Versions are numeric components, not plain text ordering
plain.text:
A version such as 2.10.3 has components. Under Semantic Versioning, a patch signals a compatible fix, a minor version compatible functionality, and a major version an incompatible public API change. That convention applies when a project adopts it; not every package follows it.

Split on the literal dot, convert components with int, then reason about numeric tuples. Lexicographic string order would place '2.10' before '2.9', which is misleading. A dependency pin improves repeatability but also needs an update and review policy. Do not claim that pinning alone makes an environment reproducible across every operating system and Python version.
plain.code:
parts = "2.10.3".split(".")
numbers = []
for part in parts:
    numbers.append(int(part))
major, minor, patch = numbers
print(major, minor, patch)
print((2, 10, 3) > (2, 9, 8))
plain.check: Which part of your README states the Python and dependency versions you actually tested?

plain.title: Evidence is stronger than a readiness checkbox
plain.text:
For this lab, finish two small workflows using a tested core: the CLI workflow and an API or automation workflow. Keep sample data synthetic, verify a clean install, and demonstrate CI's ability to fail. Explain one design tradeoff and one bug found by a test.

A release checklist records actions you have actually performed. A dictionary of True values only models that checklist; it cannot certify that a person understands the implementation. If you used generated code or outside help, record where and show you can explain, adapt, and debug it. Keep unfinished features and untested platforms visible rather than turning them into implied guarantees.
plain.check: Can another person reproduce your main workflow using only the repository and README?

plain.title: Start an unfamiliar task by clarifying its contract
plain.text:
Before coding, identify inputs, output type, allowed invalid values, ordering, tie rules, and whether input may change. Clarifying is programming work: it prevents implementing a plausible answer to the wrong question. Write one ordinary example and one boundary example before choosing an algorithm.

For a timed rehearsal, spend a few minutes stating assumptions and then build the smallest coherent result. You can look up syntax while still doing the reasoning yourself. Record any generated solution or outside guidance honestly. The goal is evidence that you can adapt and debug, not repeat a remembered answer.
plain.check: For a ranking request, what happens when two scores tie and when the requested limit is zero?

plain.title: Sorting keys: priority and tie order are separate decisions
plain.text:
sorted(items, key=function) asks the key function for a comparable value for each item. The function is passed without calling it first. A tuple key compares its first component, then uses the next component to break ties. Negating a numeric component reverses its numeric direction while leaving a later string component ascending.

A lambda is a small anonymous function: lambda word: len(word) means the same result as a named function returning len(word). Use a named def when you need comments or several steps. Sorting produces a new list. A final slice limits the ordered result; a negative slice endpoint has a real meaning in Python, so handle a contract's nonpositive limit explicitly rather than relying on slicing accidentally.
plain.check: Which tuple component makes longer words come first, and which orders equal lengths?

plain.title: Windows are contiguous ranges of positions
plain.text:
A window is a contiguous region of a sequence. Contiguous means no skipped positions. Left and right indices describe its boundaries; if both ends are included, its length is right - left + 1. Python's slice syntax excludes its stop, so the matching slice is text[left:right + 1].

A fixed-size window can slide one position at a time, dropping the old first item and adding the next item. A variable-size window grows or shrinks to maintain a rule. First identify that rule in words. Do not copy an update expression without explaining which positions it represents and why the window remains valid.
plain.code:
text = "planet"
left = 1
right = 3
print(text[left:right + 1])
print(right - left + 1)
for start in range(len(text) - 2):
    print(text[start:start + 3])
plain.check: Why is the slice endpoint one greater than the included right index?

plain.title: Remember positions and move a boundary only forward
plain.text:
A dictionary can associate a character with the last index where it appeared. enumerate(text) yields index/character pairs, so you can compare a remembered occurrence with the current window. An occurrence before left is outside the active window; it should not force left backward.

The monotonic rule is that left never decreases. If a constraint requires excluding an old position, the new boundary must be at least one past that position and at least its current value. max selects the larger bound. This is a boundary concept to apply in the practice task, not a complete implementation. Trace a repeated character inside the window and one whose old occurrence is already outside it.
plain.code:
last_position = {"x": 1, "y": 4}
left = 3
old_x = last_position["x"]
old_y = last_position["y"]
print(old_x < left)
print(max(left, old_x + 1))
print(max(left, old_y + 1))
plain.check: Which old occurrence is already irrelevant to the window beginning at index 3?

plain.title: Explain complexity in terms of actual work
plain.text:
Define n before saying O(n): it might be characters, records, or vertices. One full scan performs work proportional to n when its inner operations have constant average cost. A nested loop is not automatically O(n²); count how often each index advances. A sliding boundary that only moves forward can advance at most n times.

Dictionary and set membership have constant average-time behavior in the usual analysis, while sorting a general list costs O(n log n). Keeping a map can use O(n) extra space in the worst case. A concise expression can still hide a full scan or copy, so inspect slicing and repeated sorting. State assumptions and the clearest correct approach before proposing an optimization.
plain.check: If you sort records and then take a small slice, does the slice remove the cost of sorting all records?

plain.title: Validation and normalization are separate stages
plain.text:
Validation asks whether data meets the contract; normalization converts equivalent accepted representations into one form. A title might be accepted only as a nonempty stripped string, then normalized to lowercase. Check type before .strip, and decide whether bool is excluded from integer fields. A valid zero must not disappear through a truthy fallback.

Keep different policies distinct: first wins, latest wins, and sum by key describe different aggregations. A timestamp is a time representation, not a duration; the task may supply comparable integers without asking you to parse real calendar dates. Read the specified rule rather than inferring it from one example.
plain.code:
raw_label = "  Observatory "
normalized = raw_label.strip().lower()
quantity = 0
print(normalized)
print(type(quantity) is int)
print(quantity >= 0)
plain.check: At which stage should an all-whitespace label be rejected?

plain.title: A useful test matrix is small but deliberate
plain.text:
For an unseen task, choose tests from the contract instead of generating many arbitrary inputs. Cover an ordinary result, empty input, a precise boundary, invalid data where relevant, duplicates, ties, and mutation policy. Not every task needs every category; explain which apply.

Store a separate snapshot before calling a function when testing input preservation. A shallow list copy shares nested dictionaries, so nested mutation tests may need copy.deepcopy or a deliberately reconstructed expected value. Use independent expected results calculated by hand; calling the function itself to compute the expected value would merely compare the implementation with itself.
plain.code:
from copy import deepcopy
original = [{"name": "lamp", "count": 2}]
snapshot = deepcopy(original)
original[0]["count"] = 9
print(snapshot[0]["count"])
print(original == snapshot)
plain.check: Why would original.copy() fail to preserve the nested count in this example?

plain.title: Existing-code debugging is a separate skill
plain.text:
An independent assessment should include reading and changing unfamiliar code. Reproduce one bug with the smallest input, read the traceback or failed assertion, identify the responsible boundary, and add a test before fixing it. Make a focused change and rerun related tests. Preserve a reproduction and explain the cause, not just the final patch.

For SQL practice, use the chapter 16 tools in a separate temporary database: write a join, aggregate, and filtering query, then explain whether duplicate joined rows affect counts. For Git, use a focused branch, inspect staged changes, and write a reviewable PR. These demonstrate different abilities from solving one Python function.
plain.check: Can you show a test failing for the original bug and passing after your change?

plain.title: A timed take-home needs priorities and a handoff
plain.text:
Timebox the rehearsal to the lab's stated duration. First capture acceptance examples, then implement a narrow complete workflow, then tests, then run instructions. Avoid spending the whole session on packaging or appearance while the main behavior is unfinished. Keep a short list of deliberate omissions.

Your handoff should say what works, which command demonstrates it, which tests passed, assumptions, limitations, and help used. If time ends, a documented coherent subset is more useful than broad claims over half-finished features. Do not silently change acceptance criteria to make the result appear complete.
plain.check: Which single end-to-end behavior will you finish before adding optional features?

plain.title: Use evidence to choose the next practice session
plain.text:
Readiness is a collection of demonstrated skills, not a completion percentage or employment guarantee. Ask whether you can start a small program, explain a loop, test a boundary, debug an unfamiliar error, use Git, query data, and hand a project to another person. Repeat an unfamiliar variation after a delay to separate understanding from recent memory.

Explain one project aloud in two minutes: problem, approach, a tradeoff, a failure, and verification. If you cannot explain a generated component, mark that as a learning gap and revisit it. Use the weakest observed skill to plan the next week; role-specific frontend, data, embedded, or engine work may need further learning beyond this foundation.

grind.title: Practice grind
grind.text:
Fundamentals stick through many repetitions, not one good attempt. Each drill here is small, aimed at a single idea from that week's chapter. Aim to solve each one with no hints in under 15 minutes.

If a drill takes much longer, that's useful information: go back to the chapter's plain-English section, then try again tomorrow. Speed comes later; accuracy comes first.

bugs.title: Bug hunts
bugs.text:
Each quest gives you code that looks reasonable but is wrong. Your job is to find the bug and fix it with the smallest possible change. This is the skill that matters most now that AI writes so much code: someone has to check it.

The method:
1. Run the checks first, without changing anything. Find the failing case.
2. Trace the code by hand with that exact input, writing down each variable.
3. Stop at the first line where reality differs from what the code should do. Name the bug in one sentence in your notes.
4. Fix only that, then rerun everything.

Resist rewriting the whole function. In a real job, the smallest correct fix is the one that gets approved.
bugs.code:
Common bug families you'll meet:
  off-by-one        > vs >=, range(n) vs range(n + 1)
  wrong default     .get(key, 0) when 0 is a real value
  aliasing          b = a does not copy a list or dict
  early return      return inside a loop's else branch
  order             checking after adding instead of before
  min/max swap      'at least 0' means max(0, x)

sql.title: SQL
sql.text:
SQL is how you ask a database questions. It's on your resume, it's what data and BI roles test first, and you'll use it in almost any engineering job. These quests use a small game-library database with three tables: players, games, and sessions (who played what, for how long, and when).

You write a single SELECT statement. Forge runs it against two different datasets and compares your rows (including their order) with the expected answer, so a query has to be truly correct, not just right for one set of data.

A query reads in this order, even though you write SELECT first: FROM (which tables) → JOIN (connect them) → WHERE (filter rows) → GROUP BY (make groups) → HAVING (filter groups) → SELECT (pick columns) → ORDER BY (sort). When a query confuses you, read it in that order.
sql.code:
SELECT g.title, SUM(s.minutes) AS total      -- 6. pick columns
FROM sessions AS s                            -- 1. start here
JOIN games AS g ON g.id = s.game_id           -- 2. connect tables
WHERE s.played_on >= '2026-10-01'             -- 3. filter rows
GROUP BY g.id                                 -- 4. one row per game
HAVING SUM(s.minutes) > 60                    -- 5. filter groups
ORDER BY total DESC, g.title;                 -- 7. sort

interview.title: Interview gauntlet
interview.text:
These are classic entry-level interview problems. Treat each one like a real interview:
1. Restate the problem and ask yourself about edge cases (empty input, duplicates, negatives).
2. Describe a brute-force solution, even if it's slow.
3. Improve it, and say why it's faster.
4. Code it, then test it on a small example out loud.
5. State the time and space complexity.

After you clear one, come back in a few days and solve it from a blank file while talking out loud. Recall under light pressure is what interviews actually measure.

test.title: HackerRank practice
test.text:
Online coding tests look different from Forge's usual quests. Nobody calls your function. You write a whole program: it reads its input with input(), works out the answer, and prints it. The site runs your program on hidden test cases and compares what you printed, exactly.

Three habits win points:
1. Read the input format first, and parse it before you think about the algorithm.
2. Never prompt. input("Enter a number") prints that text, and it counts as wrong output.
3. Print only the answer. Remove debugging prints before you finish.

Easy problems are worth doing quickly and correctly. The hidden tests aim at empty input, a single item, ties, negative numbers, and big inputs, so think about those before you run.

These quests are all open from the start, in any order. The timed test puts you under the real conditions: three problems, 60 minutes, no hints. The object-oriented chapter is separate practice on classes.
test.code:
# Reading common input shapes
n = int(input())                        # one number
values = list(map(int, input().split()))  # a line of numbers
a, b = map(int, input().split())        # two numbers on a line
for _ in range(n):                      # n more lines
    row = input().split()

hardware.title: Hardware lab
hardware.text:
These quests are the software side of embedded work: turning raw sensor readings into decisions. They use the same ideas as your capstone (barometric pressure and GPS) and run right here in the browser.

To try the real thing, get a Raspberry Pi Pico (or Pico W) starter kit with a breadboard, jumper wires, a push button, an LED, and a BMP280 barometric sensor (roughly $30–50 total). Install the MicroPython firmware, use the Thonny editor, and build in this order:
1. Blink the LED. Then read the button and light the LED while it's pressed.
2. Count button presses using your debounce logic from these quests.
3. Read the BMP280 over I2C and print pressure every second.
4. Convert pressure to altitude with your formula, smooth it with your moving average, and drive the LED as an alarm with hysteresis.

Write every line yourself. If you lose track of time doing this, embedded or test engineering may be your direction.
hardware.code:
# MicroPython on a Pico: blink the onboard LED
from machine import Pin
import time

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)
while True:
    led.toggle()
    time.sleep(0.5)
