sections.text:
Python runs your code. VS Code is the editor where you write and save it. They are separate programs. If both are already installed, move to step 2.

Install Python 3 from python.org, then VS Code from code.visualstudio.com. Open VS Code. Click Extensions in its left sidebar, search for Python, and install the extension published by Microsoft. Complete the required GitHub workspace guide from the lab brief before finishing this lab. It sets up your private Forge Work repository. Paid AI tools are not required.

sections.title: Download and extract this week's kit
sections.text:
Use the download button below. A ZIP is a compressed folder: extract it before editing or running anything.

Create a folder named Forge Work in Documents (or another place you can find). On Windows, right-click the downloaded ZIP and choose Extract All. On macOS, double-click it. On Linux, use your file manager's Extract option. Put the extracted files in a week folder inside Forge Work. For week 1, name it week-01.

Open that week folder. You should see README.md, core.py, main.py, test_core.py, and cases.json together. The files must sit directly inside Forge Work/week-01 (or the matching week number). If extraction added an extra folder layer, use your file manager to move the kit files up into the week folder before continuing. This keeps the later cd .. Git routine pointing to Forge Work. Keep each week's files in its own folder.

sections.title: Open the folder and a terminal
sections.text:
In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and select the folder containing core.py. On macOS the menu may say Open instead. If asked about trusting files, review the folder and trust your own downloaded Forge kit.

The Explorer on the left should list core.py and test_core.py. Choose Terminal → New Terminal. The terminal is the panel where you type commands; Python code goes in .py files in the editor.

Type the command below in the terminal and press Enter. Do not type a prompt such as PS C:\...>. You should see a Python 3 version number.
sections.after: On Windows, if py is not recognized but python --version works, use python instead of py when creating the environment in step 4. If neither works, finish installing Python and close and reopen VS Code. If Python opens a store instead of printing a version, install it from python.org and reopen VS Code.

sections.title: Give this lab its own Python environment
sections.text:
An environment is a folder named .venv that keeps this project's Python tools together. Your program files stay beside it, outside .venv.

Run the first command and wait for the terminal prompt to return; creating the environment may print nothing. Then run the second command. You should see a Python 3 version number again.
sections.after: The commands on this page call the environment's Python directly. You do not need to activate it or change PowerShell's execution policy. In VS Code, open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+P on macOS), choose Python: Select Interpreter, and select this folder's .venv. If it is not listed, choose Enter interpreter path and browse to the Python executable used above.

sections.title: Run one file before doing the lab
sections.text: In VS Code's Explorer, click New File and name it hello.py. Type the code below in that file, then save it (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on macOS). This is a tool check, separate from your lab exercise.
sections.after: Run the command in the terminal. Success means the terminal prints My computer can run Python. If you see that sentence, your editor, file, terminal, and interpreter are working together. You can keep hello.py as a reminder.

sections.title: Run the supplied tests and read the result
sections.text: A test calls a function and compares its result with an expected value. The kit's tests check the checkpoint function in core.py. Save your files, then run:
sections.after:
FAILED with assertion failures is expected before you implement core.py. It means Python found and ran the tests, but the unfinished function did not produce the expected result. Read the first failure: which input was used, and which two values differed?

An ERROR importing core or a missing-file message means setup needs attention; see the help below. Ran 0 tests is not success: check that the open folder contains test_core.py. OK means the tests that ran passed. It does not verify the whole lab or every possible input.

sections.title: Build a small piece yourself
sections.text:
Return to the lab brief. First write an example input and the output you want. Explain the steps in ordinary words. Then implement one small part, save the file, and rerun the tests.

core.py holds calculations and rules. main.py is the starting place for the complete program: call your functions, display results, and later read input. test_core.py is where you add tests of your own. cases.json supplies the existing test inputs; changing it to make a failure disappear does not fix your code. README.md describes the task and is where you record how to run your work.

To use one of your core.py functions from main.py, put an import at the top of main.py. For example, if you named a function describe_weather in core.py, the import is from core import describe_weather. Use your actual function name, not this example name. You can then call that function in main.py and print its returned value. The import names the file without .py. Keep both files in the same folder.

An import makes a definition available; it does not call the function. Read the existing from core import line in test_core.py to see the same idea in the supplied tests.

When you have added program behavior to main.py, run it with the command below. The untouched starter only prints a reminder; that is not a finished lab.

sections.title: Write a test of your own
sections.text:
Open test_core.py. The supplied file already imports unittest, imports the checkpoint function from core, and defines a CoreTests class. A class groups the test methods; you do not need to design your own class yet.

Add the example below inside CoreTests, after the existing test method and before the final if line. Keep four spaces before def and eight before self.assertEqual. Save, then rerun the test command from step 6. The new test should appear by name.

A test method name starts with test_. self is how the method accesses unittest's checking tools. assertEqual(actual, expected) compares two values and fails if they differ. This example checks Python's len function only to demonstrate the structure; it is not evidence that your lab works.
sections.after:
Now add a test for a function you wrote: choose an input, calculate its expected result by hand, call the function, and compare the result with assertEqual. If it is a new function, add its name to the from core import line at the top of the file. Name the test for the behavior, such as test_exact_cutoff.

Temporarily change the expected result of your new test to an incorrect value and rerun. Confirm that this test fails, then restore the correct value. That proves the test is being discovered and checks what you think it checks. Keep the supplied tests intact.

sections.title: Check the full program and keep your work
sections.text:
Passing the supplied tests finishes only the checkpoint function. Follow the lab's build steps, add your own tests, and try the actual program with ordinary and boundary inputs. Compare the result with each acceptance criterion.

In your README, record the run command, one example input and output, and anything unfinished. Back up your week folder to a place you control. Forge's progress export saves browser notes and code; it does not include files on your computer.

Back in Forge, check only the criteria you have tried and write a short evidence note: what you ran, what happened, one problem you fixed, and any help you used. You can then continue to the next week. Use section 5 of the lab brief to commit and push this chapter folder to your required GitHub learning repository. Paste the full commit ID and confirm that GitHub shows the latest files. A local commit alone has not backed the work up to GitHub.

problems.title: Python cannot find the file, or cannot import core
problems.text: Check VS Code's Explorer: core.py, main.py, and test_core.py must be in the folder you opened. Open a new terminal after opening that folder. Run dir on Windows or ls on macOS/Linux; those filenames should appear. Extract the ZIP first, and check that you have not opened the outer folder above the actual files.

problems.title: The environment command cannot be found
problems.text: Run the creation command in step 4 from your week folder. On Windows use the Windows commands in a PowerShell terminal. On macOS/Linux use that platform's commands. If you moved the week folder after creating .venv, create the environment again in its new location.

problems.title: Creating .venv says ensurepip or venv is unavailable
problems.text: Some Linux distributions package venv separately. Use your distribution's instructions to install its Python 3 venv package, then rerun step 4. On Windows/macOS, check the Python installation using the official setup reference below.

problems.title: My changes do not appear when I run tests
problems.text: Save the file first. Check that you are editing the same week folder that the terminal uses. Read the failure's filename and line number. Work on one failure at a time, then run all the tests again.

workspace.title: Set up your GitHub learning workspace
workspace.intro: Required before your first independent lab. This is a separate setup session: create one private repository for your own practice, then keep one chapter folder inside it. Reading and browser practice can begin before this setup.

sections.title: Install Git and VS Code; open your GitHub account
sections.text:
Git records versions of files on your computer. GitHub keeps a remote copy online. A commit is a local save point; a push sends commits to GitHub. You will use both from your first lab.

Install VS Code and Git if needed. On Windows use the Git for Windows installer and keep Git Credential Manager selected. On macOS/Linux follow Git's instructions for your platform. Close and reopen VS Code after installing Git.

Sign in to your GitHub account in a browser, or create an account. You will use that same account when Git asks you to sign in. In VS Code, choose Terminal → New Terminal, type the command below, and press Enter.
sections.after: Success: the terminal prints a Git version number. If git is not recognized, finish installing it and reopen VS Code. Nothing on this page asks you to paste a password or token into Forge.
sections.confirm: Git prints its version, VS Code opens, and I can sign in to GitHub.

sections.title: Create and open a separate Forge Work folder
sections.text:
In your file manager, open Documents (or another place you can find). Create a folder named Forge Work. In VS Code, choose File → Open Folder and open that folder. Open a new terminal after opening the folder.

This folder holds your own learning work. Use a separate folder from the Forge application you launch or download. The files you write belong in Forge Work, with a week-01 folder for chapter 1, week-02 for chapter 2, and so on. Each chapter gets its own .venv later.

If you already started a lab, move its folder inside Forge Work using the file manager before creating its environment. Keep your existing files. Never create a second Git repository inside a chapter folder.
sections.after: Success: the terminal location ends in Forge Work. Git setup commands in this guide run from that parent folder. Lab Python commands later run from inside a chapter folder. The guide will tell you when to switch.
sections.confirm: VS Code and its terminal are open in my separate Forge Work folder.

sections.title: Start Git and set your commit identity
sections.text:
From the Forge Work terminal, run git init -b main. It creates Git's history folder and names the initial branch main. A branch is a named line of work; main is enough to begin.

Then set the name and email recorded on your commits. Replace Your Name with your preferred author name. In GitHub, open your profile menu → Settings → Emails. Copy your GitHub-provided noreply email if you want to keep your email private; otherwise use an email verified on your GitHub account. Replace YOUR_EMAIL before running the command. Keep the quotes.

These settings apply to this repository. Your Git author name is a label, not a login, and need not match your GitHub username.
sections.command:
git init -b main
git config user.name "Your Name"
git config user.email "YOUR_EMAIL"
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
git config user.name
git config user.email
sections.after: Success: the repository root ends in Forge Work, and the last two commands show the identity you intended. If the root points elsewhere, return to step 2 before adding files. If the folder already has Git history, inspect git status and keep that history; you do not need to initialize it again.
sections.confirm: Git's root is Forge Work, and my commit name and email are set.

sections.title: Ignore generated files and make your first commit
sections.text:
In VS Code's Explorer, select New File and create .gitignore directly inside Forge Work. The leading dot matters. Paste the ignore rules below into that file and save. These rules keep chapter environments, caches, local databases, and credentials out of Git. A .gitignore affects untracked files; it does not remove files already committed.

Create a second file named README.md at the same level. Write a title such as # Forge Work and one sentence explaining that this is your programming practice. Save it. Your chapter folders will sit beside these two files.

Run the terminal commands below in Forge Work. git add chooses the two files to include. git diff --staged lets you inspect exactly what the commit will save. After checking the diff, run the commit command.
sections.command:
git status
git add .gitignore README.md
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Start my Forge learning workspace"
git log --oneline -1
sections.after: Success: the log shows a short commit ID followed by your message. If a long diff opens in a pager, press q to return to the terminal. Author identity unknown means step 3 still needs your real values. An initial README commit does not require your unfinished lab tests to pass.
sections.confirm: My first commit contains the root README and .gitignore.

sections.title: Create an empty private repository on GitHub
sections.text:
Open GitHub's new-repository page using the link below. Choose your own account as Owner, enter forge-work as the name, and choose Private. Leave Add a README, .gitignore, and license initialization off: you already created your first files locally. Select Create repository.

If you already have a repository for your learning folder, use it and preserve its history. The Forge app's source repositories are separate from this learning repository.

On the new repository page, select HTTPS in Quick setup and copy the URL. Paste that repository address into Forge below. A normal browser address ending in your repository name also works; Forge will show the HTTPS Git URL in the next step.
sections.after: Success: the repository page says Private and is empty, ready for your existing local commit. If it contains files you initialized on GitHub, keep them and use the troubleshooting guide before pushing.
sections.confirm: I created or identified my private learning repository and pasted its URL.

sections.title: Connect your folder to that repository
sections.text:
Return to the terminal in Forge Work. The command below uses the repository address you recorded. origin is the local nickname for the GitHub destination; adding it connects the folder but does not upload files.

Run git remote -v afterward and compare the destination with your learning repository in your browser. You should see the same owner and repository name on the fetch and push lines.
sections.after: Success: origin points to your private learning repository. If remote origin already exists, inspect it rather than adding another. If it is already correct, keep it. If it is wrong, use the troubleshooting instructions to update the address.
sections.confirm: git remote -v shows my learning repository as origin.

sections.title: Sign in and push your first commit
sections.text:
Run git push -u origin main from Forge Work. -u connects your local main branch to origin/main, so later you can use git push.

On Windows, Git Credential Manager can open a browser sign-in. Use your GitHub account and authorize the login. If no browser opens and authentication fails, run the Windows sign-in command below, then retry the push.

On macOS/Linux, the commands below use GitHub CLI for browser sign-in. Install it from the official link if gh is unavailable. Complete its browser authorization, then let gh configure Git authentication. Do not use your GitHub account password as a Git HTTPS password.
sections.windows:
git push -u origin main

# If authentication fails, sign in and retry:
git credential-manager github login --browser
git push -u origin main
sections.mac:
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web
gh auth setup-git
git push -u origin main
sections.linux:
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web
gh auth setup-git
git push -u origin main
sections.after: Success: the push completes and main tracks origin/main. If a sign-in was already saved on this computer, no new login window may be needed. A rejected push is not a completed backup; use the help below and keep your local files.
sections.confirm: My first push to origin/main completed successfully.

sections.title: Verify the copy on GitHub, then start your lab
sections.text:
Refresh your repository page on GitHub. Open README.md and .gitignore to check they match your local files. Open the commit history and compare the latest commit with the result of git log --oneline -1.

Run git status -sb in Forge Work. After your push it should show main...origin/main without ahead or behind counts; after the first two files are committed, there should be no uncommitted changes unless you already have a chapter folder waiting to add.

Your required workspace setup is now recorded when the URL and all eight confirmations are complete. Forge saves your confirmations; it cannot inspect your private repository. Continue to the chapter's Python/lab setup, then push each finished lab using the routine on its brief.
sections.confirm: I opened the repository on GitHub and verified the first commit and both files.

problems.title: git or gh is not recognized
problems.text: Install the named tool using its official link and close and reopen VS Code. Git for Windows normally includes Git Credential Manager; macOS/Linux instructions use GitHub CLI for browser authentication. Check git --version or gh --version after reopening.

problems.title: Author identity unknown
problems.text: Return to step 3. Run the name and email commands in Forge Work with your own values replacing the examples. Then retry the commit. These settings identify commits; they do not sign you in.

problems.title: remote origin already exists
problems.text: Run git remote -v. If it already shows the right learning repository, keep it and continue. To correct a wrong destination, use the exact command shown after entering your valid repository URL below. Changing origin changes the destination, not your files or local history.

problems.title: Repository not found or permission denied
problems.text: Open the repository address in your browser while signed in. Check the owner and name, and confirm your account can access it. Then repeat the sign-in in step 7 and retry the push. A private repository may look missing to an account without access.

problems.title: Push rejected: remote contains work you do not have
problems.text: Keep your local files. Do not force-push or delete either history. If you accidentally initialized files on GitHub, use a new, empty private learning repository and update origin to its URL, or ask for help combining the histories. If it is an established shared repository, fetch and review its changes with help before merging.

problems.title: Not a git repository, or the root points to the Forge app
problems.text: Open your separate Forge Work folder in VS Code and open a new terminal there. Run git rev-parse --show-toplevel. Its output should end in Forge Work. Do not run Git setup inside a chapter folder or the Forge application folder.
